school-c7-english.title: Class 7 English
school-c7-english.description: Class 7 English: Honeycomb prose and poems chapter by chapter in our own words, plus grammar and writing skills, with practice tests.

courses.title: Ch 1 · Three Questions & The Squirrel
courses.summary: A wise tale about a king who wants three answers — the right time, the right person and the right thing to do — and finds them through kindness; plus a playful poem about a squirrel. Retold in our own words with themes, model answers, vocabulary and grammar.
outcomes: Learners can retell the story of the king and the hermit in sequence
Learners can explain the three answers and the message of the story
Learners can describe the squirrel in the poem and the poet's images
Learners can use unit vocabulary and write short answers with evidence
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

lessons.title: The story in our own words

scenes.text: A king believes that if he always knew the best time to act, the best people to listen to and the most important thing to do, he would never fail.
He announces a big reward for anyone who can answer his three questions.
Learned men give many different answers. Unsatisfied, he goes in plain clothes to a wise hermit in the forest.

steps.title: What happens (summary)
steps.body:
- The learned men disagree: some say make a timetable, others say keep a council of wise men; some say scientists, others priests or soldiers are most important.
- The king visits a **hermit** who lives in a wood and meets only ordinary people. He leaves his bodyguards behind.
- The hermit, old and weak, is **digging flower beds**. He does not answer, so the king takes the spade and digs for hours.
- As the sun sets, a **bearded man** runs out of the wood, bleeding from a stomach wound, and faints. The king washes and bandages the wound and cares for him through the night.
- In the morning the man confesses: he was the king's **enemy**, who had come to kill him because the king had executed his brother and taken his property. The king's bodyguards had recognised and wounded him. Now the king has saved his life, and he begs forgiveness and offers to serve him.
- The king forgives him and promises to return his property.

steps.title: The hermit's three answers
steps.body:
- **The most important time is now** — the present moment is the only time we have power over.
- **The most important person is the one you are with** at that moment.
- **The most important thing is to do good to that person.**

Had the king not stayed to dig, the enemy would have attacked him on his way back; because he cared for the wounded man, he made a friend.

steps.title: Model answer 1
steps.body:
Q: Why did the king go to the hermit in plain clothes?

A: The hermit met only ordinary people, so the king dressed simply and left his bodyguards behind in order to be received like anyone else.

steps.title: Model answer 2
steps.body:
Q: How did the king's kindness save his own life?

A: By staying to dig and then caring for the wounded man, the king avoided the ambush on the road and turned his enemy into a grateful friend.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the hermit answered at once — he answered only after the events showed the answers.
- Thinking the bearded man was a random traveller — he was the king's enemy.

activity.prompt: Put the events of the story in order.
items: The king offers a reward for answers to three questions
Learned men give different answers
The king visits the hermit and digs his beds
A wounded bearded man arrives and the king tends him
The man confesses he came to kill the king and asks forgiveness
The hermit explains the three answers

quiz.q: Why did the king want the three answers?
options: He believed he would never fail
He wanted to become a hermit
quiz.why: The king believed he would never fail if he knew the right time, the right people and the most important thing. That is why he wanted the three answers.

quiz.q: What was the hermit doing when the king arrived?
quiz.why: When the king arrived, the hermit was digging flower beds in front of his hut.

quiz.q: The bearded man had come to
quiz.why: The bearded man had come to kill the king, as he wanted revenge. He was waiting to attack him on his way back.

quiz.q: The most important time, says the hermit, is
quiz.why: The hermit says the most important time is now, because the present is the only time we have power over.

quiz.q: The most important thing is to
options: do good to the person you are with
quiz.why: The most important thing is to do good to the person you are with, since we do not know if we will meet them again.

scenes.text: Your friend is upset at lunch, but you want to finish a game.
The story says: the person you are with now matters most.
You sit and listen. Later, your friend thanks you — the most important thing was to help.

steps.title: Themes
steps.body:
- **Living in the present**: plans and advisers cannot replace attention to the present moment.
- **Kindness and service** turn enemies into friends.
- **Humility**: a king learns from a simple hermit by working with his hands.
- **Forgiveness**: the king forgives his enemy.

steps.title: Characters
steps.body:
- **The king**: thoughtful, keen to rule well, humble enough to dig and nurse a stranger, forgiving.
- **The hermit**: wise, patient, teaches through experience rather than lecture.
- **The bearded man**: driven by revenge, but honest enough to confess and grateful when saved.

steps.title: Model answer (long)
steps.body:
Q: 'Remember then: there is only one time that is important — now.' Explain with reference to the story. (80–100 words)

A: The king wasted effort searching for perfect advice about future timing. The hermit shows that only the present is in our control. When the king stayed to help the tired hermit, he escaped an ambush; when he cared for the wounded man, he made peace with an enemy. Each good result came from acting well in the present moment, not from plans. So the lesson is to give full attention to what we are doing now and to the person in front of us.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing only the summary when asked for the theme — link events to the idea.
- Forgetting to use evidence from the text.

activity.prompt: Match the character to the quality shown.

quiz.q: A main theme of the story
options: the importance of the present moment and kindness
quiz.why: A main theme is the importance of the present moment and of doing good to those in front of us. It is not about war or magic.
The king showed humility by digging for the hermit, a simple task for a king. He did not use his power.
The hermit taught mainly through experience and events, not through books or long lectures. The king learned by living the day.

quiz.q: The bearded man's feelings changed from
quiz.why: The bearded man came for revenge, but after the king saved him, he felt gratitude. His feelings changed from revenge to gratitude.

options: Do good to the person you are with, now
quiz.why: The best moral is to do good to the person you are with, now. 'Never trust anyone' and 'kings know best' do not match the story.

scenes.text: A squirrel sits on a branch nibbling a nut, its bushy tail curled.
When you come near, it dashes round the tree trunk and peeps from the other side.
The poet watches it play hide-and-seek — and never quite catches it.

steps.title: What the poem says
steps.body: The poet describes a squirrel in playful images: its curly tail looks like a **question mark**, its grey fur like an **overcoat**. It sits up straight to eat, then **frisks** about, and plays a game of **hide-and-seek** around a tree trunk with the speaker, running round to the opposite side whenever someone approaches. The poem is light and affectionate.

steps.title: Poetic devices
steps.body:
- **Metaphor**: the tail is called a question mark; the fur is called an overcoat (comparisons without 'like' or 'as').
- **Personification**: the squirrel 'wears' clothes and plays games like a person.
- **Rhyme**: alternate lines rhyme, giving a bouncy rhythm.

steps.title: Model answer 1
steps.body:
Q: Why does the poet say the squirrel wore a question mark for a tail?

A: Its bushy tail curves up and curls at the tip, which looks like the shape of a question mark.

steps.title: Model answer 2
steps.body: Q: What game does the squirrel play and with whom? → Hide-and-seek, with the speaker (people who come near), by running round the tree trunk.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling 'question mark for tail' a simile — there is no 'like'/'as'; it is a metaphor.
- Thinking the squirrel actually wears a coat.

items.back: Metaphor — the curly tail looks like a ?
It runs to the other side of the trunk when someone comes near

quiz.q: The squirrel's tail is compared to a
quiz.why: The poem compares the squirrel's tail to a question mark because of its curved shape.

quiz.q: Its grey fur is called an
quiz.why: The squirrel's grey fur is called an 'overcoat' in the poem, a way of saying it wears fur like a coat.
'Frisk' means to move about playfully and lively, as squirrels do.
The squirrel plays hide-and-seek, running round the tree trunk. It is not playing chess or cricket.

quiz.q: The squirrel "wearing" a coat is an example of
quiz.why: The squirrel 'wearing' a coat gives an animal human qualities, which is personification. Onomatopoeia imitates sounds.

lessons.title: Vocabulary and grammar from the unit

scenes.text: Ria finds new words in the story: hermit, bodyguard, spade, wound, forgive.
She makes word cards with meanings and her own sentences.

steps.title: Useful words
steps.body:
- **hermit**: a person who lives alone, often for religious reasons
- **learned** (adj., two syllables: learn-ed): having much knowledge
- **bodyguard**: a person who protects someone
- **spade**: a digging tool
- **wound** (noun): an injury; **bandage**: cloth to cover a wound
- **forgive**: stop being angry with someone
- **reward**: something given for a service

steps.title: Grammar focus: adverbs of manner
steps.body:
Adverbs of manner tell **how** an action is done, often ending in -ly: The king dug **steadily**. The hermit spoke **gently**. The man ran **weakly** out of the wood.

Also note **-self words** (reflexive pronouns): The king bandaged the wound **himself**.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Fill in an adverb: The squirrel ran ___ round the tree. → **quickly / swiftly**

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Make a sentence with 'forgive': → 'The king chose to forgive his enemy.'

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Pronouncing 'learned' (adjective) as one syllable; as an adjective it is learn-ed.
- Using adjectives for adverbs: 'He dug slow' ✗ → 'He dug slowly' ✓.

activity.prompt: Fill in the blanks with words from the unit.
activity.text: The king went to a ___ in the forest. He dug the beds with a ___. He tied a bandage over the man's ___.

options: a person living alone, often for religion
quiz.why: A hermit is a person who lives alone, often for religious reasons. A king, farmer or soldier lives differently.
'Gently' tells how the hermit spoke, so it is the adverb. 'Spoke' is the verb and 'hermit' the noun.
'Hard' is an adverb meaning with effort, as in 'He worked hard'. 'Hardly' means almost not, so 'worked hardly' is wrong.
'Himself' is a reflexive pronoun, as it ends with -self and refers back to the subject. 'Him' and 'his' are not reflexive.
The opposite of 'forgive' is 'blame'. Pardon, release and excuse mean something like forgive.

questions.q: The king wanted to know
options: three things: right time, right people, most important thing
questions.why: The king wanted to know three things: the right time to act, the right people to listen to and the most important thing to do.

questions.q: The hermit lived in a
questions.why: The hermit lived in a wood, a forest, in a simple hut.

questions.q: The squirrel's coat was
questions.why: The squirrel's overcoat is grey, so its coat is grey.

questions.q: The king left his bodyguards behind because
options: the hermit met only ordinary people
questions.why: The king left his bodyguards behind because the hermit met only ordinary people. He wanted to look like a common person.

questions.q: Who wounded the bearded man?
questions.why: The king's bodyguards wounded the bearded man when they found him, as they recognised him as the enemy.

questions.q: Why had the bearded man wanted to kill the king?
options: The king had executed his brother and taken his property
He was hired by the hermit
questions.why: The bearded man wanted to kill the king because the king had executed his brother and taken his property. He wanted revenge.

questions.q: "He wore a question mark for tail" is an example of
questions.why: 'He wore a question mark for tail' says directly that the tail is a question mark, without 'like' or 'as'. So it is a metaphor.

questions.q: Assertion (A): The king escaped an attack because he stayed with the hermit. Reason (R): His enemy was waiting to ambush him on the way back.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true: because the king stayed with the hermit, he avoided the ambush on the way back. So the reason explains why he escaped.

questions.q: Assertion (A): The learned men all gave the same answers. Reason (R): They were all wise.
questions.why: The assertion is false: the learned men gave different answers, not the same. The reason, that they were wise, may be true, but it does not make the assertion true.

questions.q: The hermit gives his answers
options: after the events of the day
questions.why: The hermit gives his answers after the events of the day, once the king has seen them. He teaches through experience.

questions.q: In the poem, the squirrel plays hide-and-seek by
questions.why: In the poem, the squirrel plays hide-and-seek by running round the tree trunk. It does not hide in water or a hole.

questions.q: Case: Ravi is rushing to a party but sees an old woman struggling with heavy bags. Which lesson of the story applies?
options: The most important person is the one in front of you; help her now
questions.why: The story teaches that the most important person is the one in front of you and the right time is now. So Ravi should help the old woman.

questions.q: Case: A student writes, "The hermit was rude because he did not answer the king." Best response?
options: The hermit never met the king
He answered through events, teaching by experience
questions.why: The hermit was not rude: he answered through the events of the day, teaching by experience. So the best response says that.

questions.q: Which word best describes the king at the end?
questions.why: At the end the king forgives the bearded man who wanted to kill him. So the word 'forgiving' fits him best.

questions.q: Which sentence uses an adverb of manner correctly?
options: The king carefully bandaged the wound.
The careful king bandaged carefully careful.
The king bandaged careful the wound.
The king careful bandaged the wound.
questions.why: An adverb of manner describes how an action is done. 'Carefully' tells how the king bandaged the wound, and it is placed correctly.

questions.q: What links the poem and the story in this unit?
options: Close attention to the present moment and the living things around us
Both are set in a palace
questions.why: Both the poem and the story ask us to pay close attention to the present moment and to the living things around us.

courses.title: Ch 2 · A Gift of Chappals & The Rebel
courses.summary: A warm story about children whose kindness to a hungry kitten and a barefoot beggar lands them in trouble, and a witty poem about a rebel who always does the opposite. Themes of compassion, responsibility and individuality.
outcomes: Learners can retell the main events of the chappals story
Learners can discuss kindness versus acting without permission
Learners can explain the pattern and message of the poem The Rebel
Learners can use unit vocabulary and reported speech basics
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

lessons.title: The story: a kitten, a beggar and missing chappals

scenes.text: At their grandmother's house, Ravi and Meena secretly feed a stray kitten with milk, helped by their visiting cousin Mridu.
Their elder cousin Lalli has a music lesson; the music master leaves his chappals at the door.
A beggar with burnt, blistered feet asks for something to protect them from the hot road…

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- The children hide a hungry kitten and feed it milk without letting the elders, especially the grandmother (Paati), find out.
- Lalli practises the violin with her music master, who is not very pleasant.
- A poor beggar at the gate complains that the hot road burns his feet. Feeling sorry for him, the children give him a pair of chappals lying at the door — which turn out to be the **music master's**.
- When the lesson ends, the master cannot find his chappals and is upset. The elders are embarrassed, and the family gives him another pair of chappals from the house so he can go home.
- The children learn that being kind is good, but giving away what is not ours causes trouble for others.

steps.title: Model answer 1
steps.body:
Q: Why did the children give the chappals to the beggar?

A: They felt sorry for him because the hot road had blistered his bare feet, and they wanted to help immediately.

steps.title: Model answer 2
steps.body:
Q: How did the elders solve the problem of the missing chappals?

A: The children's mother gave the music master another pair of chappals from the house, so he could leave without walking barefoot.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the children gave their own chappals — they gave away the music master's.
- Forgetting the kitten sub-plot, which also shows the children's kindness.

activity.prompt: Put the events in order.
items: The children secretly feed a hungry kitten
The music master arrives for Lalli's violin lesson
A beggar with blistered feet asks for help
The children give him chappals lying at the door
The music master cannot find his chappals
The mother gives him another pair to wear home

quiz.why: The children secretly fed a stray kitten. The story is about their kindness.

quiz.q: Lalli was learning to play the
quiz.why: Lalli was learning to play the violin. A violin is a stringed instrument.

options: the hot road burnt his feet
he was going to a wedding
quiz.why: The beggar wanted footwear because the hot road burnt and blistered his feet.
The chappals given away were the music master's, which caused trouble. They were not Paati's or the beggar's.
The children's act shows kindness without thinking of the consequences. They wanted to help, but did not ask first.

scenes.text: Helping someone in need is wonderful.
But if we give away something that belongs to someone else, we hurt them.
Asking an adult first often finds a better way to help.

steps.title: Themes
steps.body:
- **Compassion**: children feel for animals and poor people.
- **Responsibility**: kindness should not harm others; take permission.
- **Family life**: the elders scold but also solve the problem with understanding and humour.

steps.title: Model answer (value question)
steps.body:
Q: Were the children right to give away the chappals? Give your view.

A: Their intention was kind — the beggar was suffering. But the chappals belonged to the music master, who was left without footwear. They should have asked an adult, who might have given the beggar an old pair from the house. Kindness is best when it does not create a problem for someone else.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing only 'yes' or 'no' in opinion questions — give reasons on both sides.
- Ignoring the elders' role in solving the problem.

a.text: A barefoot man outside your gate says the road is burning his feet. Your father's guest has left shoes at the door. What do you do?

choices.label: Ask an adult for an old pair to give him
Give him the guest's shoes
choices.feedback: Kind, but the guest will be left barefoot.

c.text: The guest searches for his shoes and is upset. What now?

choices.label: Tell the truth and ask an adult to help

b.text: Your mother finds an old pair for the man and some water too. Everyone is helped.

quiz.why: The story mainly praises compassion, the feeling of care for those who are in need.
The children should have asked an adult first before giving away the chappals. Then they could have helped without causing trouble.
The elders responded with understanding and a practical solution. They did not use violence or call the police.
Good opinion answers include reasons and examples that support the view. One word is not enough.
Kindness is best when it does not harm others. Using others' things without asking can cause problems.

scenes.text: When everyone grows their hair long, the rebel cuts his short.
When everyone is talking, he keeps quiet.
Whatever others do, the rebel does the reverse!

steps.title: What the poem says
steps.body: The poem describes a **rebel** — a person who deliberately does the **opposite** of what others do. If everyone keeps their hair short, he grows his long (and the reverse); if everyone chatters in class, he is silent, and if everyone is silent, he makes a disturbance; when everyone dresses alike, he dresses differently; when everyone praises something, he points out the opposite view. The poem ends with the idea that it is good for society to **have** rebels — they make us think and prevent dull sameness — even if it may not be easy to **be** one.

steps.title: Structure and devices
steps.body:
- **Repetition** of the pattern 'When everybody…, the rebel…' builds humour.
- **Contrast** between the crowd and the rebel.
- The tone is light and witty, with a thoughtful ending.

steps.title: Model answer 1
steps.body: Q: Who is a rebel? → Someone who refuses to follow the crowd and does the opposite of what others do.

steps.title: Model answer 2
steps.body: Q: Why might it be good to have rebels? → They make us question habits and stop everyone from being the same.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking the poem says rebels are bad — it suggests they are useful, though being one is hard.
- Missing the humour created by repetition.

statements.s: A rebel follows the crowd.
The poem uses a repeated pattern.
The poet thinks rebels are useful to society.
The tone is completely sad.

quiz.why: A rebel is someone who does the opposite of what others do. The poem uses this idea.
The poem's main device is repetition and contrast: it repeats a pattern in which the rebel does the opposite of others.

quiz.q: The poem suggests it is good to
quiz.why: The poem suggests it is good to have rebels in society, as they bring new ideas. It does not say rebels should be punished.
The poem's tone is humorous and thoughtful. It makes us smile and also think.

quiz.q: If everyone wears blue, the rebel will
quiz.why: A rebel does the opposite of others, so if everyone wears blue, the rebel wears another colour.

lessons.title: Vocabulary and grammar: reported speech basics

scenes.text: The music master said, "Where are my chappals?"
Meena reports: The music master asked where his chappals were.

steps.title: Useful words
steps.body:
- **blister**: a painful bubble on the skin from heat or rubbing
- **scold**: speak angrily to someone for doing wrong
- **embarrassed**: feeling awkward or ashamed
- **rebel**: (noun) a person who resists; (verb, re-BEL) to resist

steps.title: Reported speech (basics)
steps.body:
Direct: He said, "I am tired." → Reported: He said that **he was** tired.

- Remove quotation marks; use 'that' (optional).
- Change pronouns (I → he/she).
- Shift tense back one step after a past reporting verb: am/is → was, are → were, will → would, can → could.
- Questions: He asked, "Where are my chappals?" → He asked **where his chappals were** (no question mark).

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Mridu said, "The kitten is hungry." → Mridu said that the kitten **was** hungry.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: The beggar said, "My feet are burning." → The beggar said that **his** feet **were** burning.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Keeping the question order: 'He asked where were his chappals' ✗ → 'where his chappals were' ✓.
- Forgetting to change pronouns.

activity.prompt: Change into reported speech.
activity.text: Ravi said, "I am happy." → Ravi said that he ___ happy. Meena said, "We will help." → Meena said that they ___ help.

quiz.q: Reported form of "I can sing" (she said)
options: She said that I can sing.
She said that she could sing.
quiz.why: In reported speech, 'I can sing' becomes 'she could sing', since 'can' shifts to 'could' and 'I' becomes 'she'. So 'She said that she could sing.'

options: He asked where was the kitten?
He asked where is the kitten.
He asks where the kitten is?
He asked where the kitten was.
quiz.why: In reported questions, the word order is as in a statement, and the tense goes back. So 'He asked where the kitten was.'

options: a painful bubble on the skin
quiz.why: A blister is a painful bubble on the skin, caused for example by hot ground or rubbing shoes.
To scold means to speak angrily to someone about something wrong they did.
In reported speech, 'will' usually becomes 'would'. This is part of the backshift in tense.

questions.q: The children hid
questions.why: The children hid a kitten, a stray they were secretly looking after.

questions.q: Lalli played the
questions.why: Lalli played the violin.

questions.q: A rebel
questions.why: A rebel does the opposite of what others do, and does not just follow them.

questions.q: The beggar's feet were
questions.why: The beggar's feet were blistered by the hot road, which is why he needed chappals.

questions.q: The music master's chappals were
questions.why: The music master's chappals were given to the beggar by the children. They did it out of kindness.

questions.q: Reported: "I am hungry," said the beggar →
options: The beggar said that he is hungrily.
The beggar says he is hungry?
The beggar said I was hungry.
The beggar said that he was hungry.
questions.why: In reported speech, 'I am hungry' becomes 'he was hungry': the pronoun changes to 'he' and 'am' becomes 'was'. So 'The beggar said that he was hungry.'

questions.q: The poem The Rebel uses
questions.why: The poem The Rebel uses repetition of a pattern, in which the rebel keeps doing the opposite. This gives it structure.

questions.q: Assertion (A): The children's act caused trouble. Reason (R): They gave away something that was not theirs.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true: the children caused trouble because they gave away something that was not theirs. The reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Assertion (A): The poet says rebels are useless. Reason (R): Rebels do the opposite of others.
questions.why: The assertion is false: the poet does not say rebels are useless, but sees value in them. The reason is a true description of rebels.

questions.q: Who solved the problem of the missing chappals?
questions.why: The children's mother found a practical way to solve the problem of the missing chappals. The kitten and beggar could not.

questions.q: "Where are my chappals?" asked the master → reported
options: The master asked where were my chappals?
The master asked where are his chappals.
The master said where my chappals are.
The master asked where his chappals were.
questions.why: In reported questions, the pronoun and tense change and the word order is normal: 'The master asked where his chappals were.'

questions.q: Case: You see a classmate without a lunchbox. You give her your friend's tiffin without asking. What does the story teach?
options: Be kind, but share what is yours or ask first
questions.why: The story teaches that kindness is good, but we should share what is ours or ask first. Taking a friend's tiffin without asking repeats the children's mistake.

questions.q: Case: In a class where everyone wants to watch a film, Arjun suggests a debate instead. In the poem's terms he is
questions.why: A rebel does the opposite of what others do. Arjun suggests a debate when everyone wants a film, so in the poem's terms he is a rebel.

questions.q: Which word best describes the children?
questions.why: The children acted out of care for a kitten and a beggar, so they are compassionate. They were not cruel or greedy.

questions.q: The poem suggests it is good to have rebels but
options: it may not be easy to be one
questions.why: The poem suggests it is good to have rebels, but it may not be easy to be one, since a rebel stands apart from others.

questions.q: Identify the error: "She asked where was the kitten."
options: Word order — should be "where the kitten was"
questions.why: In a reported question, the order is subject then verb, so it should be 'where the kitten was'. 'Where was the kitten' keeps the direct question order.

courses.title: Ch 3 · Gopal and the Hilsa Fish & The Shed
courses.summary: A comic tale of the clever court jester Gopal, who accepts the king's challenge to carry a hilsa fish through town without anyone talking about it, and a poem about a child's fear and curiosity about an old shed.
outcomes: Learners can retell how Gopal wins the king's challenge
Learners can explain the humour and Gopal's cleverness
Learners can describe the mood and the speaker's feelings in The Shed
Learners can use unit vocabulary and degrees of comparison
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

scenes.text: It is hilsa season. Everyone in the kingdom talks only about hilsa fish — in the market, at court, at home.
The king, tired of it, challenges Gopal: buy a hilsa and bring it to the palace without anyone asking about it.
Gopal accepts — and comes up with a ridiculous disguise.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- The king is fed up with all the hilsa talk. He dares his clever court jester **Gopal** to buy a hilsa and bring it to the palace with **no one** mentioning the fish.
- The next day Gopal appears **half-shaved**, his body smeared with **ash**, wearing only a rag, and carrying the fish.
- People stare and talk only about his strange appearance — some think he is mad — and nobody asks about the hilsa.
- Even at the palace, people are busy discussing his looks rather than the fish. The king laughs, admits Gopal has won, and Gopal explains that he made himself so odd that no one noticed the fish.

steps.title: Why it is funny
steps.body: The king's challenge seems impossible, but Gopal uses people's nature — they notice what is strange. His foolish look hides a clever mind: **appearances distract attention**.

steps.title: Model answer 1
steps.body: Q: Why was the king annoyed? → Everyone in the kingdom, even at court, talked only about hilsa fish.

steps.title: Model answer 2
steps.body: Q: How did Gopal make sure no one asked about the fish? → He dressed so strangely — half-shaved, smeared with ash, in rags — that people talked only about his looks.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying Gopal hid the fish — he carried it openly.
- Saying the king punished Gopal — he enjoyed the trick and conceded.

activity.prompt: Order the events.
items: Everyone in the kingdom talks about hilsa
The king challenges Gopal
Gopal disguises himself oddly
People talk only about his looks, not the fish
Gopal reaches the palace with the hilsa
The king admits Gopal has won

quiz.why: Gopal was the king's court jester, a clever man who entertained and advised him.

quiz.q: The challenge was to bring a hilsa
quiz.why: The challenge was to bring a hilsa fish without anyone asking about it. It was a test of cleverness.
Gopal's disguise included a half-shaved face and ash, which made him look odd. It was meant to draw attention away from the fish.
People thought Gopal was mad because of his odd looks. So they asked about him, not about the fish.
The trick worked because strange looks attract attention, so people stared at Gopal and not at the fish.

scenes.text: Court jesters often act foolish but are the cleverest people at court.
Gopal thinks about people, not just about the fish.

steps.title: Characters
steps.body:
- **Gopal**: witty, confident, understands human nature, willing to look silly to win.
- **The king**: playful, likes challenges, sporting enough to admit defeat.

steps.title: Themes
steps.body:
- Intelligence beats impossible-looking problems.
- **People notice the unusual** — attention can be redirected.
- Humour as a tool.

steps.title: Model answer
steps.body:
Q: What does the story tell us about Gopal's character? (50 words)

A: Gopal is quick-witted and fearless. Instead of hiding the fish, he understood that people talk about whatever is most unusual, so he made himself the most unusual sight in town. He was ready to look foolish to prove his point, which shows confidence and humour.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling Gopal foolish — he only pretends.
- Writing a summary instead of describing character traits with evidence.

activity.prompt: Match the trait with evidence.
pairs: Plans a disguise so people ignore the fish
Turns the problem into a joke

quiz.q: Gopal can best be described as
quiz.why: Gopal can best be described as witty, as he uses clever ideas to solve problems. He is not shy or cruel.

quiz.q: The king's reaction at the end
quiz.why: At the end the king laughed and accepted defeat, since Gopal won the challenge. He was a good sport.

quiz.q: A main idea of the story
quiz.why: A main idea is that clever thinking can solve odd problems. Gopal used cleverness, not force.

quiz.q: Why is Gopal called a "wise fool"?
options: He acts silly but thinks cleverly
quiz.why: Gopal is called a 'wise fool' because he acts silly but thinks cleverly. The word 'fool' is ironic.
Character answers need traits with evidence from the story. A trait without an example is not convincing.

scenes.text: At the bottom of the garden stands an old shed with a cobwebbed window and a creaky door.
The speaker's older brother says someone lives inside — a ghostly face, perhaps.
The child keeps saying "One of these days I'll go in" — but not yet!

steps.title: What the poem says
steps.body: The speaker is both **afraid** of and **curious** about an old shed. It has a door that creaks, a cobweb-covered window and floorboards that might make strange noises. The speaker's brother has told stories to scare him — that someone is inside, watching. The child keeps promising to open the door 'one of these days', which shows fear mixed with growing courage.

steps.title: Mood and devices
steps.body:
- **Mood**: mysterious, slightly spooky, playful.
- **Repetition** of 'one of these days' shows the speaker's hesitation.
- **Imagery**: creaky door, cobwebs, a face at the window.

steps.title: Model answer 1
steps.body: Q: Why hasn't the speaker gone inside the shed? → He is scared, partly because of his brother's stories about someone living there.

steps.title: Model answer 2
steps.body: Q: What does 'one of these days' suggest? → He wants to go in and plans to, but keeps putting it off — curiosity fighting fear.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating the ghost as real — the poem suggests the brother was teasing.
- Missing the mix of fear and curiosity.

statements.s: The speaker is curious about the shed.
The speaker has gone inside many times.
The brother's stories make the shed seem scary.
The poem's mood is mysterious.

quiz.why: The shed's window has cobwebs, which shows it is old and unused. This adds to the mysterious mood.

quiz.q: Who told scary stories about the shed?
quiz.why: The speaker's brother told scary stories about the shed, making it seem haunted.
'One of these days' shows hesitation and an intention to go in, but only later. He keeps putting it off.
The mood of the poem is mysterious, as the shed is dark and unknown. It is not sad or boring.
The speaker feels fear and curiosity together. He wants to look inside but is afraid.

lessons.title: Vocabulary and grammar: degrees of comparison

scenes.text: This hilsa is big. That one is bigger. The king's hilsa is the biggest of all!
Let us work through it step by step, then try the activity and quiz.

steps.title: Useful words
steps.body:
- **jester**: a person employed to entertain a king with jokes
- **disguise**: clothes or appearance that hide who you are
- **hilsa**: a fish popular in Bengal
- **creak**: a harsh squeaking sound (of a door)
- **cobweb**: a spider's web

steps.title: Degrees of comparison
steps.body:
- **Positive**: big, clever, interesting
- **Comparative** (two things): bigger, cleverer/more clever, more interesting — use 'than'
- **Superlative** (three or more): biggest, cleverest, most interesting — use 'the'
- Irregular: good → better → best; bad → worse → worst; many → more → most; little → less → least

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Gopal was ___ (clever) than all the courtiers. → **cleverer / more clever**

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: It was the ___ (strange) sight in town. → **strangest**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Double comparatives: 'more bigger' ✗ → 'bigger' ✓.
- Using the superlative for two things: 'the best of the two' ✗ → 'the better of the two' ✓.

activity.prompt: Use the correct degree.
activity.text: The shed was ___ (old) than the house. It was the ___ (dark) place in the garden. Gopal's plan was ___ (good) than the king expected.

quiz.why: The comparative of 'good' is 'better'. It is irregular, so 'gooder' is wrong, and 'best' is the superlative.
The superlative of 'bad' is 'worst'. 'Worse' is the comparative, and 'baddest' is wrong.

options: Gopal was the most cleverest courtier.
quiz.why: 'Cleverest' is already a superlative, so we say 'the cleverest'. 'Most cleverest' and 'more cleverer' wrongly double the form.
A jester is an entertainer at a royal court, like Gopal. He is not a fisherman or soldier.

options: an appearance that hides who you are
quiz.why: A disguise is an appearance that hides who you are, such as odd clothes or a changed face. Gopal used one in the story.

questions.q: Gopal was
questions.why: Gopal was the king's court jester, a clever entertainer.

questions.q: The king challenged Gopal to bring a
questions.why: The king challenged Gopal to bring a hilsa fish without anyone asking about it.

questions.q: The shed's door
questions.why: In the poem, the shed's door creaks. A creaking sound adds to the spooky feeling.

questions.q: Comparative of "old"
questions.why: The comparative of 'old' is 'older'. 'Oldest' is the superlative.

questions.q: Gopal's trick worked because
options: people talked about his odd looks
questions.why: Gopal's trick worked because people talked about his odd looks, so nobody asked about the fish.

questions.q: In The Shed, the speaker keeps saying he will go in
questions.why: In The Shed, the speaker keeps saying he will go in 'one of these days'. That repeated phrase shows he puts it off.

questions.q: Superlative of "good"
questions.why: The superlative of 'good' is 'best'. 'Better' is the comparative and 'goodest' is wrong.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Gopal won the challenge. Reason (R): Nobody asked him about the hilsa.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true: Gopal won because nobody asked about the hilsa, as people were busy with his odd looks. The reason explains the win.

questions.q: Assertion (A): The speaker in The Shed is completely fearless. Reason (R): He keeps putting off going in.
questions.why: The assertion is false: the speaker is not fearless, as he is afraid of the shed. The reason is true, since he keeps putting off going in.

questions.q: Who made the shed seem haunted?
questions.why: The speaker's brother told scary tales that made the shed seem haunted.

questions.q: Correct the error: "This is the more interesting story of all."
questions.why: 'Of all' needs a superlative, so we say 'the most interesting story of all'. 'More interesting' compares only two things.

questions.q: Case: A magician waves a bright scarf so the audience doesn't see his other hand. This is like
options: Gopal using his odd looks to distract people
questions.why: The magician's scarf draws attention away from his other hand, like Gopal's odd looks drawing attention away from the fish. Both are distractions.

questions.q: Case: Your friend fears the dark storeroom because of a cousin's ghost stories, but says he will check it someday. He is like
questions.why: The friend is afraid but curious and keeps delaying, like the speaker in The Shed. Gopal and the king do not fit.

questions.q: Which word best describes the mood of The Shed?
questions.why: The mood of The Shed is mysterious, because the shed is dark and unknown. It is not joyful or peaceful.

questions.q: What does Gopal's story suggest about human nature?
options: People notice and talk about what is most unusual
People love fish more than gossip
questions.why: Gopal's story suggests that people notice and talk about what is most unusual. His odd looks drew attention away from the fish.

questions.q: Choose the correct sentence.
options: Of the two brothers, Ravi is the tallest.
Ravi is most tall than his brother.
Of the two brothers, Ravi is the taller.
questions.why: When comparing two things, we use the comparative form: 'the taller'. The superlative is for three or more, and 'more taller' is a double form.

courses.title: Ch 4 · The Ashes That Made Trees Bloom & Chivvy
courses.summary: A Japanese folk tale in which honesty and kindness are rewarded and greed is punished, as a faithful dog's magic passes from a gift of gold to a mortar to ashes that make dead trees bloom; plus Chivvy, a poem about the endless orders adults give children.
outcomes: Learners can retell the folk tale and identify its magical turns
Learners can contrast the honest old couple with the greedy neighbours
Learners can explain the irony in Chivvy
Learners can use imperative sentences and unit vocabulary
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

lessons.title: The folk tale in our own words

scenes.text: In old Japan, a kind farmer and his wife had no children; they loved their little dog as their own.
One day the dog sniffed and scratched at a spot in the garden. The farmer dug and found gold!
Their greedy neighbours wanted the same luck…

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- The greedy neighbours borrow the dog and force it to find treasure. When they dig they find only rubbish, and in anger they **kill the dog** and bury it under a pine tree.
- The dog appears to the grieving farmer in a dream and tells him to cut down the pine and make a **mortar** from it. The mortar brings the old couple wealth (gold).
- The neighbours borrow the mortar, but it gives them nothing good, so they **burn** it.
- In another dream, the dog tells the farmer to collect the **ashes** and sprinkle them on withered **cherry trees**. The dead trees burst into bloom!
- The **daimyo** (feudal lord of the area) sees the miracle and rewards the farmer richly.
- The greedy neighbour tries the trick too, but the ashes blow into the daimyo's eyes; he is punished.

steps.title: Folk-tale features
steps.body:
- Repeated pattern of three (gold, mortar, ashes)
- Magic and dreams
- Clear contrast: **good is rewarded, greed is punished**
- Setting in a traditional society (daimyo, cherry blossoms)

steps.title: Model answer 1
steps.body:
Q: What did the dog tell the farmer in his dreams?

A: First, to cut the pine tree and make a mortar from its wood; later, to collect the mortar's ashes and sprinkle them on withered cherry trees.

steps.title: Model answer 2
steps.body: Q: Why was the daimyo pleased with the old man? → The ashes made dead cherry trees bloom beautifully in front of him.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the neighbours found gold — they found only rubbish.
- Mixing the order of magic: gold → mortar → ashes.

activity.prompt: Order the magical events.
items: The dog leads the farmer to buried gold
Greedy neighbours kill the dog and bury it under a pine
A mortar made from the pine brings the old couple wealth
The neighbours burn the mortar
The ashes make withered cherry trees bloom
The daimyo rewards the old farmer

quiz.why: The old couple loved their dog like a child. It is the dog that brings the good things in the story.

options: the pine tree over the dog's grave
quiz.why: The mortar was made from the pine tree that grew over the dog's grave, as the dog told the farmer in a dream.
The ashes of the burnt mortar made dead cherry trees bloom. This was the miracle in the story.

options: a feudal lord in old Japan
quiz.why: A daimyo is a feudal lord in old Japan. He is not a farmer or a tree.
The greedy neighbour's ashes blew into the daimyo's eyes, which was his punishment. They did not make trees bloom.

scenes.text: One old man shares, grieves for his dog and stays honest.
The other copies, grabs and destroys.
The story rewards the first and punishes the second.

steps.title: Contrast
steps.body:
- **Old farmer and wife**: kind, loving, honest, patient, grateful.
- **Neighbours**: greedy, jealous, cruel, impatient — they want rewards without goodness.

steps.title: Model answer
steps.body:
Q: 'Greed leads to loss.' Explain with reference to the story.

A: Each time the neighbours copied the farmer to get rich — borrowing the dog, the mortar and finally the ashes — they ended up with nothing and, finally, punishment from the daimyo. Their greed made them cruel and foolish, while the farmer's kindness brought lasting reward.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Summarising without explaining the moral.
- Forgetting that the dog's loyalty continues after death in the dreams.

activity.prompt: Who showed this quality?

items.text: Loved the dog like a child

options: kindness is rewarded; greed is punished
quiz.why: The main moral is that kindness is rewarded and greed is punished. The couple's kindness is rewarded, while the neighbours' greed is punished.
The neighbours were greedy and jealous, as they copied the farmer only to get rewards. They were not kind or generous.
The farmer was honest and kind, so the dog's spirit helped him. He was neither cruel nor greedy.
The dog showed loyalty even after death, by helping its owners through dreams and ashes.
Folk tales often have a clear moral and some magic. They are not maps or news reports.

scenes.text: "Sit up straight! Don't talk with your mouth full! Say please! Don't stare!"
All day, children hear instructions from grown-ups.
Then the grown-up asks: why can't you think for yourself?

steps.title: What the poem says
steps.body: **Chivvy** means to tell someone repeatedly to do something; to nag. The poem is a list of **commands** adults give children — about manners, posture, speaking up, keeping quiet, not interrupting, using a handkerchief, not dragging feet, and so on. At the very end, the adult asks why the child cannot make up their own mind — **ironic**, because the child has been told exactly what to do all the time and never allowed to decide.

steps.title: Devices
steps.body:
- **Imperative sentences** throughout (commands).
- **Irony** in the last line.
- Short lines create a nagging rhythm.
- **Tone**: humorous but critical of over-instruction.

steps.title: Model answer 1
steps.body: Q: What is ironic about the poem's ending? → After controlling every action, adults expect children to think independently — but the constant orders never let them practise.

steps.title: Model answer 2
steps.body: Q: Are all the instructions bad? → No — many teach good manners. The poem's point is that too many orders, with no room to decide, stop children from learning to think for themselves.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking the poem says children should never be taught manners.
- Missing the irony of the last line.

statements.s: Chivvy means to nag or harass someone to do things.
The poem is mostly made of commands.
The ending is ironic.
statements.why: Asked to think after being told everything.

statements.s: The poet wants children to have no manners.

quiz.why: 'Chivvy' means to nag repeatedly, telling someone again and again to do something. It is not praise or singing.

quiz.q: The poem is mainly a list of
quiz.why: The poem is mainly a list of commands given by adults to children, like 'Get up' and 'Hurry up'.
The last line is ironic, as it turns the poem's meaning around. Irony means saying something that is the opposite of what we expect.
'Sit up straight' is a command, so the sentence is imperative. It is not a question or an exclamation.

options: a chance to decide for themselves
quiz.why: The poem suggests that children need a chance to decide for themselves, after being told what to do all the time. It does not say they need more orders.

scenes.text: The class writes rules: "Raise your hand to speak." "Please keep the room tidy." "Don't run in the corridor."
Let us work through it step by step, then try the activity and quiz.

steps.title: Imperative sentences
steps.body:
Imperatives give **commands, requests, advice or instructions**. The subject 'you' is usually understood, and the verb comes first.

- Command: Shut the door.
- Request: Please pass the salt.
- Advice: Drink more water.
- Negative: Don't run. / Never touch wires.

They end with a full stop, or an exclamation mark for strong feeling.

steps.title: Unit words
steps.body:
- **mortar**: a bowl in which grain/spices are pounded
- **withered**: dried up, dead-looking
- **bloom**: to flower
- **feudal lord**: a landowner with power over people on his lands
- **nag / chivvy**: to keep telling someone to do things

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Change into an imperative: 'You should close the window.' → **Close the window, please.**

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Identify the type: 'Please help me carry this.' → **imperative (request)**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding a subject: 'You sit down' is fine but often the imperative omits 'you'.
- Putting a question mark after an imperative request without a question form.

activity.prompt: What kind of imperative?

items.text: Mix the flour and water, then knead.
Could you please open the door. (polite)

quiz.q: An imperative sentence usually begins with
quiz.why: An imperative sentence usually begins with a verb, like 'Close' or 'Sit'. The subject 'you' is understood.
'Close the gate.' is a command, so it is imperative. The other sentences are a statement, a question and an exclamation.
'Withered' describes a plant that has dried up and lost its freshness. It is the opposite of flowering.
A mortar is a bowl in which grain or spices are pounded with a pestle. It is not used to dig or carry water.
'Please be quiet.' politely asks someone to do something, so it is a request. It is not a question or a plain statement.

questions.q: The old couple's dog first found
questions.why: In the story, the old couple's dog first found gold when it dug in the ground. Later it led them to ashes and trees.

questions.q: Chivvy means
questions.why: 'Chivvy' means to nag, which is to keep telling someone to do something. It does not mean praise or dance.

questions.q: A daimyo is a
questions.why: A daimyo is a feudal lord in old Japan. He is not a farmer, a tree or a dog.

questions.q: Imperative sentences give
questions.why: Imperative sentences give commands or requests, such as 'Sit down' or 'Please come'. They are not for questions or news.

questions.q: The neighbours buried the dog under a
questions.why: The neighbours buried the dog under a pine tree, and the farmer later made a mortar from that tree. It was not under a mango or cherry tree.

questions.q: The ashes made
questions.why: The ashes made withered trees bloom, which was the miracle. They did not make gold or rain.

questions.q: "Don't stare!" is
questions.why: 'Don't stare!' is a command not to do something, so it is imperative. It is not a statement or question.

questions.q: Assertion (A): The neighbours were punished at the end. Reason (R): Their ashes blew into the daimyo's eyes.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true: the neighbours were punished at the end because their ashes blew into the daimyo's eyes. The reason explains the punishment.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Chivvy praises adults for giving many orders. Reason (R): The poem lists commands.
questions.why: The assertion is false: Chivvy gently criticises adults who give too many orders, not praises them. The reason is true, since the poem lists commands.

questions.q: Which pattern is typical of folk tales?
options: events in threes and a clear moral
questions.why: Folk tales usually have events in threes and a clear moral. They do not read like timetables or statistics.

questions.q: The irony in Chivvy is that
options: children are told to think for themselves after being told everything
questions.why: The irony in Chivvy is that children are told to think for themselves after being given orders about everything. The advice contradicts the commands.

questions.q: Case: A neighbour copies your science project to win a prize but it fails. Which story moral fits?
options: Copying greedily without effort brings loss
questions.why: The neighbour copying greedily and failing matches the greedy neighbours in the story, who copied the farmer and were punished. So copying greedily without effort brings loss.

questions.q: Case: A parent gives a child 20 instructions before breakfast, then asks why she can't decide what to wear. This mirrors
questions.why: A parent who gives 20 instructions and then asks why the child cannot decide mirrors Chivvy, where adults give orders and then say 'think for yourself'. That is the irony.

questions.q: Change to imperative: "You must wash your hands."
questions.why: To change 'You must wash your hands' into a command, write 'Wash your hands.' That is the imperative form.

questions.q: What does the dog's appearance in dreams show?
questions.why: The dog's appearance in dreams shows loyalty that continues after death, as it helps its owners again. It does not show anger or kindness of the neighbours.

questions.q: Which line would fit in Chivvy?
options: Keep your elbows off the table!
questions.why: 'Keep your elbows off the table!' is a command given to a child, like the orders in Chivvy. The other lines belong to other stories.

courses.title: Ch 5 · Quality & Trees
courses.summary: John Galsworthy's moving story of the Gessler brothers, bootmakers who would rather starve than compromise on quality, and a gentle poem that praises the many gifts of trees.
outcomes: Learners can retell the story of the Gessler brothers through the narrator's eyes
Learners can discuss quality versus advertising and big business
Learners can list the gifts of trees described in the poem
Learners can use unit vocabulary and write character sketches
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

scenes.text: In a small London shop, two German brothers, the Gesslers, make boots by hand.
Their boots fit perfectly and last for years — they are made "with the soul".
But big firms with advertisements are taking away their customers.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- The narrator has known **Mr Gessler** since childhood. The brothers' boots are made only to order, with perfect skill and the best leather; they never advertise.
- Mr Gessler is hurt when the narrator once wears boots bought from a **large firm**; he complains that big firms win customers by **advertisement, not by work**, and take away the trade of honest craftsmen.
- Because their boots last so long, customers order rarely. The brothers grow poorer.
- On later visits, the narrator finds the **elder brother has died** and the shop has shrunk. Mr Gessler looks older and thinner, but his boots are still excellent.
- Finally the narrator learns that Mr Gessler has **died of slow starvation**: he worked day and night, spent everything on the best leather, never let anyone else touch his work, and charged fair prices — so he earned too little to live.
- A young Englishman takes over the shop.

steps.title: Model answer 1
steps.body: Q: Why did Mr Gessler dislike big firms? → They attracted customers through advertising rather than quality work, and took business away from honest craftsmen.

steps.title: Model answer 2
steps.body: Q: How did Mr Gessler die? → From slow starvation; he gave all his time and money to making perfect boots and charged little.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying Mr Gessler was a poor craftsman — he was the best; he was poor because of the market.
- Mixing up which brother died first (the elder brother died first).

activity.prompt: Order the events.
items: The narrator orders boots from the Gesslers as a young man
Mr Gessler complains about big firms and advertising
Business declines; the shop shrinks
The elder brother dies
The narrator orders boots after a long gap; they are perfect
He learns Mr Gessler died of slow starvation

quiz.why: The Gesslers were bootmakers. They made fine boots by hand for their customers.
Their boots were perfectly made and lasted a very long time. That quality was their pride.
Mr Gessler felt that big firms won customers by advertisement, not by better work. He refused to follow that way.
Mr Gessler died of slow starvation, as orders had become so few. It was a sad end for such a skilled craftsman.

quiz.q: Who took over the shop at the end?
quiz.why: A young Englishman took over the shop at the end. He took over the business from Gessler.

scenes.text: A shiny advertisement says "Best boots in town!"
In a quiet shop, an old man stitches boots that really are the best.
Which one will most people notice?

steps.title: Themes
steps.body:
- **Dedication to quality** and pride in craft.
- **Big business and advertising** overpowering small craftsmen.
- **Integrity**: Mr Gessler would not lower standards even to survive.
- Tragedy of a good man defeated by the market.

steps.title: Model character sketch
steps.body: Mr Gessler (80–100 words): Mr Gessler was a German bootmaker in London, dedicated to his craft. He made every pair by hand with the finest leather and judged his worth by the quality of his work, not by profit. Honest and proud, he refused to advertise or rush. He was hurt when customers chose big firms. Even when poor and weak, he kept making perfect boots, and he finally died of slow starvation. He is a symbol of integrity and true craftsmanship.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling Mr Gessler greedy — he charged fairly and spent on quality.
- Writing only events in a character sketch — describe traits with evidence.

activity.prompt: Match trait and evidence.
pairs: Made boots by hand, never let others do the work
Hurt when the narrator bought factory boots

options: quality and integrity versus commercial pressure
quiz.why: The main theme is quality and integrity versus commercial pressure. Mr Gessler keeps his standards even when it costs him.
Mr Gessler refused to advertise, believing good work should speak for itself. This is a sign of his integrity.

quiz.q: The narrator felt towards Mr Gessler
quiz.why: The narrator feels respect for Mr Gessler's craft and sympathy for his hardship. He does not hate or fear him.
A character sketch should include traits supported by evidence from the story, such as actions and words. A list of events or dates is not enough.
The story criticises a world where advertising takes the place of real quality. It praises good craftsmanship.

scenes.text: A tree stands quietly in a field; cows rest in its shade and birds gather in its branches.
It gives fruit, wood for houses, and new green buds each spring.
It catches the first light of morning and holds the last light of evening.

steps.title: What the poem says
steps.body: The poet calls trees among the **kindest things** he knows: they do no harm, they simply grow. They give **shade** to sleepy cows, gather **birds** among their branches, give **fruit**, **wood** to build houses, **leaves** (to burn in autumn festivals) and fresh **buds** in spring. They are the first to touch the morning sun and the last to hold the light as evening turns into night.

steps.title: Devices
steps.body:
- **Personification**: trees are 'kind', 'gather' birds.
- **Rhyming couplets** give a calm, flowing music.
- **Imagery** of seasons and times of day.

steps.title: Model answer 1
steps.body: Q: List four gifts of trees from the poem. → Shade, fruit, wood for houses, homes for birds (also leaves and spring buds).

steps.title: Model answer 2
steps.body: Q: Why are trees called 'kind'? → They give so much and harm no one, asking for nothing.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling 'trees are kind' a simile — it is personification.
- Missing the time imagery (first/last light).

activity.prompt: Thank a tree — this week I will:
items: Find out the name of a tree near my home
Notice birds that visit it
Water a young plant
Avoid wasting paper
Draw the tree in morning and evening light

quiz.why: The poet calls trees 'the kindest things', because they give so much to us. They are not useless or scary.
The poem says trees give shade to sleepy cows. That image shows how trees care for living things.

quiz.q: Trees are the first to touch
quiz.why: The poem says trees are the first to touch the morning sun. This is an image of the early morning.
Calling trees 'kind' gives a tree a human quality, which is personification. It is not a comparison with 'like' or 'as'.

quiz.q: Wood from trees is used to
quiz.why: Wood from trees is used to build houses. It cannot be used to make glass, plastic or metal.

lessons.title: Vocabulary and writing: describing a person

scenes.text: Write about someone you admire who works with their hands — a potter, tailor, cobbler or carpenter.
Let us work through it step by step, then try the activity and quiz.

steps.title: Words from the story
steps.body:
- **craftsman**: a skilled worker who makes things by hand
- **firm**: a business company
- **advertisement**: a public notice to promote a product
- **starvation**: suffering or death from lack of food
- **integrity**: honesty and strong moral principles

steps.title: Writing a description of a person
steps.body:
1. Introduce the person (who, where).
2. Describe appearance briefly.
3. Give 2–3 traits with examples.
4. End with your feelings or what you learnt.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: "Ramu Kaka, our neighbourhood cobbler, sits under a neem tree with his tools. His hands are rough but quick. He never hurries a repair; every stitch is tight and even. He charges little and often fixes children's sandals for free. Like Mr Gessler, he takes pride in doing a job well."

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Listing appearance only — show character through actions.
- Forgetting a conclusion.

activity.prompt: Fill in with unit words.
activity.text: A skilled ___ makes things by hand. Big ___ spend money on ___ to attract customers.

quiz.why: Integrity means honesty and strong moral principles. It is not about speed, fame or wealth.
A firm is a business company that makes or sells things. It is not a shoe, a tree or a farm.
Starvation is suffering or dying from lack of food. It does not mean eating too much or sleeping.

quiz.q: A good description of a person includes
quiz.why: A good description shows a person's traits through their actions. Only clothes or height tell little about character.
A craftsman makes things skilfully, often by hand, like the Gesslers' boots. He is not just a seller or a banker.

questions.q: The Gesslers were
questions.why: The Gesslers were German bootmakers living in London. They made fine boots by hand.

questions.q: Trees give shade to
questions.why: The poem says trees give shade to sleepy cows. Ships, whales and mountains do not need shade from trees.

questions.q: Mr Gessler made boots
questions.why: Mr Gessler made boots by hand, with great skill. He did not use factories or machines only.

questions.q: Integrity means
questions.why: Integrity means honesty and strong principles. It does not mean speed, size or money.

questions.q: Mr Gessler was hurt when
options: the narrator wore boots from a large firm
questions.why: Mr Gessler was hurt when the narrator wore boots from a large firm. It felt like a sign that his craft was being ignored.

questions.q: Who died first?
questions.why: The elder brother died first, and then Mr Gessler died later of slow starvation. The narrator and the young Englishman are alive at the end.

questions.q: In "Trees", leaves are mentioned as
options: something to burn in autumn and new buds in spring
questions.why: The poem mentions leaves as something that burns in autumn and new buds in spring. These are gifts trees give through the seasons.

questions.q: Assertion (A): The Gesslers grew poor. Reason (R): Their boots lasted so long and they would not advertise, so orders were few.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true: the Gesslers grew poor because their boots lasted so long and they would not advertise, so few orders came. The reason explains the poverty.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Mr Gessler lowered his quality to earn more. Reason (R): Big firms were taking his customers.
questions.why: The assertion is false: Mr Gessler never lowered his quality, even when poor. The reason is true, as big firms took his customers.

questions.q: The poem "Trees" uses mainly
questions.why: The poem 'Trees' uses personification and rhyme: it calls trees kind and its lines rhyme. It does not use dialogue or numbers.

questions.q: What does the title "Quality" refer to?
options: the excellence of Mr Gessler's boots and character
questions.why: The title 'Quality' refers to the excellence of Mr Gessler's boots and of his character. It is not the name of a shop or brand.

questions.q: Case: A local potter's handmade pots last years but a shop selling cheap, advertised pots gets more buyers. This mirrors
questions.why: A potter's lasting handmade pots losing buyers to cheap advertised ones mirrors Quality. The theme is good craft against cheap commercial products.

questions.q: Case: A student writes, "Mr Gessler was foolish to care so much." Give a balanced view.
options: His dedication was admirable, but the market did not reward it fairly
questions.why: A balanced view says his dedication was admirable, but the market did not reward it fairly. He was not greedy or lazy.

questions.q: Which line best sums up the poem "Trees"?
options: Trees give generously and harm no one
questions.why: The poem sums up that trees give generously and harm no one. They are not dangerous.

questions.q: What does Mr Gessler's death suggest about society?
options: It may fail to value honest craftsmanship
questions.why: Mr Gessler's death suggests that society may fail to value honest craftsmanship. He was ignored, though his work was excellent.

questions.q: Which word best describes the narrator's final feeling?
questions.why: The narrator's final feeling is sorrow for Mr Gessler, who deserved better. He is not angry at Gessler.

courses.title: Ch 6 · Expert Detectives & Mystery of the Talking Fan
courses.summary: A story in which two children turn amateur detectives and learn that first impressions can mislead, and a funny poem about a fan that seemed to chatter. This course focuses on reading skills — clues, inference, judging people fairly — with our own examples; read the textbook chapter for the full plot.
outcomes: Learners can identify clues and make inferences while reading
Learners can explain why judging people by appearance is unfair
Learners can explain the humour and personification in the fan poem
Learners can write a short mystery paragraph using clues
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

scenes.text: Two children notice a quiet neighbour who lives alone and rarely goes out.
They start imagining he is hiding something and collect "clues".
As in the textbook story, they discover that the truth is kinder — and sadder — than their suspicions.

steps.title: What detectives do
steps.body:
- **Observe** details (clues).
- **Infer**: work out what is not directly said.
- **Test** ideas against evidence; change them if evidence disagrees.
- Avoid jumping to conclusions.

steps.title: Inference in reading
steps.body: Authors often do not state everything. If a character shivers and pulls a shawl tighter, we infer it is cold. If a neighbour always keeps curtains closed and has scars, we must not infer he is a criminal — we need real evidence.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Clue: 'Her eyes were red and she held a crumpled tissue.' Inference: she had been crying.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Clue: 'The man had a scarred face and lived alone.' Fair inference? → Only that he may have been hurt in the past; nothing proves he is dangerous.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating guesses as facts.
- Ignoring evidence that does not fit your theory.

activity.prompt: Fact (stated) or inference (worked out)?

quiz.why: An inference is a conclusion drawn from clues, not directly stated. A stated fact is already in the text.
Good detectives test their ideas against the evidence. They do not ignore clues or trust rumours.
Scars on a face prove nothing about a person's character. We cannot say someone is a criminal from their looks.

quiz.q: "He shivered and pulled his coat tighter" suggests
quiz.why: Shivering and pulling a coat tighter are signs of feeling cold. So we infer that it was cold.
A clue is a piece of evidence that helps solve a mystery.

story.title: Don't judge a book by its cover

scenes.text: A shabby old book can hold a wonderful story.
A quiet, scarred neighbour may be a brave or kind person with a painful past.
Empathy means trying to understand someone's life before judging.

steps.title: Themes of the chapter
steps.body:
- **First impressions can mislead**.
- **Empathy** for people who are lonely, hurt or different.
- Children's imagination can be fun, but suspicion can hurt others.

steps.title: Model answer
steps.body:
Q: What lesson do the children learn? (Write in your own words.)

A: They learn that appearance and rumours are not proof. When they find out the real story of the person they suspected, they feel sorry for having misjudged him and understand the value of kindness and empathy.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing that suspicious-looking people are always guilty.
- Forgetting to mention the change in the children's feelings.

a.text: A new neighbour never smiles and walks with a limp. Your friends say he is "scary". What do you do?

choices.label: Say hello politely and learn more before judging
Spread a rumour that he is dangerous

c.text: Other children start avoiding him. He looks hurt. Want to change course?

b.text: You learn he was injured helping people during a flood. First impressions were wrong!

quiz.why: A key lesson is that first impressions can mislead. A person may seem suspicious but be innocent.
Empathy means understanding others' feelings. It helps us avoid judging people unfairly.
Rumours can hurt innocent people, because they spread without proof. They do not prove facts.
Before judging someone, we should learn the facts. Gossip and looks can mislead us.

quiz.q: "Don't judge a book by its cover" means
quiz.why: 'Don't judge a book by its cover' means we should not judge by appearance. What is inside may be different.

lessons.title: Poem: Mystery of the Talking Fan

scenes.text: An old electric fan whirs and rattles as it spins — it almost sounds as if it is talking!
Someone tightens a loose part and oils it.
Now the fan is silent — the "mystery" is solved.

steps.title: What the poem says
steps.body: The poem humorously describes an electric fan that seemed to **talk** — it whirred, clicked and chattered all day, and people wondered what it was saying. When it was finally **mended**, it stopped 'talking'. The 'mystery' was just a loose or worn part.

steps.title: Devices
steps.body:
- **Personification**: the fan 'talks' like a person.
- **Humour**: an ordinary noise is treated like a mystery.
- **Onomatopoeia** may be used for sounds (whirr, click).

steps.title: Model answer
steps.body: Q: Why did the fan stop talking? → Because it was repaired; the noise came from a fault, not real talking.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Taking the 'talking' literally.
- Missing the light, joking tone.

statements.s: The fan really spoke words.
The poem uses personification.
Mending the fan made it quiet.
The tone is humorous.

quiz.why: In the poem, the fan seems to talk, giving it a human ability. That is where the humour comes from.
The 'mystery' of the talking fan was solved when the fan was mended. The noise then stopped.
The poem's tone is humorous. It makes light of a puzzling noise.

quiz.q: Giving a fan human abilities is
quiz.why: Giving a fan the ability to talk is personification, as it gives a non-living thing a human quality.
'Whirr' imitates the sound of a fan, so it is onomatopoeia. It is not a comparison or a rhyme.

scenes.text: Write a 100-word mystery with three clues and a surprising but fair solution.
Let us work through it step by step, then try the activity and quiz.

steps.title: Plan
steps.body:
1. **Set-up**: place, characters, a puzzle (something missing, a strange noise).
2. **Clues** (three): leave hints the reader can notice.
3. **False lead**: a suspect who seems guilty.
4. **Solution**: explained by the clues, not by luck.
5. **Ending**: how the characters feel.

steps.title: Model paragraph
steps.body: "Every night, a tapping sound came from the attic. Ria found tiny scratches on the window frame, crumbs on the floor, and a feather by the box of old clothes. Her brother insisted it was a ghost. With a torch, Ria climbed up quietly. In the box sat a pigeon with three chicks! It had come in through a gap in the broken window. Feeling silly and happy, the family fixed a small nesting box outside and closed the gap."

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- A solution with no clues before it ('it was magic').
- Too many characters for a short piece.

activity.prompt: Write the opening two sentences of your own mystery and list three clues you will hide in it.
activity.hint: Clues can be sounds, objects, footprints, smells or something out of place.

quiz.why: A good mystery solution is explained by the clues given earlier. It should not appear from nowhere.

options: a suspect who seems guilty but is not
quiz.why: A false lead is a suspect or clue that seems important but turns out to be wrong. It adds suspense.

quiz.q: In the model paragraph, the noise came from
quiz.why: In the model paragraph, the noise came from a family of pigeons, an ordinary cause behind a spooky mystery.

quiz.q: First step in planning a mystery
options: set the scene and the puzzle
quiz.why: The first step in planning a mystery is to set the scene and the puzzle. Then clues and the solution follow.
Clues should be noticeable but not too obvious, so readers can think but not guess at once. Hiding them or leaving them out would be unfair.

questions.q: An inference is
questions.why: An inference is a conclusion drawn from evidence. It is not a stated fact, a title or a rhyme.

questions.q: The fan in the poem seemed to
questions.why: The fan in the poem seems to talk, which is personification.

questions.q: Empathy means
questions.why: Empathy means understanding others' feelings. It is the opposite of ignoring or judging them.

questions.q: A clue is
questions.why: A clue is evidence that helps solve a puzzle. It is not a lie or a joke.

questions.q: Good detectives
questions.why: Good detectives change their ideas when the evidence disagrees. They do not trust rumours or ignore facts.

questions.q: The fan stopped talking because
questions.why: The fan stopped 'talking' because it was repaired. The humour is that the cause was ordinary.

questions.q: A key theme of Expert Detectives
questions.why: A key theme of Expert Detectives is not to judge by appearance. First impressions can mislead.

questions.q: Assertion (A): We should not judge a person only by scars or looks. Reason (R): Appearance does not show a person's character or story.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true: we should not judge a person by scars or looks, because appearance does not show character or story. The reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Assertion (A): The fan in the poem actually spoke words. Reason (R): The poem uses personification.
questions.why: The assertion is false: the fan only seemed to talk, and it did not really speak words. The reason is true, as the poem uses personification.

questions.q: "She clutched her umbrella and shook water from her hair." Inference?
questions.why: Clutching an umbrella and shaking water from her hair suggests it was raining. This is an inference, not a stated fact.

questions.q: Which is a fact, not an inference?
questions.why: 'He lives alone' is a stated fact. 'Probably', 'might' and 'must be' are signs of inference or guessing.

questions.q: Case: Students blame a new classmate for a missing pen because he is quiet. The pen is found in a bag. Lesson?
questions.why: Blaming the quiet classmate without proof was unfair, and the pen was found in a bag. So we should not accuse without evidence.

questions.q: Case: A noisy ceiling fan keeps everyone guessing at night until an electrician tightens it. Which poem?
questions.why: A noisy fan that keeps people guessing until it is tightened matches the poem Mystery of the Talking Fan.

questions.q: Which makes a mystery fair to the reader?
questions.why: A mystery is fair to the reader when clues are given before the solution. A surprise with no clues is not fair.

questions.q: Why might children enjoy "detective" games yet need care?
options: Imagination is fun, but suspicion can hurt real people
questions.why: Detective games use imagination and are fun, but suspicion can hurt real people. So we must be careful not to accuse anyone.

questions.q: Which device is common to both The Shed and the fan poem?
options: a mystery that turns out ordinary or uncertain
questions.why: In both The Shed and the fan poem, a mystery turns out ordinary or uncertain. That is a shared device.

courses.title: Ch 7 · The Invention of Vita-Wonk & Dad and the Cat and the Tree
courses.summary: A fantasy episode with Roald Dahl's inventor Mr Willy Wonka, who sets out to make a medicine that makes people older, and a comic poem about a dad whose rescue of a cat goes hilariously wrong.
outcomes: Learners can explain the idea behind Vita-Wonk and the humour of fantasy
Learners can describe Mr Wonka's character
Learners can retell the events of the Dad and the cat poem and explain its irony
Learners can use unit vocabulary and make words with prefixes
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

scenes.text: Mr Wonka, a brilliant and eccentric chocolate-maker, once made a medicine that made people younger.
Some people took too much of it, and now he must undo the effect.
So he decides to invent the opposite — Vita-Wonk — to make people older.

steps.title: The idea in our own words
steps.body: In this fantasy episode, Mr Wonka explains to Charlie how he set about inventing **Vita-Wonk**, a mixture meant to make people **older**.
