His plan was to collect tiny amounts from the **oldest things** in the world — very old trees and other ancient things — because, he reasons, something made from the oldest of old things should add years to a person. He describes his search with wild excitement and comic exaggeration.

steps.title: Why it is fun
steps.body:
- **Fantasy**: an impossible invention described as if it were real science.
- **Hyperbole** (exaggeration) and invented words make the language playful.
- Mr Wonka's fast, excited talk shows his character.

steps.title: Model answer 1
steps.body: Q: What is Vita-Wonk meant to do? → Make people older (the opposite of his earlier youth medicine).

steps.title: Model answer 2
steps.body: Q: Why did Mr Wonka collect things from the oldest objects? → He believed the essence of very old things would add age.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating the science as real — it is fantasy.
- Saying Vita-Wonk makes people younger.

statements.s: Vita-Wonk is meant to make people older.
Mr Wonka uses the oldest things he can find.
The story is a real science report.
The author uses exaggeration for humour.

quiz.why: Vita-Wonk is meant to make people older, which is the opposite of the usual idea of a youth potion. This is part of the story's humour.
Mr Wonka is an inventive, eccentric chocolate-maker. He is not a detective, a king or a farmer.

quiz.q: The story belongs to the genre of
quiz.why: The story is fantasy, with imaginary inventions and magical events. It is not news or a science textbook.
Exaggeration for effect is called hyperbole. A simile compares using 'like' or 'as'.

options: the oldest things in the world
quiz.why: For Vita-Wonk, Mr Wonka collected material from the oldest things in the world. This fits the idea of ageing people.

scenes.text: Mr Wonka jumps from idea to idea, waving his arms.
He invents words and makes huge claims — but he truly loves inventing.

steps.title: Mr Wonka's character
steps.body:
- **Inventive and curious**: tries things no one else would.
- **Enthusiastic**: speaks quickly, with excitement.
- **Eccentric**: strange in a lovable way.
- **Responsible in his own way**: tries to fix the problem his earlier invention caused.

steps.title: Model answer
steps.body: Q: Describe Mr Wonka in 50 words. → Mr Wonka is a brilliant, eccentric inventor bursting with energy. He talks rapidly and dramatically, exaggerating everything. He is never discouraged; when his first medicine causes trouble, he immediately sets out to invent its opposite. His curiosity and imagination make him both funny and admirable.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling him evil — he is quirky and well-meaning.
- Not giving evidence for traits.

activity.prompt: Match the trait with evidence.
pairs: Plans a medicine to make people older
Tries to undo the trouble caused by his earlier invention

options: unusual or odd in a harmless way
quiz.why: Eccentric means unusual or odd, but in a harmless way. It does not mean cruel or shy.
Mr Wonka speaks quickly and excitedly, full of ideas. He is not slow or sad.

quiz.q: Mr Wonka can best be described as
quiz.why: Mr Wonka can best be described as imaginative, as he invents wonderful things. He is not lazy or fearful.
Invented words in fantasy add playfulness and fun. They do not add sadness.
He invents Vita-Wonk to undo an earlier problem, in which something he made had gone wrong. It was not by accident or only for money.

lessons.title: Poem: Dad and the Cat and the Tree

scenes.text: The family cat is stuck high up in a tree, meowing.
Dad says, "Leave it to me!" and climbs up, ignoring Mum's warnings.
He slips, dangles and gets stuck — while the cat calmly jumps down by itself!

steps.title: What happens
steps.body: Dad confidently decides to rescue the cat, refuses help and tries one method after another (standing on things, climbing the branches). Each attempt goes wrong in a funny way. In the end, the cat simply **jumps down on its own**, and **Dad is the one stuck in the tree**.

steps.title: Devices
steps.body:
- **Situational irony**: the rescuer needs rescuing.
- **Humour** through Dad's over-confidence.
- Lively narrative style with dialogue.

steps.title: Model answer 1
steps.body: Q: What is ironic about the ending? → The cat, which needed help, gets down easily, while Dad, the rescuer, ends up stuck.

steps.title: Model answer 2
steps.body: Q: What does the poem show about Dad? → He is over-confident and stubborn but well-meaning.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying Dad rescued the cat successfully.
- Missing the irony.

activity.prompt: Order the events of the poem.
items: The cat is stuck in the tree
Dad says he will rescue it
Dad ignores warnings and climbs
Dad's attempts go wrong
The cat jumps down by itself
Dad is stuck in the tree

quiz.q: Who needed rescuing at the end?
quiz.why: At the end of the poem, Dad is the one who needs rescuing, and not the cat. That is the irony.
Dad was over-confident, so he climbed the tree to rescue the cat and got stuck. He was not scared or lazy.
The cat got down by jumping down itself, while Dad was stuck. So the cat did not need rescuing.

quiz.q: The ending is an example of
quiz.why: The ending, in which the rescuer needs rescuing, is irony. What happens is the opposite of what we expect.

quiz.q: The tone of the poem is
quiz.why: The tone of the poem is comic, since it makes us laugh at Dad's mishap.

scenes.text: Mr Wonka wants to undo, redo and reinvent!
Let us work through it step by step, then try the activity and quiz.

steps.title: Prefixes
steps.body:
A **prefix** is added to the start of a word to change its meaning.

- **un-** (not / reverse): happy → unhappy, do → undo
- **re-** (again): invent → reinvent, write → rewrite
- **dis-** (not / opposite): agree → disagree, appear → disappear
- **im-/in-** (not): possible → impossible, correct → incorrect
- **mis-** (wrongly): understand → misunderstand

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: Add a prefix: 'The trick was ___possible.' → **impossible**; 'Dad ___judged the climb.' → **misjudged**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'unpossible' ✗ → 'impossible' ✓.
- Spelling: dis + satisfied = dissatisfied (double s).

activity.prompt: Match the prefix word with its meaning.

quiz.why: The opposite of 'agree' is 'disagree'. 'Dis-' is the prefix that gives an opposite meaning here.
The prefix 're-' means again, as in 'rewrite'. It does not mean not or before.
The word 'impossible' uses 'im-' before p, which gives the meaning 'not possible'. 'Inpossible' and 'unpossible' are wrong.
'Mis-' means wrongly, so 'misjudged' means judged wrongly. Dad judged the branch badly.
In 'unhappy', 'un-' is the prefix meaning not. The root word is 'happy'.

questions.q: Vita-Wonk was meant to make people
questions.why: Vita-Wonk was meant to make people older. This is the opposite of what we might expect.

questions.q: In the poem, Dad tried to rescue
questions.why: In the poem, Dad tried to rescue a cat that was stuck in a tree.

questions.q: A prefix is added
options: at the beginning of a word
questions.why: A prefix is added at the beginning of a word, like 'un-' in 'unhappy'. A suffix is added at the end.

questions.q: Mr Wonka is
questions.why: Mr Wonka is an inventor who makes wonderful and strange things.

questions.q: The story of Vita-Wonk is
questions.why: The story of Vita-Wonk is fantasy, with magical inventions. It is not history or news.

questions.q: At the end of the poem, the cat
questions.why: At the end of the poem, the cat jumps down by itself. Dad is the one who is stuck.

questions.q: Opposite of "appear"
questions.why: The opposite of 'appear' is 'disappear'. 'Dis-' gives the opposite meaning, while 're-' in 'reappear' means again.

questions.q: Assertion (A): The poem's ending is ironic. Reason (R): The rescuer ends up needing rescue.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true: the poem's ending is ironic because the rescuer ends up needing rescue. The reason explains the irony.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Mr Wonka's invention is a real scientific medicine. Reason (R): He uses old things.
questions.why: The assertion is false: Vita-Wonk is a fantasy invention, not a real scientific medicine. The reason is true, as he uses old things, but that does not make it real.

questions.q: Dad's main flaw in the poem
questions.why: Dad's main flaw in the poem is over-confidence, which leads him into trouble. He is not cruel or afraid of cats.

questions.q: Word with prefix meaning "again"
questions.why: 'Redo' has the prefix 're-', which means again. Undo, outdo and misdo have other prefixes.

questions.q: Case: Your uncle insists on fixing the TV antenna himself, falls off the stool, and the TV starts working when your cousin simply restarts it. Which text is similar?
options: Dad and the Cat and the Tree
questions.why: Your uncle trying to fix things himself and failing while someone else simply solves it is like Dad climbing the tree and the cat getting down alone. It is comic irony.

questions.q: Case: A scientist in a cartoon invents a ray that makes plants talk. This is like Vita-Wonk because
options: it is fantasy presented as science
questions.why: A scientist inventing a ray that makes plants talk is fantasy dressed as science, like Vita-Wonk. It is not a real report.

questions.q: Which word describes Mr Wonka's language?
questions.why: Mr Wonka's language is exaggerated and playful, with invented words. It is not dull or legal.

questions.q: Correct spelling
questions.why: 'Dissatisfied' is spelt with a double s, as dis- + satisfied. The other spellings are wrong.

questions.q: What do both texts in this unit have in common?
questions.why: Both texts get their humour from unexpected results, such as Vita-Wonk's odd purpose and Dad needing rescue. They have no detective clues or tragic endings.

courses.title: Ch 8 · Fire: Friend and Foe & Meadow Surprises
courses.summary: An informative chapter on what fire needs, how it helps and harms us, and how fires are put out safely; plus a poem inviting us to look closely and discover the hidden wonders of a meadow.
outcomes: Learners can explain the three things fire needs
Learners can describe fire as a friend and as a foe
Learners can explain how fires are controlled and what to do in a fire emergency
Learners can describe the surprises in the meadow poem
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

lessons.title: What fire needs and how it helps

scenes.text: A campfire needs wood, air and a spark to start.
Cover a candle with a glass — it goes out. No oxygen!
Fire cooks our food, warms our homes and runs factories.

steps.title: Three things for fire
steps.body: Fire needs **fuel** (something that burns: wood, paper, gas), **oxygen** (from the air) and **heat** (enough to reach the **ignition temperature**). Remove any one, and the fire goes out. This is the **fire triangle**.

steps.title: Fire as a friend
steps.body:
- Cooking food and heating water
- Warmth and light
- Industries: melting metals, making glass, running engines
- Early humans used fire for protection from animals
- Discovery of fire (by rubbing stones/sticks) changed human life

steps.title: Model answer 1
steps.body: Q: Why does a candle go out when covered with a glass? → The oxygen inside is used up, and fire needs oxygen.

steps.title: Model answer 2
steps.body: Q: Name two uses of fire in industry. → Melting metals and making glass.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting heat as a requirement — fuel and air alone do not start a fire.
- Thinking fire produces oxygen; it uses oxygen.

activity.prompt: Match the fire triangle part with an example.
pairs: A spark or flame to reach ignition temperature
Clear dry leaves around a forest fire
Cover with sand or a blanket

quiz.why: Fire needs fuel, oxygen and heat. This is called the fire triangle, and removing one puts the fire out.

quiz.q: Covering a candle with a jar puts it out because
quiz.why: Covering a candle with a jar puts it out because the oxygen inside gets used up. Fire needs oxygen to burn.

quiz.q: Fire is a friend when it
quiz.why: Fire is a friend when it cooks food or gives heat and light. Burning forests and homes is fire as a foe.

quiz.q: The lowest temperature at which something catches fire
quiz.why: The lowest temperature at which a substance catches fire is its ignition temperature. Melting and boiling points are different things.
Fire uses oxygen from the air to burn. It does not use water or carbon dioxide.

lessons.title: Fire as a foe and fire safety

scenes.text: The school fire alarm rings during a drill.
Students walk quickly — not run — to the exits, covering their noses.
The teacher calls 112; the fire brigade arrives with hoses.

steps.title: Fire as a foe
steps.body: Fires can destroy homes, forests, crops and lives. Causes include careless handling of matches, candles and stoves, electrical short circuits, gas leaks, fireworks, and dry weather for forest fires.

steps.title: Putting out fires
steps.body:
- **Water** cools the burning material below its ignition temperature (not for electrical or oil fires).
- **Sand or a blanket** cuts off oxygen.
- **Fire extinguishers** (e.g. carbon dioxide) cut off oxygen; useful for electrical and oil fires.
- Fire brigades use powerful hoses, ladders and protective suits.

steps.title: If there is a fire
steps.body:
- Shout to warn others; call **112**.
- Do not use lifts; use stairs.
- Crawl low under smoke; cover nose and mouth with a wet cloth.
- If clothes catch fire: **Stop, Drop and Roll**.
- Never pour water on an electrical or oil fire.

steps.title: Model answer
steps.body: Q: Why should water not be used on an oil fire? → Oil floats on water and spreads, making the fire bigger; use sand, a lid or an extinguisher to cut off oxygen.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Running when clothes catch fire — it fans the flames; stop, drop and roll.
- Using water on electrical fires — risk of electric shock.

a.text: Oil in a frying pan catches fire in the kitchen. What do you do first?

choices.label: Switch off the stove and cover the pan with a lid

c.text: Water makes burning oil splash and spread. Try again.

choices.label: Switch off the stove and cover with a lid

b.text: The flames die down. The kitchen is smoky. What next?

choices.label: Open windows, leave the pan covered, tell an adult; call 112 if fire continues

d.text: Well done. Remember: fuel, oxygen and heat — remove one and the fire stops.

quiz.q: Water puts out fire mainly by
quiz.why: Water puts out fire mainly by cooling the burning material below its ignition temperature. It does not add fuel or oxygen.
For an electrical fire, use a CO₂ extinguisher, since water can conduct electricity and cause shock. Never throw water on it.
If your clothes catch fire, stop, drop and roll to smother the flames. Running makes the fire burn faster.
During a fire, avoid lifts, as power may fail and trap you. Use the stairs instead.
The emergency number in India is 112. 911 is used in the USA and 999 in the UK.

scenes.text: At first a meadow looks like just grass.
Look closely: a butterfly sipping nectar, a rabbit's hidden home, a bird's nest on the ground.
Blow on a dandelion and its seeds float away like tiny parachutes.

steps.title: What the poem says
steps.body: The poem invites readers to **walk gently and look carefully** in a meadow, because it is full of **surprises**: small creatures and hidden homes, insects feeding on flowers, and seeds carried by the wind. The meadow's wonders reveal themselves only to those who are patient and observant.

steps.title: Devices
steps.body:
- **Imagery** of sights, textures and movement.
- **Metaphor/personification** may describe nature playfully (e.g. seeds as parachutes).
- Gentle, inviting tone.

steps.title: Model answer
steps.body: Q: Why does the poet say we must look closely? → The meadow's living things are small and well hidden; only careful, quiet observation reveals them.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Reading the poem as just a list — focus on the message of patient observation.
- Missing the gentle tone.

activity.prompt: Meadow (or park) observation walk:
items: Walk slowly and quietly
Look under leaves and near the ground
Spot one insect feeding on a flower
Find a seed that travels by wind
Do not pluck or harm anything
Write three surprises you found

quiz.why: The poem asks us to observe carefully, so we notice the little wonders of the meadow.
Meadow surprises are hidden creatures and natural wonders that we notice when we look closely.
Dandelion seeds are light and have fluffy parts, so they travel by wind.

quiz.q: The tone of the poem is
quiz.why: The tone of the poem is gentle and inviting, asking us to look closely at the meadow.
The main device in the poem is imagery, words that help us see and feel the meadow.

scenes.text: The school wants a notice inviting students to a fire-safety demonstration.
Let us work through it step by step, then try the activity and quiz.

steps.title: Notice format
steps.body:
1. Name of the institution
2. The word **NOTICE**
3. Date
4. Heading (short title)
5. Body: what, when, where, who, why (in 50 words)
6. Name and designation of the writer

steps.title: Model notice
steps.body:
**Green Valley School, Pune**

**NOTICE**

12 November 2026

**Fire Safety Demonstration**

All students of Classes 6–8 are informed that the city fire brigade will hold a fire-safety demonstration on 18 November 2026 at 10 a.m. in the school playground. Students will learn to use extinguishers and practise evacuation. Attendance is compulsory.

Anil Kumar
Head Boy

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Missing date, time or venue.
- Writing a long letter instead of a short notice.
- Forgetting the writer's name and designation.

activity.prompt: Arrange the parts of a notice.
items: Name of the institution
NOTICE
Date
Heading
Body (what, when, where, who)
Name and designation of writer

quiz.why: A notice is short, about 50 words, so it is easy to read quickly.

quiz.q: Which is NOT needed in a notice?
quiz.why: A notice needs the date, venue and writer's name, but not a long story. It must be brief.

quiz.q: The word written at the top centre
quiz.why: The word NOTICE is written at the top centre of a notice, followed by the title.
The body of a notice tells what, when, where and who. It gives the main details briefly.

options: the writer's post, like Head Boy
quiz.why: A designation is the writer's post or position, such as Head Boy or Secretary. It is not the title or date.

questions.q: Fire needs fuel, heat and
questions.why: Fire needs fuel, heat and oxygen. This is the fire triangle.

questions.q: If clothes catch fire
questions.why: If clothes catch fire, stop, drop and roll to put out the flames. Running or fanning makes it worse.

questions.q: Emergency number
questions.why: The emergency number in India is 112.

questions.q: The meadow poem asks us to
questions.why: The meadow poem asks us to observe closely, so we notice small surprises.

questions.q: Sand puts out fire by
questions.why: Sand puts out fire by cutting off the oxygen supply. It covers the flames.

questions.q: Ignition temperature is
options: the lowest temperature at which a substance catches fire
questions.why: Ignition temperature is the lowest temperature at which a substance catches fire. It is not the boiling or freezing point.

questions.q: A notice must include
questions.why: A notice must include the date, venue and writer. A long story or poem does not belong in it.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Water should not be used on an electrical fire. Reason (R): Water conducts electricity and can cause shock.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true: water should not be used on an electrical fire because water conducts electricity and can cause a shock. The reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Fire produces oxygen. Reason (R): Fire needs oxygen to burn.
questions.why: The assertion is false: fire does not produce oxygen, it uses it. The reason is true, since fire needs oxygen to burn.

questions.q: Clearing dry leaves to stop a forest fire removes
questions.why: Clearing dry leaves removes fuel, so the forest fire has nothing to spread on. This breaks the fire triangle.

questions.q: During a fire, why crawl low?
options: Cleaner air is near the floor
questions.why: In a fire, smoke rises, so the cleaner air is near the floor. Crawling low helps you breathe.

questions.q: Case: A pan of oil catches fire. Best action?
options: Switch off the stove and cover with a lid
questions.why: For an oil fire, switch off the stove and cover the pan with a lid to cut off oxygen. Water would make burning oil spread.

questions.q: Case: A student wants to inform the school about a nature walk to a meadow. Best format?
questions.why: A notice is the right format to inform the school about an event like a nature walk. A diary or poem is not for announcing.

questions.q: Which shows fire as a friend?
questions.why: Melting metals in industry uses fire for a useful purpose, so it shows fire as a friend. Burns and fires in homes and forests are harmful.

questions.q: A CO₂ extinguisher works mainly by
questions.why: A CO₂ extinguisher works mainly by cutting off oxygen, as the gas covers the flames. It does not add heat or fuel.

questions.q: What links the two texts in this unit?
options: careful understanding of nature — fire's power and the meadow's small wonders
questions.why: Both texts ask for a careful understanding of nature: fire's power and the meadow's small wonders. They have nothing to do with cricket or kings.

courses.title: Ch 9 · A Bicycle in Good Repair & Garden Snake
courses.summary: Jerome K. Jerome's comic account of an over-eager friend who "repairs" a perfectly good bicycle into pieces, and a poem about a child's fear of a harmless garden snake.
outcomes: Learners can retell the humorous events of the bicycle story
Learners can explain how humour is created by exaggeration and irony
Learners can describe the speaker's change of feeling in Garden Snake
Learners can use phrasal verbs from the unit
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

scenes.text: The narrator plans an early bicycle ride. His friend arrives even earlier.
The friend says the front wheel "wobbles" and offers to put it right.
Soon the bicycle is in pieces on the ground, and tiny steel balls have rolled everywhere.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- The narrator's friend insists the bicycle needs attention, though it is working fine.
- He takes off the front wheel and spins it, takes the gear-case apart and loses the small **steel balls** from the bearing; they hunt for them on the ground.
- He over-tightens and loosens parts, struggles with the chain, and gets covered in oil and dirt, while being very confident and cheerful.
- By the end, the bicycle is in worse shape than before and the ride is ruined. The narrator decides that bicycles should be left to experts — or left alone!

steps.title: How the humour works
steps.body:
- **Exaggeration** of the friend's confidence and the mess he makes.
- **Irony**: 'good repair' makes it worse.
- The narrator's polite, mock-serious tone.

steps.title: Model answer 1
steps.body: Q: Why does the friend start taking the bicycle apart? → He believes the front wheel wobbles and wants to 'fix' it, though the bicycle is fine.

steps.title: Model answer 2
steps.body: Q: What is ironic about the title? → The bicycle was in good repair until the friend tried to repair it.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking the friend was an expert mechanic.
- Missing the narrator's sarcastic tone.

activity.prompt: Order the events.
items: The friend arrives early
He says the front wheel wobbles
He takes off the wheel and opens the gear-case
Steel balls from the bearing roll away
He struggles with the chain and gets covered in oil
The bicycle ends up worse than before

quiz.why: The friend thought the front wheel wobbled, and that was his excuse for taking the bicycle apart.

quiz.q: Small parts that rolled away were
quiz.why: The small parts that rolled away were steel balls from the bearing. They were very hard to find again.
The friend was over-confident, as he believed he could repair it without being a skilled mechanic.
The title is ironic, since the bicycle was not in good repair after his help. It ended up worse.

quiz.q: At the end, the bicycle was
quiz.why: At the end, the bicycle was worse than before, as the friend's repair had made things worse.

scenes.text: Everyone has met someone who "helps" by making things worse.
The narrator stays polite — and that makes it funnier.

steps.title: Characters
steps.body:
- **The friend**: enthusiastic, over-confident, careless, cheerful.
- **The narrator**: patient, polite, quietly sarcastic.

steps.title: Tone
steps.body: **Mock-serious** and **humorous** — the narrator reports disaster calmly, which increases the comedy.

steps.title: Model answer
steps.body: Q: How does the narrator show his feelings without shouting? → He describes the friend's actions in polite, exaggerated detail, letting the reader see the absurdity.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling the narrator angry and rude — he is restrained.
- Not giving examples of humour.

activity.prompt: Match.

quiz.why: The narrator's tone is mock-serious, pretending to be serious about a funny disaster. He is not furious or scared.
The friend meant to help, though the result was a mess. He did not mean harm.
Sarcasm means saying the opposite of what you mean in order to mock. It is not sincere praise.

quiz.q: Humour in the story comes from
quiz.why: The humour in the story comes from exaggeration and irony. It is not from statistics or sad events.
A lesson from the story is to leave expert jobs to experts. Taking things apart without skill can make things worse.

scenes.text: A child sees a snake slide through the garden and runs away screaming.
Mother explains: it is a harmless garden snake.
The child learns it even helps the garden — and fear turns to curiosity.

steps.title: What the poem says
steps.body: The speaker is frightened by a snake in the garden, but learns that this kind of **garden snake** is **harmless** and useful (it eats small pests). The speaker's feelings change from **fear** to **understanding** and even friendliness.

steps.title: Theme
steps.body: Fear often comes from not knowing. Learning about an animal can replace fear with respect. (Real-life note: some snakes are venomous — never touch a snake; tell an adult.)

steps.title: Model answer
steps.body: Q: How do the speaker's feelings change? → From fear on seeing the snake to calm understanding after learning it is harmless.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Concluding all snakes are harmless — the poem is about a harmless garden snake.
- Ignoring the change in feeling.

statements.s: The speaker is first afraid.
The garden snake is harmful.
Learning removes some fear.
You should pick up any snake you see.

quiz.why: The speaker's first feeling on seeing the snake is fear. He later learns it is harmless.
The garden snake is harmless. It is not venomous or imaginary.
The poem's theme is that knowledge can replace fear. Once the speaker understands the snake, he is no longer afraid.

quiz.q: In real life, on seeing a snake you should
options: keep away and tell an adult
quiz.why: In real life, keep away from a snake and tell an adult. Chasing, catching or throwing stones is dangerous.
The speaker's feelings change from fear to understanding. He learns something about the snake.

scenes.text: The friend took the bicycle apart but could not put it back together!
Let us work through it step by step, then try the activity and quiz.

steps.title: Phrasal verbs
steps.body:
A **phrasal verb** = verb + small word (preposition/adverb) with a new meaning.

- take apart = separate into pieces
- put back = return to place
- look for = search
- give up = stop trying
- turn up = arrive
- set off = start a journey
- run away = escape

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: Choose: The friend ___ (turned up / gave up) at six in the morning. → **turned up** (arrived).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Translating word by word: 'give up' does not mean 'give upwards'.
- Wrong particle: 'look after' (take care) vs 'look for' (search).

activity.prompt: Match the phrasal verb to its meaning.

quiz.q: "They looked for the steel balls" means
quiz.why: 'Looked for' means searched for. They were trying to find the steel balls.
'Give up' means stop trying. It does not mean donate or lift.

quiz.q: "The child ran away from the snake" means
quiz.why: 'Ran away from the snake' means he escaped from it. He did not chase or catch it.

quiz.q: Choose: We ___ early for the ride.
quiz.why: 'Set off' means to start a journey, so 'We set off early for the ride' fits. 'Set up' means to arrange.
'Look after' means take care of someone or something. It does not mean search.

questions.q: The friend tried to repair a
questions.why: The friend tried to repair a bicycle. That is the source of the story's comedy.

questions.q: The garden snake was
questions.why: The garden snake was harmless, so the speaker's fear was not needed.

questions.q: "Turn up" means
questions.why: 'Turn up' means arrive, often unexpectedly. It does not mean leave.

questions.q: The bicycle story is
questions.why: The bicycle story is humorous. It makes us laugh at the friend's attempt to repair it.

questions.q: The friend lost
questions.why: The friend lost the steel balls from the bearing. That is why repairing it became so hard.

questions.q: The speaker in Garden Snake first felt
questions.why: The speaker in Garden Snake first felt afraid on seeing the snake. His feelings change later.

questions.q: "Take apart" means
questions.why: 'Take apart' means to separate something into pieces. It does not mean paint or ride.

questions.q: Assertion (A): The title "A Bicycle in Good Repair" is ironic. Reason (R): The friend's repair left the bicycle worse.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true: the title is ironic because the friend's repair left the bicycle worse, not in good repair. The reason explains the irony.

questions.q: Assertion (A): The poem teaches that all snakes are harmless. Reason (R): The garden snake was harmless.
questions.why: The assertion is false: the poem does not teach that all snakes are harmless, as some snakes are dangerous. The reason is true, because the garden snake was harmless.

questions.q: The narrator's tone is
questions.why: The narrator's tone is mock-serious, with polite and calm humour about the disaster.

questions.q: Correct phrasal verb: "Don't ___; try once more!"
questions.why: 'Give up' means to stop trying, so 'Don't give up; try once more' fits. The other phrasal verbs have different meanings.

questions.q: Case: A cousin insists on "improving" your working phone settings and it stops working. Which story?
questions.why: A cousin 'improving' working settings and breaking the phone is like the friend whose repair made the bicycle worse. It is similar comedy.

questions.q: Case: A child screams at a lizard; her father explains it eats insects and is harmless; she watches it calmly. Which poem?
questions.why: A child who screams at a lizard, learns it is harmless and watches it calmly goes from fear to understanding, like Garden Snake.

questions.q: Which phrasal verb means "search"?
questions.why: 'Look for' means search. 'Look after' means take care of and 'look up to' means admire.

questions.q: How does the narrator create humour without anger?
options: polite, exaggerated description of the disaster
questions.why: The narrator creates humour without anger by describing the disaster in a polite, exaggerated way. He does not shout.

questions.q: What do both texts suggest?
options: Understanding beats blind confidence or blind fear
questions.why: Both texts suggest that understanding is better than blind confidence or blind fear. The friend was over-confident and the speaker was afraid.

courses.title: Ch 10 · The Story of Cricket
courses.summary: How cricket grew from a village game in England into a global sport: early rules, the changing bat and ball, the first Test, how Indians took up the game, and how television and money changed cricket.
outcomes: Learners can describe the origins and early rules of cricket
Learners can explain changes in equipment and formats
Learners can describe how cricket spread in India
Learners can discuss commerce and television in modern cricket
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

story.title: A game on the village green

scenes.text: Hundreds of years ago, English villagers played cricket on open commons with a curved bat.
In 1744 the first written "Laws of Cricket" appeared.
Clubs formed, and the game slowly became organised.

steps.title: Early history
steps.body: Cricket grew in England in the **16th–17th centuries** as a village game. It was played on open land ('commons'), so the length of a match could be long and boundaries vague. The **first written Laws of Cricket were drawn up in 1744**. The pitch length was set at **22 yards**. The **Marylebone Cricket Club (MCC)**, founded in **1787**, became the guardian of the Laws.

steps.title: Equipment changes
steps.body: Early bats were curved like hockey sticks because the ball was bowled along the ground. When bowlers began to pitch the ball (bounce it), bats became straight. Pads, gloves and later helmets were introduced for safety. Materials changed, but the basic willow bat stayed.

steps.title: Model answer
steps.body: Q: Why were early cricket bats curved? → The ball was rolled along the ground, so a curved bat like a hockey stick suited it.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying cricket began in India or Australia — it began in England.
- Mixing 1744 (first written laws) with 1787 (MCC founded).

activity.prompt: Arrange the early history of cricket.

events.text: First Test match, England vs Australia

quiz.why: Cricket began in England, where it developed over centuries. It later spread to other countries.
The first written laws of cricket were drawn up in 1744. 1877 was the first Test match.
A cricket pitch is 22 yards long, which is about 20 metres. So the correct answer is 22 yards.
The Marylebone Cricket Club (MCC) was founded in 1787. It later became the keeper of the Laws.

options: the ball was bowled along the ground
quiz.why: Early bats were curved because the ball was bowled along the ground. The curve helped hit a rolling ball.

story.title: Five days to a few hours

scenes.text: Test matches can last five days and still end in a draw.
One-day matches and Twenty20 games finish in a day or an evening.
Shorter formats suit television and big crowds.

steps.title: Formats
steps.body:
- **Test cricket**: the first Test was played between **England and Australia in 1877** (Melbourne). Tests can last up to five days.
- **One-day internationals (ODIs)**: limited overs; the first World Cup was held in **1975**.
- **Twenty20 (T20)**: 20 overs per side; very fast and popular.

steps.title: Unusual features of cricket
steps.body:
- A Test can end in a **draw** after five days.
- The **size of the ground** is not fixed (unlike football fields), only the pitch length.

steps.title: Model answer
steps.body: Q: Why are shorter formats popular? → They finish quickly, are exciting, and suit television schedules and audiences.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking the size of the cricket field is fixed by rule like a football pitch.
- Mixing the first Test (1877) with the first World Cup (1975).

activity.prompt: Test cricket, ODI or T20?

items.text: Can end in a draw after days of play

quiz.why: The first Test match was played in 1877 between England and Australia. India's first Test was in 1932.
T20 cricket has 20 overs per side. It is much shorter than a Test or a 50-over match.

quiz.q: Test matches can end in a
quiz.why: Test matches can end in a draw, if time runs out before a result. This is unusual among sports.

quiz.q: The size of a cricket ground is
quiz.why: The size of a cricket ground is not fixed exactly, but the pitch is always 22 yards. This is unlike football.
The first Cricket World Cup was held in 1975. India won in 1983.

scenes.text: In 19th-century Bombay, the Parsi community were the first Indians to take up cricket seriously.
A Parsi team toured England in 1886.
Much later, in 1983, India won the World Cup!

steps.title: How the game spread
steps.body:
- The **Parsis** in Bombay founded the **Oriental Cricket Club in 1848** — the first Indian cricket club.
- A **Parsi team toured England in 1886**.
- Other communities formed teams; tournaments were often organised by community (later criticised as divisive).
- **India played its first Test in 1932** (at Lord's, England).

steps.title: Modern Indian cricket
steps.body:
- India won the **1983 World Cup** under **Kapil Dev**, which made one-day cricket hugely popular.
- India also won the first T20 World Cup in **2007**.
- Today India is a centre of world cricket, with large audiences and commercial power.

steps.title: Model answer
steps.body: Q: Which community first took up cricket in India and where? → The Parsis, in Bombay (Mumbai); they founded the Oriental Cricket Club in 1848.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing up 1932 (first Test) and 1983 (World Cup win).
- Thinking Indians played cricket before the British arrived.

activity.prompt: Indian cricket timeline.

events.text: Oriental Cricket Club founded by Parsis in Bombay
India wins the first T20 World Cup

quiz.q: First Indian community to take up cricket
quiz.why: The Parsis were the first Indian community to take up cricket, in Bombay.
The Oriental Cricket Club, the first Indian cricket club, was founded in 1848 by the Parsis.
India played its first Test in 1932, at Lord's in England.

quiz.q: India won the World Cup in
quiz.why: India won the Cricket World Cup in 1983, under Kapil Dev.
A Parsi team toured England in 1886. It was the first Indian cricket tour abroad.

lessons.title: Commerce, television and the modern game

scenes.text: Television brought cricket into every home.
Companies pay huge amounts to broadcast matches and to sponsor players.
Players became celebrities; the game's centre shifted towards South Asia.

steps.title: Commerce and TV
steps.body: From the 1970s, **television** and **commercial sponsorship** transformed cricket. Broadcasters paid cricket boards for rights; advertisers paid to reach huge audiences. Players earned more and became stars. Coloured clothing, white balls, floodlights and shorter formats were introduced partly to suit TV viewers.

steps.title: Effects
steps.body:
- Cricket spread to smaller towns and new fans.
- More money for boards and players.
- Concerns: pressure of too many matches, commercial interests over sport.

steps.title: Model answer
steps.body: Q: How did television change cricket? → It took matches to millions, attracted advertisers and sponsors, made players famous, and encouraged changes like coloured clothes and day–night matches.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking TV changed only viewing — it changed rules, formats and money.
- Ignoring disadvantages.

activity.prompt: Interview an elder: how did they follow cricket when they were your age — radio, TV, newspapers? What has changed?
activity.hint: Note down three changes and one thing that has stayed the same.

options: companies paying to be linked with a sport
quiz.why: Commercial sponsorship means companies pay to be linked with a sport, such as by putting their names on kits. It is not free tickets.
Television helped cricket by reaching millions of viewers and bringing in money. It increased the sport's popularity.
Coloured clothing and floodlights were introduced partly for TV, so the game could be shown clearly in the evening.

options: too many matches and money pressure
quiz.why: A concern about commercial cricket is that there are too many matches and pressure from money. It is not a lack of fans or sponsors.
Cricket's centre has shifted towards South Asia, where the largest audiences and money are.

questions.q: Cricket originated in
questions.why: Cricket began in England and then spread to other countries.

questions.q: First written Laws of Cricket
questions.why: The first written Laws of Cricket were made in 1744.

questions.q: Pitch length
questions.why: The cricket pitch is 22 yards long.

questions.q: India won the World Cup in
questions.why: India won the World Cup in 1983, under Kapil Dev.

questions.q: First Test match
questions.why: The first Test match was in 1877, between England and Australia.

questions.q: First Indian cricket club
questions.why: The Oriental Cricket Club, founded in 1848 by the Parsis, was the first Indian cricket club.

questions.q: T20 means
questions.why: T20 means 20 overs per side.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Early bats were curved. Reason (R): The ball was bowled along the ground.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true: early bats were curved because the ball was bowled along the ground. The reason explains the shape.

questions.q: Assertion (A): The size of a cricket ground is fixed exactly by the Laws. Reason (R): The pitch is 22 yards long.
questions.why: The assertion is false: the Laws fix the pitch at 22 yards, but not the exact size of the ground. The reason is true.

questions.q: MCC stands for
questions.why: MCC stands for Marylebone Cricket Club, founded in 1787 in London.

questions.q: India's first Test was played in
questions.why: India played its first Test in 1932, at Lord's. 1947 was the year of Independence.

questions.q: Case: A board introduces floodlit evening matches with coloured kits to attract more viewers. This reflects
options: the influence of television and commerce
questions.why: Floodlit evening matches and coloured kits to attract viewers reflect the influence of television and commerce. They are not old features.

questions.q: Case: A student says, "Cricket was invented by the Parsis." Correct?
options: No — it began in England; Parsis were the first Indians to take it up
questions.why: Cricket did not begin with the Parsis. It began in England, and the Parsis were the first Indians to take it up.

questions.q: Which is unusual about Test cricket compared with most sports?
options: A match can last days and still end in a draw
questions.why: A Test match can last for days and still end in a draw, which is unusual among sports.

questions.q: Arrange: India wins World Cup; first Test; MCC founded; first written laws
options: World Cup → first Test → MCC → laws
first written laws (1744) → MCC (1787) → first Test (1877) → India wins World Cup (1983)
first Test → laws → MCC → World Cup
MCC → laws → World Cup → first Test
questions.why: In order: first written laws (1744), MCC founded (1787), first Test (1877) and India's World Cup win (1983).

questions.q: Give one advantage and one concern of commercial cricket.
options: More money and reach; but heavy schedules and commercial pressure
questions.why: Commercial cricket brings more money and reach, but it can also mean heavy schedules and commercial pressure. This answer gives both sides.

courses.title: Grammar for Class 7
courses.summary: The grammar a Class 7 student needs: parts of speech, tenses, subject–verb agreement, active and passive voice basics, direct and reported speech, articles and prepositions, and sentence types — with solved examples and practice.
outcomes: Learners can identify parts of speech in sentences
Learners can use present, past and future tenses correctly
Learners can apply subject–verb agreement rules
Learners can change simple sentences from active to passive voice and direct to reported speech

lessons.title: Parts of speech and sentence types

scenes.text: "The clever jester quickly crossed the busy market." Sana labels each word.
Article, adjective, noun, adverb, verb, article, adjective, noun!

steps.title: Eight parts of speech
steps.body:
- **Noun**: name of a person, place, thing, idea (king, Delhi, courage)
- **Pronoun**: replaces a noun (he, they, it, himself)
- **Adjective**: describes a noun (clever, old)
- **Verb**: action or state (run, is)
- **Adverb**: describes a verb/adjective/adverb (quickly, very)
- **Preposition**: shows relation (in, on, under, between)
- **Conjunction**: joins (and, but, because)
- **Interjection**: shows sudden feeling (Oh! Hurray!)

steps.title: Sentence types
steps.body:
- **Declarative** (statement): The fan is noisy.
- **Interrogative** (question): Is the fan noisy?
- **Imperative** (command/request): Switch off the fan.
- **Exclamatory**: What a noisy fan!

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Identify: 'Wow! Meena and Ravi happily fed the tiny kitten.' → Wow (interjection), Meena/Ravi/kitten (nouns), and (conjunction), happily (adverb), fed (verb), the (article/determiner), tiny (adjective).

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Type: 'How beautiful the cherry trees look!' → **exclamatory**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- The same word can be different parts of speech: 'fast' (adjective: a fast car; adverb: run fast).
- Missing the full stop or question mark that shows sentence type.

activity.prompt: Which part of speech?

quiz.q: In "The old bootmaker worked carefully", "carefully" is
quiz.why: 'Carefully' tells how he worked, so it is an adverb. It describes the verb 'worked'.
'Between' shows a relation of position, so it is a preposition. It is not a verb or a conjunction.
'Hurray!' expresses sudden feeling, so it is an interjection.
'Close the door.' gives a command, so it is imperative.
In 'a fast train', 'fast' describes the noun 'train', so it is an adjective.

scenes.text: Yesterday the king visited the hermit. Today the hermit is digging. Tomorrow the king will return.
Let us work through it step by step, then try the activity and quiz.

steps.title: The main tenses
steps.body:
- **Simple present**: habits/facts — She plays cricket. Water boils at 100 °C.
- **Present continuous**: now — She is playing.
- **Present perfect**: past action linked to now — She has played twice this week.
- **Simple past**: finished past — She played yesterday.
- **Past continuous**: ongoing in past — She was playing when it rained.
- **Past perfect**: earlier past — She had played before lunch.
- **Simple future**: She will play tomorrow.
- **Future continuous**: She will be playing at 4 p.m.

steps.title: Signal words
steps.body:
- always, usually, every day → simple present
- now, at the moment → present continuous
- already, just, ever, yet, since, for → present perfect
- yesterday, ago, last year → simple past
- tomorrow, next week → future

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Fill: Mr Gessler ___ (make) boots for forty years when the narrator met him. → **had been making / had made** (past perfect).

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Correct: 'I have seen him yesterday.' → **I saw him yesterday.** (simple past with 'yesterday').

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Present perfect with a past time word ('has gone yesterday') ✗.
- Missing -s in third person singular: 'He play' ✗ → 'He plays' ✓.

activity.prompt: Use the correct tense.
activity.text: The squirrel ___ (sit) on the branch right now. Gopal ___ (win) the challenge yesterday. We ___ (visit) the meadow tomorrow.

quiz.why: 'She has finished her work' uses has + past participle, which is present perfect. It links the past to the present.
With 'he' in the simple present, the verb takes -s or -es: 'goes'. 'Go' is for I/you/we/they.

quiz.q: "I was reading when the bell rang." Tense of "was reading"
quiz.why: 'Was reading' is was + -ing, which is past continuous. It shows an action in progress in the past.
'Already' is a signal word for the present perfect, as it links to now. 'Ago' and 'yesterday' go with simple past.
The simple future is 'will' plus the base verb: 'They will play'.

scenes.text: The dog barks. The dogs bark.
Each of the boys ___ (has/have) a bicycle? → has!

steps.title: Rules
steps.body:
- Singular subject → singular verb: The boy **runs**.
- Plural subject → plural verb: The boys **run**.
- **Each, every, either, neither, everyone, somebody** → singular: Everyone **is** here.
- Two subjects joined by **and** → plural: Ravi and Meena **are** cousins.
- With **either…or / neither…nor**, the verb agrees with the nearer subject: Neither the teacher nor the students **were** late.
- Words between subject and verb do not change it: The box of chocolates **is** on the table.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: The quality of these boots ___ excellent. → **is** (subject: quality).

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Neither Gopal nor the courtiers ___ worried. → **were** (nearer subject: courtiers).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Matching the verb with the nearest noun instead of the real subject: 'The box of pens are' ✗.
- 'Everyone have' ✗ → 'Everyone has' ✓.

activity.prompt: Match subject with the correct verb.
pairs: Neither the boys nor the girl

quiz.why: 'Everyone' is singular, so it takes 'is': 'Everyone is invited.' 'Are' and 'were' are wrong.
The subject is 'list', which is singular, and not 'names'. So the verb is 'is': 'The list of names is long.'
'My friends and I' is a plural subject, so it takes 'are'. 'Am' goes only with 'I' alone.

quiz.q: "Either the cat or the dogs ___ the milk."
quiz.why: With 'either... or', the verb agrees with the nearer subject, 'dogs', which is plural. So 'drink' is correct.
Mathematics, though it ends in -s, is treated as singular, so it takes 'is'. 'Mathematics is my favourite subject.'

lessons.title: Active and passive voice; direct and reported speech

scenes.text: Active: The friend broke the bicycle.
Passive: The bicycle was broken by the friend.

steps.title: Active and passive (basics)
steps.body:
In the **active** voice, the subject does the action. In the **passive**, the subject receives the action.

Passive = object becomes subject + form of **be** + **past participle** (+ by + doer).

- Simple present: They make boots. → Boots **are made** (by them).
- Simple past: The king asked a question. → A question **was asked** by the king.
- Future: She will write a letter. → A letter **will be written** by her.

Use passive when the doer is unknown or less important: 'The shop was closed.'

steps.title: Direct and reported speech (review)
steps.body:
- Statements: He said, "I am ready." → He said that he was ready.
- Questions (yes/no): She asked, "Are you coming?" → She asked **if/whether** I was coming.
- Wh-questions: He asked, "Where do you live?" → He asked where I lived.
- Commands: The teacher said, "Sit down." → The teacher **told** us **to sit** down.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Passive: 'Mr Gessler made these boots.' → These boots **were made** by Mr Gessler.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Reported: Mother said, "Don't touch the snake." → Mother told me **not to touch** the snake.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Wrong participle: 'was broke' ✗ → 'was broken' ✓.
- Keeping question marks and question word order in reported questions.

activity.prompt: Active or passive?

items.text: The fish was carried by the jester.

quiz.q: Passive of "The cat drank the milk."
options: The cat was drunk the milk.
The milk is drink by the cat.
The milk was drunk by the cat.
quiz.why: In the passive, the object 'milk' becomes the subject with 'was drunk' (be + past participle), and the doer follows 'by'. So 'The milk was drunk by the cat.'

quiz.q: Passive of "They will build a school."
options: A school is built by them.
They will be built a school.
A school will be built by them.
quiz.why: The future passive is 'will be' plus the past participle: 'A school will be built by them.' The other options are wrong in form.

options: She asked if was I hungry.
She asked if I was hungry.
quiz.why: In a reported yes/no question, we use 'if' or 'whether' and the statement order, with the tense shifted back. So 'She asked if I was hungry.'

options: He told that close the window.
He told me to close the window.
quiz.why: A reported command uses 'told' + object + 'to' + verb. So 'He told me to close the window.'
'Write' is irregular: write, wrote, written. The past participle is 'written'.

questions.q: "Quickly" is
questions.why: 'Quickly' tells how something is done, so it is an adverb of manner.

questions.q: "What a lovely day!" is
questions.why: 'What a lovely day!' expresses strong feeling, so it is an exclamatory sentence.

questions.q: Simple past of "go"
questions.why: 'Go' is irregular, and its simple past is 'went'. 'Gone' is the past participle.

questions.q: "Each of the girls ___ a prize."
questions.why: 'Each' is singular, so it takes 'gets': 'Each of the girls gets a prize.' 'Get' is for plural subjects.

questions.q: Present perfect of "She eats"
questions.why: The present perfect is 'has/have' plus the past participle. So 'She eats' becomes 'She has eaten.'

questions.q: Passive of "Ravi wrote a poem."
options: A poem is written by Ravi.
A poem was written by Ravi.
questions.why: The passive of 'Ravi wrote a poem' is 'A poem was written by Ravi', with 'was' and the past participle 'written'.

questions.q: "Under" in "under the tree" is a
questions.why: 'Under' shows the position of something in relation to a tree, so it is a preposition.

questions.q: Assertion (A): "Everyone are happy" is correct. Reason (R): "Everyone" refers to many people.
questions.why: The assertion is false: 'Everyone' takes a singular verb, so it should be 'Everyone is happy'. The reason is true, since 'everyone' means many people, but it is grammatically singular.

questions.q: Assertion (A): "I have seen him yesterday" is incorrect. Reason (R): The present perfect is not used with a finished past time like "yesterday".
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true: 'I have seen him yesterday' is wrong because present perfect is not used with a finished time like 'yesterday'. We should say 'I saw him yesterday.'

questions.q: Reported: Ravi said, "I will come."
options: Ravi said that he would come.
Ravi said that I will come.
questions.why: In reported speech, 'I will come' becomes 'he would come' and 'I' becomes 'he'. So 'Ravi said that he would come.'

questions.q: "Neither the teacher nor the students ___ ready."
questions.why: With 'neither... nor', the verb agrees with the nearer subject, 'students', which is plural. So 'were' is right.

questions.q: Identify the error: "The box of pencils are on the desk."
questions.why: The subject is 'box', which is singular, not 'pencils'. So 'are' should be 'is'.

questions.q: Change to passive: "The gardener waters the plants every day."
options: The plants were watered by the gardener.
The plants are watered by the gardener every day.
questions.why: The present passive uses 'are' plus the past participle: 'The plants are watered by the gardener every day.' It stays in the present tense.

questions.q: Reported: The teacher asked, "Who broke the window?"
options: The teacher asked who broke the window?
The teacher asked that who broke the window.
The teacher asked who had broken the window.
The teacher told to break the window.
questions.why: A reported wh-question keeps the question word, uses statement order, and shifts the tense back. 'Broke' becomes 'had broken': 'The teacher asked who had broken the window.'

questions.q: Choose the correct sentence.
options: She had left before I arrived.
She has left before I arrived yesterday.
questions.why: The past perfect 'had left' shows an action that happened before another past action ('arrived'). So 'She had left before I arrived.'

questions.q: Which sentence uses the passive appropriately (doer unknown)?
options: My bicycle was stolen last night.
questions.why: The passive is used when the doer is unknown, as in 'My bicycle was stolen last night.' The other sentences are ungrammatical or illogical.

courses.title: Writing Skills for Class 7
courses.summary: Practical writing: notices and messages, paragraphs and descriptions, informal and formal letters, diary entries and stories — formats, model answers, checklists and common mistakes.
outcomes: Learners can write notices and messages in the correct format
Learners can write well-organised paragraphs and descriptions
Learners can write informal and formal letters
Learners can write diary entries and short stories

scenes.text: Aunt calls while Mum is out: "Tell her I'll come on Sunday at 4."
Ria writes a short, clear message and sticks it on the fridge.

steps.title: Message format
steps.body:
- Date and time
- Salutation (Mum,)
- Body: who called, what was said, any action needed (30–50 words, reported speech)
- Your name

steps.title: Model message
steps.body:
12 November, 11 a.m.

Mum,

Meena Aunty called. She will visit us on Sunday at 4 p.m. with Raju. She asked you to call her back about the wedding shopping.

Ria

steps.title: Notice (review)
steps.body: Institution · NOTICE · date · heading · body (what, when, where, who) · writer's name and designation. Keep to about 50 words; use formal language.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Copying the caller's exact words (use reported speech).
- Missing time/date or the writer's name.

activity.prompt: Order the parts of a message.
items: Date and time
Salutation
Who called and what they said
Action needed
Your name

quiz.why: A message should be short and clear, so the reader gets the point quickly. It should include names but need not be poetic.
Messages usually use reported speech, as they tell what someone else said. They do not use only direct speech.
A notice is written in formal language. Slang, code and emojis do not suit it.
A notice is concise, about 50 words. It should not be as long as 500 words.

quiz.q: Which is essential in a notice?
quiz.why: The date and venue are essential in a notice, so people know when and where. A joke or poem is not needed.

scenes.text: Topic: "A tree I love". Sana writes one main sentence, then supporting details, then a closing line.
Let us work through it step by step, then try the activity and quiz.

steps.title: Paragraph structure
steps.body:
1. **Topic sentence**: the main idea.
2. **Supporting sentences**: details, examples, reasons.
3. **Concluding sentence**: sums up or gives a feeling.

Use linking words: first, also, moreover, however, finally.

steps.title: Model paragraph (describing a place)
steps.body: "The neem tree outside our school is my favourite place. Its wide branches spread a cool shade where we eat lunch. In the morning, parrots and mynas chatter among its leaves, and in summer tiny white flowers fill the air with a bitter-sweet smell. Our science teacher says its leaves protect clothes from insects. Whenever I feel tired, I sit under it and feel calm again."

steps.title: Use the senses
steps.body: Describe sights, sounds, smells, textures and tastes to make writing vivid.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Several unrelated ideas in one paragraph.
- No topic sentence.

activity.prompt: Paragraph checklist:
items: One clear topic sentence
Three or more supporting details
At least two senses used
Linking words
A concluding sentence
Spelling and punctuation checked

quiz.q: The first sentence of a paragraph is the
quiz.why: The first sentence of a paragraph is usually the topic sentence, which states the main idea.
A paragraph should have one main idea, which all its sentences support. Many unrelated ideas confuse the reader.
'However' is a linking word for contrast. 'And' and 'also' add information and 'firstly' shows order.
Vivid descriptions use the senses: what we see, hear, smell, taste and feel. They need adjectives and details.
The last sentence usually sums up the paragraph. It should not start a new topic.

scenes.text: Ravi writes to his cousin about his school trip — friendly and chatty.
He also writes to the Principal requesting a sports period — polite and formal.

steps.title: Informal letter
steps.body: Sender's address · date · salutation (Dear Mridu,) · body (friendly tone, 3 paragraphs) · closing (Yours lovingly / With love,) · name.

steps.title: Formal letter
steps.body: Sender's address · date · receiver's designation and address · **Subject** line · salutation (Sir/Madam,) · body (purpose, details, request) · closing (Yours sincerely / Yours faithfully,) · name (and class).

steps.title: Model formal letter
steps.body:
14, Gandhi Nagar, Jaipur

12 November 2026

The Principal
Sunrise Public School, Jaipur

Subject: Request for a library period

Sir,

I am a student of Class 7B. Many of us wish to read more books but have no time during school. I request you to kindly allot one library period every week for our class. This will improve our reading and writing.

Thank you.

Yours sincerely,
Aman Verma
Class 7B

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Missing the subject line in formal letters.
- Using slang or emojis in formal letters.
- Mixing informal closings ('Love') in formal letters.

activity.prompt: Informal or formal letter feature?

quiz.why: A formal letter must have a subject line that tells what the letter is about. Slang, jokes and emojis do not belong.
A formal letter is addressed 'Sir/Madam'. 'Dear Bestie', 'Hi buddy' and 'Yo' are too casual.

quiz.q: An informal letter is written to
quiz.why: An informal letter is written to friends and family. A company, Mayor or Principal would get a formal letter.
'Yours sincerely' is a formal closing. 'Cheers', 'Bye!' and 'Lots of love' are informal.

quiz.q: Body of a formal letter states
quiz.why: The body of a formal letter states the purpose, gives the details and makes the request. Jokes and greetings alone are not enough.

scenes.text: After the school trip, Meena writes in her diary about the best and worst moments.
Then she turns a funny moment into a short story for the class magazine.

steps.title: Diary entry
steps.body: Date, day, time (optional) · **Dear Diary** · personal feelings in the first person, usually past tense for events · end with a reflection · name/initial (optional). About 100 words.

steps.title: Story writing
steps.body: Beginning (characters, setting) → problem → events → climax → solution → ending (moral or feeling). Use dialogue, past tense, vivid verbs. Give a title.

steps.title: Model diary entry
steps.body:
Saturday, 14 November 2026, 9 p.m.

Dear Diary,

Today was our fire-safety drill. When the alarm rang, my heart jumped, but I remembered to walk, not run. The fire officer showed us how to use an extinguisher, and I even tried it! I felt proud and a little nervous. I've decided to check our kitchen at home tomorrow. Safety first!

Meena

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing a diary like a report without feelings.
- Stories with no problem or ending.

activity.prompt: Write a diary entry (about 100 words) about a day when you helped someone, like the king in "Three Questions".
activity.hint: Include what happened, how you felt, and what you learnt.

quiz.q: A diary entry is written in the
quiz.why: A diary entry is personal, so it is written in the first person, using 'I'.
A diary entry begins with the date and 'Dear Diary'. A subject line is for formal letters.
A story needs a problem and a solution, which give it a plot. Without them it is just description.
Diary entries focus on the writer's feelings and experiences. They are not advertisements or notices.

quiz.q: Stories are usually written in the
quiz.why: Stories are usually told in the past tense, as the events have already happened.

questions.q: A message should include
options: date, time, who called, what was said
questions.why: A message includes the date, time, who called and what was said, so the person who reads it knows everything. A notice heading or subject line is not needed.

questions.q: A topic sentence
questions.why: A topic sentence states the main idea of the paragraph. It usually comes first.

questions.q: Formal letter closing
questions.why: 'Yours sincerely' is a formal closing. 'Love' and 'XOXO' are for close people.

questions.q: A diary entry is
questions.why: A diary entry is personal, as it records the writer's own thoughts and feelings.

questions.q: Which is NOT part of a notice?
questions.why: 'Dear Diary' belongs in a diary entry, not a notice. A notice has a heading, date and the writer's designation.

questions.q: Subject line appears in
questions.why: A subject line appears in formal letters. Poems, diary entries and informal letters do not need one.

questions.q: Linking word to add information
questions.why: 'Moreover' adds more information. 'However', 'but' and 'although' show contrast.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Messages are written in reported speech. Reason (R): They report what someone else said.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true: messages use reported speech because they report what someone else said. The reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Formal letters may use slang to sound friendly. Reason (R): Formal letters are written to officials.
questions.why: The assertion is false: formal letters should not use slang. The reason is true, since they are written to officials, which is why they must be formal.

questions.q: Best order of a story
questions.why: A story follows the order: beginning, problem, climax, solution and ending. Other orders confuse the plot.

questions.q: A notice is usually about
questions.why: A notice is usually about 50 words, so it is short enough to read quickly.

questions.q: Case: You must inform all Class 7 students about a book fair. Format?
questions.why: To tell all Class 7 students about a book fair, write a notice, as it is public and gives key details. A message to Mum or an informal letter is private.

questions.q: Case: You want to ask the Municipal Commissioner to repair a broken streetlight. Format?
questions.why: To ask the Municipal Commissioner for a repair, write a formal letter, an official request. A poem or story would not do this.

questions.q: Which sentence suits a formal letter?
options: I request you to kindly look into the matter.
questions.why: 'I request you to kindly look into the matter' is polite and formal. The other lines are slang or rude.

questions.q: Which improves a description most?
options: using sensory details and vivid verbs
questions.why: Sensory details and vivid verbs make a description lively. Repeating 'nice' or unrelated facts weakens it.

questions.q: A good diary entry ends with
questions.why: A good diary entry ends with a reflection or feeling. 'Yours faithfully' and a subject line belong to formal letters.

courses.title: Revision & Practice · Class 7 English
courses.summary: Revise every Honeycomb unit in one place — characters, themes, poems and devices — plus a grammar and writing quick-sheet, and a full mixed mock paper with reading, literature, grammar and writing questions.
outcomes: Learners can recall characters, events and themes of every unit
Learners can identify poetic devices in the poems
Learners can apply key grammar rules quickly
Learners can attempt a mixed English mock paper

scenes.text: Neha makes a table: unit, main character, one event, one theme.
She reads it aloud every evening for a week.

steps.title: Prose
steps.body:
- **Three Questions**: king, hermit, wounded enemy — now is the important time; the person with you; do good.
- **A Gift of Chappals**: children's kindness to a kitten and a barefoot beggar; giving away the music master's chappals — kindness with responsibility.
- **Gopal and the Hilsa Fish**: jester wins the king's challenge by a strange disguise — clever thinking.
- **The Ashes That Made Trees Bloom**: kind farmer, faithful dog, greedy neighbours; gold → mortar → ashes → blooming trees — kindness rewarded, greed punished.
- **Quality**: the Gessler brothers' perfect boots; big firms and advertising; death by slow starvation — integrity.
- **Expert Detectives**: children suspect a neighbour; first impressions mislead — empathy.
- **Vita-Wonk**: Mr Wonka's fantasy invention to make people older — imagination.
- **Fire: Friend and Foe**: fuel, oxygen, heat; uses and dangers; safety.
- **A Bicycle in Good Repair**: over-confident friend ruins a working bicycle — irony and humour.
- **The Story of Cricket**: 1744 laws, 22-yard pitch, 1877 first Test, Parsis 1848, India's first Test 1932, World Cup win 1983, TV and commerce.

steps.title: Poems and devices
steps.body:
- The Squirrel — metaphor (question-mark tail, grey overcoat), personification
- The Rebel — repetition, contrast
- The Shed — mystery, repetition ('one of these days')
- Chivvy — imperatives, irony
- Trees — personification, rhyming couplets, imagery
- Mystery of the Talking Fan — personification, humour
- Dad and the Cat and the Tree — situational irony
- Meadow Surprises — imagery, observation
- Garden Snake — fear to understanding

steps.title: Model answer
steps.body:
Q: Compare the endings of 'Quality' and 'Dad and the Cat and the Tree'.

A: 'Quality' ends tragically — Mr Gessler dies, defeated by commerce despite his skill. The poem ends comically — Dad, the would-be rescuer, is stuck while the cat walks free. Both endings are ironic: effort and skill do not bring the expected result.

steps.title: Frequent slips
steps.body:
- Calling 'question mark for tail' a simile.
- Saying Gopal hid the fish.
- Mixing up which Gessler brother died first (the elder).

activity.prompt: Match text and theme.
pairs: Live in the present; do good
The Ashes That Made Trees Bloom
Too many orders, no room to think

quiz.q: Who said the most important time is now?
quiz.why: In 'Three Questions', the hermit says the most important time is now. Gopal, Mr Wonka and Mr Gessler are from other texts.
The last line of 'Chivvy' is ironic, as it turns the poem's meaning around. It is not just rhyme or alliteration.
In 'Quality', the Gesslers made boots. They were bootmakers.
Fire needs fuel, oxygen and heat. This is the fire triangle.

quiz.q: India won the World Cup in
quiz.why: India won the Cricket World Cup in 1983. 1975 was the first World Cup and 1932 India's first Test.

scenes.text: Ravi writes ten grammar rules on a card and keeps it in his pencil box.
Let us work through it step by step, then try the activity and quiz.

steps.title: Grammar rules
steps.body:
1. Third person singular present → -s (She plays).
2. Present perfect not with 'yesterday/ago'.
3. Each/every/everyone → singular verb.
4. Comparative for two, superlative for three or more; no 'more bigger'.
5. Passive: be + past participle.
6. Reported speech: backshift tense, change pronouns, no question order.
7. Commands reported with told/asked + to.
8. Adverbs of manner often end in -ly.
9. Imperatives begin with the verb.
10. Prefixes un-, re-, dis-, im-, mis- change meaning.

steps.title: Writing formats
steps.body:
- **Notice**: institution, NOTICE, date, heading, body (50 words), name + designation
- **Message**: date/time, salutation, body in reported speech, name
- **Formal letter**: addresses, date, subject, Sir/Madam, body, Yours sincerely
- **Informal letter**: address, date, Dear…, friendly body, with love
- **Diary**: date, Dear Diary, feelings, reflection
- **Story**: title, beginning, problem, climax, solution, ending

steps.title: Solved mixed example
steps.body: Correct: 'Everyone have finished their work yesterday, so the teacher said us go home.' → **Everyone had finished their work, so the teacher told us to go home.**

steps.title: Frequent slips
steps.body:
- 'He don't' ✗ → 'He doesn't' ✓.
- 'Yours faithfully' vs 'Yours sincerely' — follow your school's convention; both are formal.

activity.prompt: Correct the verbs.
activity.text: She ___ (go) to school every day. The boots ___ (make) by hand. Each child ___ (have) a book.

quiz.why: The passive of 'They sell fruit' is 'Fruit is sold by them', with 'is' + past participle. The tense stays the present.
The comparative of 'bad' is 'worse'. 'Worst' is the superlative and 'badder' is wrong.

options: He said that he was tired.
quiz.why: In reported speech, 'I am tired' becomes 'he was tired', with the tense shifted back and the pronoun changed. So 'He said that he was tired.'
A formal letter needs a subject line. 'Dear Diary' and emojis do not belong in it.
The prefix 'im-' gives 'not' before p, as in 'impossible' (not possible). Dis- and mis- have other meanings.

scenes.text: Read the passage below and answer the questions in the quiz.
Let us work through it step by step, then try the activity and quiz.

steps.title: Passage
steps.body: Every winter, flocks of bar-headed geese fly over the Himalayas to reach the lakes of India. They travel thousands of kilometres, often at great heights where the air is thin and cold. Scientists have found that these birds breathe deeply and their blood carries oxygen efficiently, which helps them survive the journey. Along the way they rest at wetlands, where they feed and regain strength. Sadly, many wetlands are being drained for buildings and farms. If their resting places disappear, the geese may not be able to complete their long migration.

steps.title: How to answer
steps.body:
- Read the questions first, then the passage.
- Underline key words.
- Answer in your own words; use the passage for evidence.
- For vocabulary questions, use context clues.

steps.title: Model answer
steps.body: Q: Why are wetlands important for the geese? → They are resting places where the birds feed and regain strength during migration.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Answering from general knowledge instead of the passage.
- Copying long chunks instead of answering precisely.

statements.s: Bar-headed geese fly over the Himalayas.
The air at great heights is thick and warm.
Wetlands are being drained.
Geese never rest during migration.

quiz.q: Why do the geese fly to India?
options: to reach its lakes in winter
quiz.why: The geese fly to India to reach its lakes in winter, where it is warm and they find food. They do not seek deserts or escape tigers.

quiz.q: What helps them survive at heights?
options: deep breathing and efficient oxygen in blood
quiz.why: The passage says deep breathing and efficient use of oxygen in the blood help them survive at great heights. Warm air is not available there.
'Migration' here means the seasonal travel of animals from one place to another.
The main threat mentioned is the loss of wetlands, where the geese rest and feed. It is not storms or hunters.

options: Long Journey of the Bar-headed Geese
quiz.why: 'Long Journey of the Bar-headed Geese' matches the passage's main idea. The other titles are about other topics.

questions.q: In "Three Questions", the king helped the hermit by
questions.why: In 'Three Questions', the king helped the hermit by digging the flower beds. He did this to help the old man.

questions.q: The squirrel's tail is compared to
questions.why: The squirrel's tail is compared to a question mark, because of its curve. This is a metaphor.

questions.q: Gopal was a
questions.why: Gopal was a court jester, a clever entertainer of the king.

questions.q: "Chivvy" means
questions.why: 'Chivvy' means to nag, to tell someone repeatedly to do something.

questions.q: Mr Gessler died of
questions.why: In 'Quality', Mr Gessler died of slow starvation, as he had too few customers.

questions.q: Passive of "Dad climbed the tree."
options: Dad was climbed by the tree.
The tree was climbed by Dad.
The tree is climb by Dad.
questions.why: In the passive, 'the tree' becomes the subject: 'The tree was climbed by Dad.' The tense stays past.

questions.q: Format with "Subject:" line
questions.why: A 'Subject:' line is part of a formal letter. Stories, diary entries and messages do not have one.

questions.q: Assertion (A): The rescuer ends up stuck in "Dad and the Cat and the Tree". Reason (R): The cat jumps down by itself.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true: Dad, the rescuer, ends up stuck, and the cat jumps down by itself. But the cat's jump does not cause Dad to be stuck, so the reason does not explain the assertion.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Vita-Wonk makes people younger. Reason (R): Mr Wonka is an inventor.
questions.why: The assertion is false: Vita-Wonk makes people older, not younger. The reason is true, since Mr Wonka is an inventor.

questions.q: "Neither the king nor his guards ___ the hermit's answers."
questions.why: The subject nearer to the verb is 'guards', which is plural, and the sentence is in the past. So 'knew' is right.

questions.q: In "Trees", trees are called
questions.why: In the poem 'Trees', trees are called 'the kindest things'. That is the poem's opening idea.

questions.q: Case: Your class wants to tell all students about a poetry recitation. Which format and key details?
options: Notice — date, time, venue, who can take part
questions.why: To tell all students about a poetry recitation, write a notice with the date, time, venue and who can take part. A story or diary would not inform people.

questions.q: Case: A friend says, "The Rebel tells us never to follow rules." Best reply?
options: It suggests rebels make us think, but it does not say break all rules
questions.why: The poem suggests rebels make us think, but it does not say break all rules. The friend's claim overstates it.

questions.q: Reported: The teacher said, "Don't run in the corridor."
options: The teacher told to not running.
The teacher told us not to run in the corridor.
The teacher asked are we running?
questions.why: A reported command uses 'told' + object + 'not to' + verb. So 'The teacher told us not to run in the corridor.'

questions.q: Which pair is correctly matched?
questions.why: 'Chivvy' is about imperatives, commands, and irony. Quality, The Shed and Trees do not match the other descriptions.

questions.q: Correct the sentence: "This is the most tallest tree in the meadow."
options: This is the tallest tree in the meadow.
This is the more tall tree.
questions.why: 'Tallest' is already a superlative, so 'most tallest' doubles it. The correct form is 'the tallest tree in the meadow'.

questions.q: Which theme links "Three Questions", "A Gift of Chappals" and "Expert Detectives"?
questions.why: The three texts all show kindness and understanding others: the king's kindness, the children's compassion and not judging by looks. They have nothing to do with war or sports.

questions.q: Choose the best topic sentence for a paragraph on fire safety at home.
options: Simple habits can keep our homes safe from fire.
Once upon a time there was a fire.
questions.why: A topic sentence states the main idea of the paragraph. 'Simple habits can keep our homes safe from fire' does that for fire safety.

school-c7-maths.title: Class 7 Mathematics
school-c7-maths.description: Every chapter of Class 7 Maths (NCERT 2023–24 rationalised order) as its own course: integers to solid shapes, with solved examples, common mistakes, quizzes and chapter tests.

courses.title: Ch 1 · Integers
courses.summary: Positive and negative whole numbers: adding, subtracting, multiplying and dividing them, the properties that make calculation easy, and real problems with temperatures, heights and scores.
outcomes: Learners can add and subtract integers using the number line and sign rules
