courses.summary: Numbers of the form p/q: equivalent and standard forms, positive and negative rationals, placing them on the number line, comparing them, finding rationals between two rationals, and the four operations.
outcomes: Learners can recognise and write rational numbers in standard form
Learners can represent and compare rational numbers on a number line
Learners can find several rational numbers between two given ones
Learners can add, subtract, multiply and divide rational numbers

scenes.text: A weather report says the temperature in Leh is −3/2 °C.
Not an integer, not an ordinary fraction — it is negative and fractional.
Numbers like this, p/q with integers p, q and q ≠ 0, are rational numbers.

steps.title: Definition
steps.body:
A **rational number** can be written as **p/q**, where p and q are integers and **q ≠ 0**.

- Every integer is rational: −5 = −5/1
- Every fraction is rational: 3/7
- 0 = 0/1 is rational (neither positive nor negative)
- Decimals like 0.25 = 1/4 are rational.

steps.title: Positive and negative
steps.body:
- Positive rational: numerator and denominator have the **same** sign: 3/5, −2/−7
- Negative rational: **different** signs: −3/5, 4/−9

steps.title: Equivalent rational numbers
steps.body: Multiply or divide numerator and denominator by the same non-zero integer: −2/3 = −4/6 = −10/15 = 8/−12.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Write −3/4 with denominator 20 and with numerator 15.

- Denominator 20: multiply by 5 → −15/20
- Numerator 15: multiply by −5 → 15/−20

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
Is 5/−8 positive or negative?

- Signs differ → **negative**; it equals −5/8.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Allowing q = 0: 7/0 is not a rational number (not defined).
- Thinking −2/−5 is negative. Two negatives make it positive: 2/5.

activity.prompt: Positive, negative or neither?

quiz.why: A rational number p/q needs q ≠ 0. 5/0 is not defined, so it is not rational.
−6/−7 has two negative signs that cancel, so it equals 6/7, which is positive.
Multiplying the top and bottom of −2/5 by 3 gives −6/15, which is equivalent to it.
Every integer n can be written as n/1, so every integer is rational.
35 = 7 × 5, so multiply the top and bottom of 3/7 by 5: 3 × 5 = 15. So 3/7 = 15/35.

lessons.title: Standard form, number line and comparison

scenes.text: Three divers are at −3/4 m, −5/6 m and −2/3 m from the surface.
Who is deepest? Write all three with the common denominator 12: −9/12, −10/12, −8/12.
−10/12 is smallest, so the diver at −5/6 m is deepest.

steps.title: Standard form
steps.body:
A rational number is in **standard form** if its denominator is a **positive** integer and numerator and denominator have **no common factor other than 1**.

- −18/45 → divide by 9 → −2/5
- 36/−24 → divide by −12 → −3/2

steps.title: Number line
steps.body: Divide each unit into q equal parts. Positive rationals lie to the right of 0, negative to the left. −5/4 is 5 quarter-steps to the left of 0 (between −1 and −2).

steps.title: Comparison
steps.body:
- Any positive rational > 0 > any negative rational.
- To compare, write with the **same positive denominator**, then compare numerators.
- For two negatives, compare their sizes and **reverse**: since 2/3 < 4/5, −2/3 > −4/5.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Leaving a negative denominator in 'standard form'.
- Comparing negative rationals the same way as positive ones (forgetting to reverse).

activity.prompt: Match each number to its standard form.

quiz.why: 12/−16 = −12/16, and dividing by 4 gives −3/4. Standard form has a positive denominator and lowest terms.
−1/3 is closer to 0 than −1/2, so −1/3 is greater. Among negatives, the one closer to zero is larger.
−5/4 = −1.25, which lies between −2 and −1.
Negative numbers are less than 0, and 0 is less than positive ones. So in ascending order: −3/4, 0, 1/2.
−36/24 can be reduced by dividing by 12, to give −3/2. So it is not in standard form.

scenes.text: Between 1 and 2 there is no integer.
But between 1/2 and 1 there are 3/4, 5/8, 7/8…
Between any two rational numbers there are infinitely many rational numbers.

steps.title: Method 1: equivalent forms
steps.body:
Write both with a larger common denominator.

Rationals between −2/5 and 1/2: LCM 10 → −4/10 and 5/10 → −3/10, −2/10, −1/10, 0, 1/10, …

Need more? Use denominator 20, 100, …

steps.title: Method 2: mean
steps.body:
The **average** (a + b)/2 always lies between a and b. Repeat to find more.

Between 1/4 and 1/2: (1/4 + 1/2)/2 = 3/8.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Find 5 rationals between −1 and 0.

- Write as −6/6 and 0/6
- **−5/6, −4/6, −3/6, −2/6, −1/6**

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
Find 3 rationals between 2/3 and 3/4.

- LCM 12: 8/12 and 9/12 — nothing between with denominator 12
- Multiply by 4: 32/48 and 36/48
- **33/48, 34/48, 35/48**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying 'there is no number between 8/12 and 9/12'. Make the denominator bigger.
- Listing numbers outside the range.

activity.prompt: Find a rational number exactly halfway.
activity.text: Halfway between 1/3 and 2/3 is ___. Halfway between −1 and 0 is ___.

quiz.q: How many rationals lie between 0 and 1?
quiz.why: There are infinitely many rational numbers between 0 and 1, since we can always find another between any two.
Write 1/5 = 8/40 and 1/4 = 10/40. Then 9/40 lies between them.

scenes.text: A tank has 5/8 of its water. Then 3/4 of a tankful flows out over a week, but 1/2 tank is refilled.
It ends at 3/8 full. Rational operations handle gains and losses.

steps.title: Addition and subtraction
steps.body:
- Same denominator: add/subtract numerators. −3/7 + 5/7 = 2/7
- Different denominators: use the LCM. −2/3 + 3/4 = −8/12 + 9/12 = 1/12
- Subtracting: a − b = a + (additive inverse of b). 5/6 − (−1/3) = 5/6 + 2/6 = 7/6

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
Find (−9/16) × (8/−15).

- Signs: negative × negative → positive
- 9 × 8 / (16 × 15) = 72/240 = **3/10**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding denominators: 1/2 + 1/3 ≠ 2/5.
- Taking the reciprocal of a negative and making it positive: the reciprocal of −2/3 is −3/2.
- Forgetting to give the final answer in standard form.

activity.prompt: Compute 3/4 − 5/6 as a decimal rounded to 2 places (e.g. −0.08).

quiz.why: The denominators are the same, so add the numerators: 2 + (−3) = −1, giving −1/5.
The reciprocal of −7/11 is −11/7, by flipping it and keeping the sign.
Dividing by 2 is multiplying by 1/2, so (−4/5) × 1/2 = −4/10 = −2/5.
The additive inverse of −8/9 is 8/9, because −8/9 + 8/9 = 0.

questions.q: Which is a rational number?
questions.why: −9/4 is a rational number, as it has the form p/q with q ≠ 0. 5/0 and 3/0 are not defined.

questions.q: Standard form of −15/25
questions.why: −15/25, divided by 5 on top and bottom, is −3/5. This is in lowest terms with a positive denominator.

questions.q: 0 is
questions.why: 0 is neither positive nor negative. It is rational, as 0 = 0/1.

questions.q: Reciprocal of −1
questions.why: The reciprocal of −1 is −1, because (−1) × (−1) = 1.

questions.q: Which is smaller: −4/7 or −3/5?
questions.why: −4/7 = −20/35 and −3/5 = −21/35. Since −21 is less than −20, −3/5 is smaller.
A negative times a negative is positive, so (−3/4) × (−8/9) = 24/36 = 2/3.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Every integer is a rational number. Reason (R): Any integer n can be written as n/1.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true: every integer n can be written as n/1, so every integer is rational. The reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Assertion (A): 2/−3 is in standard form. Reason (R): Its numerator and denominator have no common factor other than 1.
questions.why: The assertion is false: standard form needs a positive denominator, so 2/−3 should be −2/3. The reason is true, but it is not enough.
Subtracting −1/4 is adding 1/4. Using denominator 12: −10/12 + 3/12 = −7/12.

questions.q: Case: A shop records a loss of −5/8 lakh in April and a profit of 3/4 lakh in May. Net result over two months (lakh)?
questions.why: The loss is −5/8 and the profit is 3/4 = 6/8, so the net is −5/8 + 6/8 = 1/8 lakh profit.

questions.q: Case: A rope of length 27/4 m is cut into pieces of 9/8 m each. Number of pieces?
Number of rationals between −1/3 and 1/3 with denominator 12 (excluding the ends)?
questions.why: −1/3 = −4/12 and 1/3 = 4/12. The numbers with denominator 12 strictly between are −3/12, −2/12, −1/12, 0, 1/12, 2/12 and 3/12, which is 7 numbers.

questions.q: The product of two rationals is −9/16. One is −4/3. The other is
Arrange in descending order: −2/3, 5/−9, −7/12

courses.title: Ch 9 · Perimeter and Area
courses.summary: Perimeter and area of squares, rectangles, parallelograms and triangles; circumference and area of circles; converting units; and practical problems with paths and borders.
outcomes: Learners can find perimeter and area of rectangles, squares, parallelograms and triangles
Learners can find circumference and area of a circle using π
Learners can convert between cm², m², hectares
Learners can solve problems on paths, borders and painting costs

scenes.text: Dadi's vegetable patch is 12 m long and 8 m wide.
Fence needed = perimeter = 2(12 + 8) = 40 m.
Soil to cover = area = 12 × 8 = 96 m². Perimeter is the boundary; area is the surface.

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body:
- Rectangle: P = 2(l + b), A = l × b
- Square: P = 4s, A = s²
- **Parallelogram: A = base × height**, where the height is the perpendicular distance between the base and the opposite side.

Area units are square units (cm², m²).

steps.title: Why base × height for a parallelogram
steps.body: Cut a right triangle from one side of a parallelogram and stick it on the other side — you get a rectangle with the same base and height. So the area is b × h.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
A rectangular sheet measures 500 cm by 2 m. Find its area in m² (convert units first).

- 500 cm = 5 m
- Area = 5 × 2 = **10 m²**

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
A parallelogram has base 12 cm and the corresponding height 7.5 cm. Area? If another side is 10 cm, find the height on it.

- A = 12 × 7.5 = **90 cm²**
- 90 = 10 × h → h = **9 cm**

steps.title: Solved example 3
steps.body:
Cost of fencing a square field of area 2500 m² at ₹15 per metre.

- Side = 50 m (since 50 × 50 = 2500)
- Perimeter = 200 m
- Cost = 200 × 15 = **₹3000**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the slanting side as height in a parallelogram. Height is perpendicular.
- Writing area in cm instead of cm².
- Mixing units (one side in m, the other in cm).

activity.prompt: Area of a parallelogram with base 14 cm and height 6 cm (cm²)?

quiz.q: Perimeter of a square of side 9 cm
quiz.why: The perimeter of a square is 4 × side = 4 × 9 = 36 cm.

quiz.q: Area of a rectangle 15 m × 4 m
quiz.why: Area = length × breadth = 15 × 4 = 60 m², with square units.
The area of a parallelogram is base × height. We can cut a triangle off one side and move it to make a rectangle.

quiz.q: A rectangle has area 96 cm² and length 12 cm. Breadth?
quiz.why: Breadth = area ÷ length = 96 ÷ 12 = 8 cm.

quiz.q: Wire forms a square of side 11 cm. Bent into a rectangle of length 13 cm, its breadth is
quiz.why: The wire length is the square's perimeter, 4 × 11 = 44 cm. For the rectangle 2(13 + b) = 44, so b = 9 cm.

scenes.text: Cut a square sandwich along its diagonal.
Each triangle is exactly half of the square.
Any triangle is half of a parallelogram with the same base and height: A = ½ × b × h.

steps.title: Formula
steps.body:
**Area of triangle = ½ × base × height.**

Any side may be the base; the height is the perpendicular from the opposite vertex to that base (or base extended). For a right triangle, the two legs are base and height.

steps.title: Triangles with equal bases and heights
steps.body: All triangles on the same base and between the same parallel lines have equal area, even if they look different, because b and h are the same.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Base 12 cm, height 5 cm.

- A = ½ × 12 × 5 = **30 cm²**

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
△PQR is right-angled at Q with PQ = 8 cm, QR = 6 cm, PR = 10 cm. Find the area and the altitude from Q to PR.

- Area = ½ × 6 × 8 = 24 cm²
- Also 24 = ½ × 10 × h → h = **4.8 cm**

steps.title: Solved example 3
steps.body:
A triangle has area 36 cm² and base 9 cm. Height?

- 36 = ½ × 9 × h → h = 72/9 = **8 cm**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the ½.
- Using a side that is not perpendicular to the base as the height.
- Pairing the wrong height with a base (each base has its own height).

activity.prompt: Triangle with base 15 cm and height 8 cm: area (cm²)?

quiz.why: The area of a triangle is ½ × base × height = ½ × 10 × 7 = 35.

quiz.q: Right triangle legs 9 cm and 4 cm. Area
quiz.why: The area of a right triangle is ½ × 9 × 4 = 18 cm².

quiz.q: Triangle area 48 cm², height 12 cm. Base
quiz.why: Base = 2 × area ÷ height = 96 ÷ 12 = 8 cm.

quiz.q: A triangle and parallelogram share base and height. Triangle area is
quiz.why: A triangle with the same base and height as a parallelogram has half its area: ½ b h versus b h.

quiz.q: Two triangles on the same base between the same parallels have
quiz.why: Triangles on the same base between the same parallel lines have the same height, so they have equal area.

scenes.text: Zoya's cycle wheel has radius 35 cm. How far does it go in one turn?
Circumference = 2πr = 2 × 22/7 × 35 = 220 cm.
In 100 turns she travels 220 m!

steps.title: Circumference
steps.body:
The perimeter of a circle is its **circumference**: **C = 2πr = πd**.

π (pi) is the ratio circumference ÷ diameter for every circle, about **22/7 or 3.14**. It is not exactly either; it is a never-ending, non-repeating decimal.

steps.title: Area
steps.body:
**Area of a circle = πr².**

Idea: cut a circle into many thin sectors and arrange them alternately — they form almost a rectangle of length πr (half the circumference) and breadth r. Area ≈ πr × r.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
A circular park has circumference 132 m. Find its area.

- 2 × 22/7 × r = 132 → r = 132 × 7/44 = 21 m
- A = 22/7 × 21 × 21 = **1386 m²**

steps.title: Solved example 3 (ring)
steps.body:
Find the area of a ring between circles of radii 10 cm and 7 cm (π = 3.14).

- 3.14 × (100 − 49) = 3.14 × 51 = **160.14 cm²**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the diameter in πr² (squaring d instead of r gives 4 times too much).
- Mixing C = 2πr and A = πr².
- Ring area is π(R² − r²), not π(R − r)².

bands.text: Small coin-sized circle: area under 30 cm².
Doubling the radius doubles the circumference but makes the area 4 times bigger.

quiz.q: Circumference of a circle with r = 21 cm (π = 22/7)
quiz.why: Circumference = 2πr = 2 × 22/7 × 21 = 132 cm.

quiz.q: Area of a circle with r = 14 cm

quiz.why: Area is πr², so doubling the radius gives π(2r)² = 4πr², which is 4 times the area.
Circumference = πd = 3.14 × 10 = 31.4 cm.
π is the ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter. 3.14 and 22/7 are only approximations of it.

scenes.text: A pool is 20 m × 10 m. A 2 m wide grass path runs all around it.
Outer rectangle = 24 m × 14 m = 336 m². Pool = 200 m².
Path area = 336 − 200 = 136 m² of grass to plant.

steps.title: Area units
steps.body:
- 1 cm² = 100 mm² (10 × 10)
- 1 m² = 10 000 cm² (100 × 100)
- **1 hectare = 10 000 m²**

Converting area: square the length conversion.

steps.title: Paths
steps.body:
- Path **outside**: outer length = l + 2w, outer breadth = b + 2w.
- Path **inside**: inner length = l − 2w, inner breadth = b − 2w.
- Path area = outer area − inner area.
- Cross paths through the middle: add both strips, then subtract the overlap square once.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
A path 1 m wide runs inside a 30 m × 20 m garden. Find its area.

- Inner = 28 × 18 = 504 m²
- Garden = 600 m²
- Path = **96 m²**

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
Two cross roads, each 3 m wide, run through the middle of a 60 m × 40 m park, parallel to its sides. Area of roads?

- 60 × 3 + 40 × 3 − 3 × 3 = 180 + 120 − 9 = **291 m²**

steps.title: Solved example 3
steps.body:
Convert 3.5 hectares to m².

- 3.5 × 10 000 = **35 000 m²**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 1 m² = 100 cm² is wrong — it is 10 000 cm².
- Adding the path width only once instead of twice.
- Counting the crossing square twice for cross roads.

activity.prompt: Match conversions.

quiz.why: 1 m² = 10 000 cm², so 2 m² = 20 000 cm².

quiz.q: Path 2 m wide outside a 10 m × 5 m lawn: outer dimensions
quiz.why: A 2 m path on all sides adds 2 × 2 = 4 m to each dimension, so the outer size is 14 m × 9 m.
1 hectare = 10 000 m², so 50 000 m² = 5 hectares.

quiz.q: Cross roads 2 m wide in a 20 m × 10 m field. Road area
quiz.why: One road runs 20 m × 2 m = 40 m², and the other 10 m × 2 m = 20 m². The crossing square, 2 × 2 = 4 m², is counted twice, so 40 + 20 − 4 = 56 m².

quiz.q: Cost of painting 25 m² at ₹12 per m²
quiz.why: Cost = area × rate = 25 × 12 = ₹300.

questions.q: Area of a square of side 12 cm
questions.why: The area of a square is side × side = 12 × 12 = 144 cm².

questions.q: Area of a triangle =
questions.why: The area of a triangle is ½ × base × height, half of the matching parallelogram.

questions.q: Circumference formula
questions.why: The circumference of a circle is 2πr. πr² is its area.

questions.q: 1 hectare =
questions.why: 1 hectare is 10 000 m², the area of a 100 m × 100 m square.

questions.q: Parallelogram base 9 cm, height 4 cm. Area
questions.why: The area of a parallelogram is base × height = 9 × 4 = 36 cm².

questions.q: Circle r = 7 cm. Area (π = 22/7)
questions.why: Area = πr² = 22/7 × 7 × 7 = 154 cm².

questions.q: Rectangle 25 cm × 16 cm has the same area as a square of side
questions.why: The area of the rectangle is 25 × 16 = 400 cm². A square with the same area has side √400 = 20 cm.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Doubling the radius of a circle doubles its area. Reason (R): Area = πr².
questions.why: The assertion is false: doubling the radius makes the area 4 times, since area is πr² and the radius is squared. The reason is true.

questions.q: A wire of length 88 cm is bent into a circle. Radius (π = 22/7)?
questions.why: The circumference is 88 cm, so 2πr = 88, giving 2 × 22/7 × r = 88. So r = 14 cm.

questions.q: Triangle area 54 cm², base 12 cm. Height
questions.why: Height = 2 × area ÷ base = 108 ÷ 12 = 9 cm.

questions.q: A 1.5 m wide path surrounds a 20 m × 12 m lawn. Path area
questions.why: The outer rectangle is (20 + 3) × (12 + 3) = 23 × 15 = 345 m². Subtracting the lawn (20 × 12 = 240 m²) gives a path area of 105 m².

questions.q: Case: A wheel of diameter 70 cm makes how many revolutions to cover 1.1 km? (π = 22/7)
questions.why: The wheel's circumference is 22/7 × 70 = 220 cm. The distance is 1.1 km = 110 000 cm, so it makes 110 000 ÷ 220 = 500 revolutions.

questions.q: Case: A rectangular floor 6 m × 4 m is tiled with square tiles of side 20 cm. Number of tiles?
questions.why: The floor is 24 m² = 240 000 cm², and each tile is 20 × 20 = 400 cm². So 240 000 ÷ 400 = 600 tiles.

questions.q: Area of the region between a square of side 14 cm and its inscribed circle (π = 22/7)
questions.why: The circle inscribed in a square of side 14 has radius 7, so its area is 22/7 × 49 = 154 cm². The square is 196 cm², so the region left is 196 − 154 = 42 cm².

questions.q: A circular flower bed is surrounded by a path 4 m wide. Bed diameter 66 m. Path area (π = 22/7)?
questions.why: The bed has radius 33 m, so the outer radius is 37 m. Path area = π(37² − 33²) = 22/7 × (37 − 33)(37 + 33) = 22/7 × 4 × 70 = 880 m².

questions.q: A parallelogram has sides 12 cm and 8 cm. The height on the 12 cm side is 4 cm. Height on the 8 cm side?
questions.why: The area is 12 × 4 = 48 cm². With base 8 cm, 48 = 8 × h, so h = 6 cm.

courses.title: Ch 10 · Algebraic Expressions
courses.summary: How algebraic expressions are formed, terms, factors and coefficients, like and unlike terms, monomials to polynomials, adding and subtracting expressions, finding their values, and using them as formulas and rules.
outcomes: Learners can identify terms, factors and coefficients of an expression
Learners can classify expressions as monomials, binomials, trinomials
Learners can add and subtract algebraic expressions
Learners can evaluate expressions and use them to write rules and formulas

scenes.text: One square needs 4 matchsticks. Squares in a row share sides: 4, 7, 10, 13…
For n squares the count is 3n + 1.
An expression like 3n + 1 captures the whole pattern in a few symbols.

steps.title: Forming expressions
steps.body:
Expressions are made from **variables** (x, y, n) and **constants** (5, −3) using +, −, ×, ÷.

- 'x multiplied by 5, then 3 added' → 5x + 3
- 'y squared minus 4' → y² − 4

steps.title: Terms and factors
steps.body:
**Terms** are the parts added together. In 4x² − 3xy + 5: terms 4x², −3xy, 5.

Each term is a product of **factors**: −3xy = (−3) × x × y.

A tree diagram shows expression → terms → factors.

steps.title: Coefficient
steps.body: The **numerical factor** of a term is its (numerical) coefficient: in −3xy it is −3; in x² it is 1; in −y it is −1. A coefficient can also be algebraic: in 5xy the coefficient of x is 5y.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
For 7x²y − 4xy + 9:

- Terms: 7x²y, −4xy, 9
- Factors of 7x²y: 7, x, x, y
- Coefficient of xy in −4xy: −4
- Constant term: 9

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Write expressions: 'Sum of a and b, subtracted from their product' → ab − (a + b). 'One-fourth of z, plus 7' → z/4 + 7.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Dropping the sign: in 5 − 2x the term is −2x, coefficient −2.
- Saying the coefficient of x is 0 because no number is written — it is 1.
- Treating x² as 2x.

quiz.why: 2x² + 3x − 1 has three terms: 2x², 3x and −1.
The coefficient of x² in −9x² + x is −9, the number with its sign.
'Twice m' is 2m, and '3 less than' that is 2m − 3.
The factors of −5ab are −5, a and b. The sign belongs to the numerical factor.

quiz.q: In 8 − 3y, the term containing y is
quiz.why: In 8 − 3y, the term with y is −3y, keeping its sign.

lessons.title: Like and unlike terms; monomials, binomials, trinomials

scenes.text: 3 apples + 2 bananas + 4 apples = 7 apples + 2 bananas.
Algebra works the same: 3a + 2b + 4a = 7a + 2b.
You cannot add apples to bananas — or a to b.

steps.title: Like and unlike terms
steps.body: **Like terms** have the **same algebraic factors** (same variables with the same powers): 4xy and −7yx are like; 3x² and 3x are **unlike**.

steps.title: Kinds of expressions
steps.body:
- **Monomial**: 1 term — 7xy, −5, a²
- **Binomial**: 2 unlike terms — a + b, 4x² − 3
- **Trinomial**: 3 unlike terms — x² + 2x + 1
- **Polynomial**: one or more terms (with whole-number powers of variables).

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Group like terms: 12x, 12, −25x, −25, 25y, −y, x².

- x-terms: 12x, −25x
- Constants: 12, −25
- y-terms: 25y, −y
- x² stands alone

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Classify: 4y − 7z (binomial), y² (monomial), x + y − xy (trinomial), 100 (monomial).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling 2x + 3x a binomial — they are like terms; it simplifies to 5x, a monomial.
- Thinking xy and yx are unlike. Multiplication order does not matter.

activity.prompt: Monomial, binomial or trinomial?

quiz.why: Like terms have the same variables with the same powers. 2a² and 5a² are like terms.
x² − y² has two unlike terms, so it is a binomial.
A monomial has only one term. −9pq is a single term.
5ab and −3ba are like terms, because ab and ba are the same product. The coefficients may differ.
4x + 3x simplifies to 7x, which is one term.

scenes.text: Ravi has (3x + 2) stickers; Anu has (5x − 4).
Together: 8x − 2 stickers.
Anu has (5x − 4) − (3x + 2) = 2x − 6 more than Ravi.

steps.title: Adding
steps.body:
Add **like terms only**, by adding their coefficients. Write each expression, collect like terms, simplify.

(3x² − 4x + 5) + (2x² + 7x − 9) = 5x² + 3x − 4

steps.title: Subtracting
steps.body:
Subtracting an expression = adding its **additive inverse**: change the sign of **every** term being subtracted, then add.

(5a − 3b) − (2a − 7b) = 5a − 3b − 2a + 7b = 3a + 4b

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Add 7xy + 5yz − 3zx, 4yz + 9zx − 4y, −3xz + 5x − 2xy.

- xy: 7 − 2 = 5xy
- yz: 5 + 4 = 9yz
- zx: −3 + 9 − 3 = 3zx
- Others: −4y + 5x
- **5xy + 9yz + 3zx + 5x − 4y**

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
Subtract 3a − 4b − 7c from 5a + 2b − c.

- (5a + 2b − c) − (3a − 4b − 7c)
- = 5a + 2b − c − 3a + 4b + 7c
- = **2a + 6b + 6c**

steps.title: Solved example 3
steps.body:
What should be added to x² + xy + y² to get 2x² + 3xy?

- (2x² + 3xy) − (x² + xy + y²) = **x² + 2xy − y²**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Changing the sign of only the first term when subtracting.
- 'Subtract A from B' means B − A, not A − B.
- Adding unlike terms: 3x + 2x² ≠ 5x³.

activity.prompt: Simplify.

quiz.why: Add like terms: 2a + 5a = 7a, and 3 + (−7) = −4. So the result is 7a − 4.
Subtracting 2x from 9x gives 9x − 2x = 7x.
x² − 2x² = −x², and −3x − x = −4x. So the result is −x² − 4x.
The additive inverse changes the sign of every term: −(3y − 5) = −3y + 5.
Subtract −5ab from 3ab: 3ab − (−5ab) = 3ab + 5ab = 8ab.

lessons.title: Values of expressions, formulas and rules

scenes.text: A taxi charges ₹50 plus ₹15 per km. Fare for d km: 50 + 15d.
Substituting a value gives the answer for any trip.

steps.title: Finding the value
steps.body:
Replace each variable by its given number (use brackets for negatives) and calculate.

If x = −2: 3x² − 5x + 1 = 3(4) − 5(−2) + 1 = 12 + 10 + 1 = 23.

steps.title: Formulas and rules
steps.body:
- Perimeter of square: P = 4l; of rectangle: 2(l + b)
- Area of square: l², of rectangle: l × b
- nth odd number: 2n − 1; nth even number: 2n
- Number patterns: 5, 9, 13, … → 4n + 1

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
If 2x + k = 15 when x = 4, find k.

- 8 + k = 15 → **k = 7**

steps.title: Solved example 3
steps.body:
Matchstick pattern: one 'L' uses 2 sticks; 'C' uses 3; 'E' uses 5. Sticks for n copies of 'E'?

- **5n** sticks

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- −x² with x = −3 is −9, not 9 (square first, then the sign).
- Substituting without brackets: 5 − 2x with x = −3 → 5 − 2(−3) = 11.
- Simplify first when possible — it makes substitution easier.

activity.prompt: Find the value of 5x² − 3x + 2 when x = −2.

quiz.why: For x = −5, x² = (−5) × (−5) = 25, as the product of two negatives is positive.
The terms 3, 6, 9, 12 are the multiples of 3, so the nth term is 3n.

quiz.q: Perimeter of an equilateral triangle of side s
quiz.why: An equilateral triangle has three equal sides, so its perimeter is 3s.

questions.q: Terms in 5xy − 3
questions.why: The terms of 5xy − 3 are 5xy and −3. Terms are the parts separated by + or −, with the sign.

questions.q: Coefficient of a in −a
questions.why: In −a, the coefficient of a is −1, as −a = (−1) × a.

questions.q: x + y + z is a
questions.why: x + y + z has three unlike terms, so it is a trinomial.

questions.q: Like terms
questions.why: Like terms have the same variable raised to the same power. 7p² and −p² are like terms.
3x + (−x) = 2x, and −4 + 9 = 5. So the sum is 2x + 5.

questions.q: Value of 2m² − m at m = 3
Subtract 4a − 7 from 9a + 2
Assertion (A): 3xy and −2yx are like terms. Reason (R): Like terms have the same algebraic factors.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true: 3xy and −2yx have the same variables, so they are like terms. The reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Assertion (A): 2x + 3x is a binomial. Reason (R): A binomial has two unlike terms.
questions.why: The assertion is false: 2x + 3x = 5x, which is a single term, so it is a monomial. The reason is true.

questions.q: Simplify 3(a − b) − 2(a + b)
If a = 2, b = −1, find a³ − b³
Case: A hall has r rows of 2r + 3 chairs each. Expression for total chairs, and value when r = 10?
questions.why: There are r rows with 2r + 3 chairs each, so the total is r(2r + 3) = 2r² + 3r. At r = 10 that is 200 + 30 = 230.

questions.q: Case: The sides of a triangle are (2x − 1), (x + 5) and (3x + 2) cm. Perimeter expression and value at x = 4?
questions.why: The perimeter is (2x − 1) + (x + 5) + (3x + 2) = 6x + 6. At x = 4 it is 6 × 4 + 6 = 30 cm.

questions.q: What must be subtracted from 3a² − 4b² + 5ab to get −a² − b² + 6ab?
questions.why: To find what is subtracted, take (3a² − 4b² + 5ab) − (−a² − b² + 6ab) = 3a² + a² − 4b² + b² + 5ab − 6ab = 4a² − 3b² − ab.

questions.q: If x = 2 and y = −3, value of 2x² − 3xy + y²
The nth term of 7, 12, 17, 22, … is
questions.why: The sequence 7, 12, 17, 22 goes up by 5, so the nth term is 5n + something. For n = 1 we need 7, so it is 5n + 2.

courses.title: Ch 11 · Exponents and Powers
courses.summary: Writing large numbers with exponents, the laws of exponents for multiplying, dividing and raising powers, zero exponent, and expressing very large numbers in standard form.
outcomes: Learners can write repeated multiplication in exponential form and read base and exponent
Learners can apply the laws of exponents to simplify expressions
Learners can use a⁰ = 1 and compare powers
Learners can express large numbers in standard form

scenes.text: Tara forwards a message to 2 friends; each forwards it to 2 more, and so on.
After 10 rounds: 2 × 2 × … (10 times) people receive it in that round.
That is 2¹⁰ = 1024 people. Exponents write big repeated products neatly.

steps.title: Base and exponent
steps.body:
aⁿ means a multiplied by itself n times. **a is the base, n is the exponent (power, index).**

- 10⁴ = 10 × 10 × 10 × 10 = 10 000 (read: 10 to the power 4)
- a² is 'a squared', a³ is 'a cubed'.

steps.title: Negative bases
steps.body:
(−1)^odd = −1, (−1)^even = 1. In general (−a)ⁿ is positive if n is even and negative if n is odd.

(−2)³ = −8, (−3)⁴ = 81.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Which is greater: 2⁸ or 8²?

- 2⁸ = 256, 8² = 64
- **2⁸ is greater**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 2³ = 6 is wrong (that is 2 × 3). 2³ = 8.
- −3² means −(3²) = −9, but (−3)² = 9.
- Confusing base and exponent: 3⁵ ≠ 5³.

activity.prompt: Match each power with its value.

quiz.why: In 7⁵, the base is 7, the number being multiplied repeatedly. The exponent is 5.
(−1) raised to an even power is 1, and 2026 is even. So (−1)²⁰²⁶ = 1.
3⁴ = 81 and 4³ = 64, so 3⁴ is larger.
(−4)² = (−4) × (−4) = 16, since an even power of a negative number is positive.

scenes.text: A bacterium splits into 2 every hour. After 3 hours: 2³. After 5 more hours: 2³ × 2⁵.
That is just 2 multiplied 8 times: 2⁸.
When multiplying powers of the same base, add the exponents.

steps.title: The laws (a, b non-zero; m, n whole numbers)
Why a⁰ = 1
steps.body: a³ ÷ a³ = 1, but by law 2 it is a³⁻³ = a⁰. So a⁰ = 1 for any non-zero a.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
Simplify (3²)³ × 3⁴ ÷ 3⁷.

- (3²)³ = 3⁶
- 3⁶ × 3⁴ = 3¹⁰
- 3¹⁰ ÷ 3⁷ = **3³ = 27**

steps.title: Solved example 3
steps.body:
Simplify (2⁵ × 3²) ÷ 6². First write 6² = 2² × 3².

- = 2⁵⁻² × 3²⁻² = 2³ × 3⁰ = **8**

steps.title: Solved example 4
steps.body:
Find x if 5ˣ × 5³ = 5⁹.

- x + 3 = 9 → **x = 6**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 2³ × 3² = 6⁵ is wrong — the laws need the **same base** (or same exponent for law 4).
- (a²)³ = a⁵ is wrong; it is a⁶ (multiply).
- a⁰ = 0 is wrong; a⁰ = 1.
- Adding exponents when adding numbers: 2³ + 2² ≠ 2⁵ (8 + 4 = 12).

activity.prompt: Write as a single power.

quiz.why: When multiplying powers with the same base, add the exponents: x⁴ × x⁶ = x¹⁰.
A power of a power multiplies the exponents: (2³)² = 2⁶.
Any non-zero number to the power 0 is 1, so 9⁰ = 1.
With the same exponent, a^m × b^m = (ab)^m. So 2⁴ × 5⁴ = 10⁴.
Subtract the exponents: (−3)⁵ ÷ (−3)² = (−3)³ = −27.
2⁷ ÷ 2³ = 2⁷⁻³ = 2⁴, so n = 4.

scenes.text: The Sun is about 150 000 000 km from Earth.
Counting zeros is tiring and risky.
Scientists write 1.5 × 10⁸ km — short, clear and easy to compare.

steps.title: Standard form
steps.body:
A number is in **standard form** when written as **k × 10ⁿ**, where **1 ≤ k < 10** and n is a whole number.

- 5 985 = 5.985 × 10³
- 300 000 = 3 × 10⁵
- 49 000 000 000 = 4.9 × 10¹⁰

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Write 6 400 000 (approx. Earth's radius in metres) in standard form.

- Move the decimal point 6 places left → 6.4
- **6.4 × 10⁶ m**

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
Compare 2.7 × 10¹² and 1.5 × 10⁸.

- Bigger power of 10 dominates: **2.7 × 10¹² is larger** (by about 18 000 times).

steps.title: Solved example 3
steps.body:
Write 3.08 × 10⁵ in usual form.

- Move the point 5 places right → **308 000**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing 45 × 10⁴ as standard form; k must be from 1 to less than 10 → 4.5 × 10⁵.
- Counting places wrongly; count the jumps of the decimal point.

activity.prompt: In standard form, 72 000 000 = 7.2 × 10ⁿ. What is n?

quiz.why: In standard form, a number is written as k × 10ⁿ with 1 ≤ k < 10. So 3400 = 3.4 × 10³.
9.1 × 10⁷ is in standard form, as 9.1 is between 1 and 10. The others have a first number outside that range.

scenes.text: The test question: simplify (25 × 5² × t⁸) ÷ (10³ × t⁴).
Manya plans: break every number into primes, apply the laws, then calculate.

steps.title: Strategy
steps.body:
1. Write each number as a product of prime powers (4 = 2², 9 = 3², 25 = 5², 6 = 2 × 3).
2. Collect powers of the same base.
3. Apply the laws.
4. Calculate only at the end.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
Simplify (3⁵ × 10⁵ × 25)/(5⁷ × 6⁵).

- 10⁵ = 2⁵5⁵, 25 = 5², 6⁵ = 2⁵3⁵
- Numerator: 3⁵ 2⁵ 5⁷; Denominator: 5⁷ 2⁵ 3⁵
- **= 1**

steps.title: Solved example 3
steps.body:
Express 108 × 192 in exponential form.

- 108 = 2² × 3³; 192 = 2⁶ × 3
- Product = **2⁸ × 3⁴**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting to factorise composite bases (4, 6, 10) before applying laws.
- Cancelling terms instead of factors: (2³ + 2²) ÷ 2² = 12 ÷ 4 = 3. You may not strike 2² out of just one term.

statements.s: 4² = 2⁴
2⁵ + 2⁵ = 2¹⁰

quiz.why: Any non-zero number to the power 0 is 1, so (1 + 1) × 1 = 2.
(−1)³ = −1 and (−2)² = 4, so the product is −1 × 4 = −4.

questions.q: In 4⁹, the exponent is
questions.why: In 4⁹, the exponent is 9, the small raised number.
Any non-zero number to the power 0 is 1. This is the zero exponent law.
(−1) to an odd power is −1, and 99 is odd. So (−1)⁹⁹ = −1.

questions.q: a³ × a⁷ =
questions.why: Same base, so add the exponents: a³ × a⁷ = a¹⁰.

questions.q: Standard form of 92 000
questions.why: In standard form 92 000 = 9.2 × 10⁴, since the decimal point moves 4 places and k is between 1 and 10.
(5²)³ = 5⁶, and 5⁶ ÷ 5⁴ = 5².

questions.q: Assertion (A): 2³ × 3³ = 6³. Reason (R): aᵐ × bᵐ = (ab)ᵐ.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true: 2³ × 3³ = 8 × 27 = 216 = 6³. The law a^m × b^m = (ab)^m explains it.

questions.q: Assertion (A): 2⁴ + 2⁴ = 2⁸. Reason (R): aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ.
questions.why: The assertion is false: 2⁴ + 2⁴ = 16 + 16 = 32 = 2⁵, not 2⁸. The reason is a true law, but it is for multiplication and not for addition.

questions.q: Express 1000 × 64 as powers of primes

questions.why: The exponents add: (m + 1) + 5 = 7, so m + 6 = 7 and m = 1.

questions.q: Case: The distance between Earth and Moon is about 384 000 000 m. In standard form?
questions.why: 384 000 000 = 3.84 × 10⁸, since the decimal point moves 8 places.

questions.q: Case: A hard disk holds 5 × 10¹¹ bytes; each photo is 2.5 × 10⁶ bytes. Number of photos?
Simplify (2⁵ × 7³)/(8 × 7²)
questions.why: 2⁵ ÷ 8 = 2⁵ ÷ 2³ = 2² = 4, and 7³ ÷ 7² = 7. So the result is 4 × 7 = 28.
4 = 2², so 2ˣ × 2² = 2ˣ⁺² = 128 = 2⁷. Then x + 2 = 7 and x = 5.

questions.q: Simplify (3⁴ × 9² × 27)/(3⁹)
questions.why: Write all as powers of 3: 3⁴ × 3⁴ × 3³ = 3¹¹. Dividing by 3⁹ gives 3² = 9.

courses.title: Ch 12 · Symmetry
courses.summary: Line (mirror) symmetry and lines of symmetry of regular polygons, rotational symmetry with centre, angle and order, and shapes that have both.
outcomes: Learners can identify and draw lines of symmetry
Learners can state the number of lines of symmetry of regular polygons
Learners can find the centre, angle and order of rotational symmetry
Learners can classify shapes by line and rotational symmetry

scenes.text: Riya drops paint on paper, folds it and opens it.
A perfect butterfly — the fold line is a line of symmetry.
Each half is the mirror image of the other.

steps.title: Line of symmetry
steps.body: A figure has **line symmetry** if a line divides it into two parts that match exactly when folded along the line. The line is a **line (axis) of symmetry** or mirror line.

steps.title: Regular polygons
steps.body:
A regular polygon has all sides equal and all angles equal. **A regular polygon with n sides has n lines of symmetry.**

- Equilateral triangle: 3
- Square: 4
- Regular pentagon: 5
- Regular hexagon: 6
- Circle: infinitely many

steps.title: Other shapes
steps.body:
- Rectangle (not square): 2
- Isosceles triangle: 1
- Scalene triangle: 0
- Rhombus: 2 (its diagonals)
- Parallelogram (not rectangle or rhombus): 0

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Letters with a vertical line of symmetry: A, H, I, M, O, T, U, V, W, X, Y. With a horizontal one: B, C, D, E, H, I, K, O, X.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: How many lines of symmetry does a regular octagon have? → **8**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying a rectangle's diagonals are lines of symmetry. Folding along a diagonal does not match the halves (unless it is a square).
- Saying a parallelogram has 2 lines of symmetry — usually it has none.

activity.prompt: Match the shape with its number of lines of symmetry.

quiz.q: Lines of symmetry of a circle
quiz.why: Every diameter of a circle is a line of symmetry, so there are infinitely many.
A regular polygon with n sides has n lines of symmetry. A regular pentagon has 5.

quiz.q: Which letter has no line of symmetry?
quiz.why: The letter F has no line of symmetry, since folding it never makes the two halves match. H, O and A can be folded to match.

quiz.q: A rhombus's lines of symmetry are its
quiz.why: A rhombus is symmetric about its diagonals, so folding along either diagonal makes the halves match.

quiz.q: Number of lines of symmetry of a kite
quiz.why: A kite has one line of symmetry, along its main diagonal.

scenes.text: A windmill with 4 blades turns in the wind.
After a quarter turn (90°) it looks exactly the same.
It looks the same 4 times in a full turn, so its order of rotational symmetry is 4.

steps.title: Key words
steps.body:
- **Centre of rotation**: fixed point about which the figure turns.
- **Angle of rotation**: smallest angle of turn after which the figure looks the same.
- **Order**: number of times the figure looks the same in one full turn (360°).

Order × angle = 360°.

steps.title: Examples
steps.body:
- Square: order 4, angle 90°
- Equilateral triangle: order 3, angle 120°
- Regular hexagon: order 6, angle 60°
- Rectangle: order 2, angle 180°
- Circle: any angle works

Every shape looks the same after 360°; we say a shape has rotational symmetry only if its order is **more than 1**.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
A shape has rotational symmetry of order 5. Its angle?

- 360 ÷ 5 = **72°**

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
Does the letter Z have rotational symmetry?

- Turn it 180° about its centre: it looks the same.
- **Yes, order 2.**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Counting the starting position twice (the 0° and 360° positions are the same one).
- Thinking a shape needs line symmetry to have rotational symmetry. Z and S have rotational but no line symmetry.

activity.prompt: A regular octagon: angle of rotational symmetry in degrees?

quiz.q: Order of rotational symmetry of a square
quiz.why: A square looks the same after each quarter turn (90°), so its order of rotational symmetry is 4.

quiz.q: Angle of rotation for an equilateral triangle
quiz.why: An equilateral triangle looks the same after 360° ÷ 3 = 120°. So 120° is its smallest angle of rotation.
A parallelogram looks exactly the same after a half-turn (180°), and again after a full turn (360°). That gives 2 matching positions in one turn, so its order is 2.

quiz.q: Letter N has rotational symmetry of order
quiz.why: The letter N looks the same after a half-turn (180°) but not after a quarter-turn. So it matches itself 2 times in a full turn, giving order 2.
Order 6 means the shape matches itself 6 times in one full turn of 360°. The smallest turn is 360° ÷ 6 = 60°.

scenes.text: At Diwali, Priya draws a rangoli with 8 petals.
It has 8 lines of symmetry, and it also looks the same after every 45° turn.
Many beautiful designs have both kinds of symmetry.

steps.title: Comparing
steps.body:
- Both: square, equilateral triangle, regular polygons, circle, rectangle, letters H, I, O, X
- Only line: isosceles triangle, kite, letters A, B, C, D, E, K, M, T, U, V, W, Y
- Only rotational: parallelogram (general), letters N, S, Z
- Neither: scalene triangle, letters F, G, J, L, P, Q, R

steps.title: Regular polygons link
steps.body: A regular n-gon has **n lines of symmetry** and **rotational symmetry of order n**, angle 360°/n.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Letter H: lines of symmetry 2 (vertical, horizontal); rotational order 2. **Both.**

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: A figure has 1 line of symmetry. Can it have rotational symmetry of order 2? For simple figures in Class 7 — an isosceles triangle, kite, letter A — no; with 1 line only, order is 1.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying a circle has order 360. A circle looks the same at every angle; its order is infinite.
- Forgetting that shapes with 2 perpendicular lines of symmetry also have order-2 rotational symmetry.

activity.prompt: Sort the letters.

quiz.q: Which has both line and rotational symmetry?
quiz.why: A square has 4 lines of symmetry and rotational symmetry of order 4. A kite and an isosceles triangle have only line symmetry, and a parallelogram has only rotational symmetry.

quiz.q: Which has rotational but no line symmetry?
quiz.why: S looks the same after a 180° turn, so it has rotational symmetry. No fold line splits it into two matching halves, so it has no line symmetry. E and A have lines only; O has both.

quiz.q: A regular hexagon has rotational order
quiz.why: A regular polygon with n sides has rotational symmetry of order n. A hexagon has 6 sides, so its order is 6 (turns of 60°).

quiz.q: Letter X has how many lines of symmetry?
quiz.why: In common fonts X can be folded along a vertical line and along a horizontal line, so it has 2 lines of symmetry. The diagonals do not work unless the letter is a perfect square X, so we count 2.
In a scalene triangle all sides and angles are different. No fold makes two matching halves, and no turn less than 360° brings it back, so it has neither kind of symmetry.

questions.q: Lines of symmetry of a square
questions.why: A square can be folded along 2 diagonals and 2 lines joining midpoints of opposite sides. That makes 4 lines of symmetry.

questions.q: Order of rotational symmetry of an equilateral triangle
questions.why: An equilateral triangle matches itself after every turn of 360° ÷ 3 = 120°. So it matches 3 times in a full turn, giving order 3. The number 120 is the angle, not the order.

questions.q: Which letter has a horizontal line of symmetry?
questions.why: B can be folded along a horizontal line through its middle so top and bottom match. W, A and V have only a vertical line of symmetry.

questions.q: A rectangle has how many lines of symmetry?
questions.why: A rectangle has 2 lines of symmetry: the lines joining midpoints of opposite sides. Its diagonals are not lines of symmetry, because folding along them does not match the halves.

questions.q: Angle of rotation for a regular pentagon
questions.why: A regular pentagon has order 5, so the smallest turn that matches it is 360° ÷ 5 = 72°. The 108° is its interior angle, which is a different thing.

questions.q: Which has no line of symmetry?
questions.why: A parallelogram that is not a rhombus or rectangle cannot be folded into matching halves, so it has no line of symmetry. It has only rotational symmetry of order 2. The kite, isosceles trapezium and semicircle each have one line.

questions.q: Regular decagon: lines of symmetry
questions.why: A regular polygon with n sides has n lines of symmetry. A decagon has 10 sides, so it has 10 lines. The other numbers confuse sides with angles.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Letter Z has rotational symmetry. Reason (R): Z looks the same after a 180° turn.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: A: Z looks the same after a 180° turn, so it has rotational symmetry of order 2. R is true and is exactly the reason A is true, so R explains A.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Every shape with rotational symmetry has line symmetry. Reason (R): A parallelogram has rotational symmetry of order 2.
questions.why: A is false: a parallelogram has rotational symmetry of order 2 but no line of symmetry, so it is a counter-example. R is true, but it does not support A.

questions.q: A figure has angle of rotational symmetry 40°. Its order
questions.why: Order = 360° ÷ angle of rotational symmetry = 360 ÷ 40 = 9. The shape matches itself 9 times in a full turn.

questions.q: An isosceles triangle has rotational symmetry of order
questions.why: An isosceles triangle matches itself only after a full 360° turn. That counts as order 1, which means no real rotational symmetry. It has a line of symmetry, but that is a different kind.

questions.q: Case: A ceiling fan has 3 identical blades evenly spaced. Smallest turn after which it looks the same?
questions.why: With 3 identical blades evenly spaced, the fan matches itself 3 times in a full turn. The smallest turn is 360° ÷ 3 = 120°.

questions.q: Case: A logo looks the same after turns of 60°, 120°, 180°… Its order is
questions.why: The smallest turn that matches is 60°, so order = 360° ÷ 60° = 6. The logo matches itself 6 times in a full turn.

questions.q: Which pair has the same order of rotational symmetry?
questions.why: A rectangle and a rhombus both look the same after a half-turn but not a quarter-turn, so both have order 2. A square has order 4, a triangle 3 and a hexagon 6, so those pairs differ.

questions.q: A shape has 4 lines of symmetry and is a quadrilateral. It must be a
questions.why: Of the quadrilaterals, only the square has 4 lines of symmetry. A rhombus and a rectangle have 2 each, and a kite has 1.

questions.q: Total lines of symmetry of: equilateral triangle + regular hexagon + rectangle
questions.why: Equilateral triangle 3 + regular hexagon 6 + rectangle 2 = 11 lines of symmetry. Regular polygons have as many lines as sides.

courses.title: Ch 13 · Visualising Solid Shapes
courses.summary: Plane figures and solid shapes, faces, edges and vertices, nets for building 3-D shapes, drawing solids with oblique and isometric sketches, and seeing sections and shadows of solids.
outcomes: Learners can name faces, edges and vertices of common solids
Learners can identify nets of cubes, cuboids, cylinders, cones and pyramids
Learners can draw oblique and isometric sketches
Learners can describe cross-sections, shadows and views from different directions

scenes.text: Kabir counts his gift box: 6 flat faces, 12 edges, 8 corners.
His football has no flat face, no edge, no corner at all.
Solids are described by their faces, edges and vertices.

steps.title: 2-D and 3-D
steps.body: Plane (2-D) figures have length and breadth: square, circle, triangle. Solid (3-D) shapes also have height (depth): cube, cuboid, cylinder, cone, sphere, pyramid, prism.

steps.title: Key counts
steps.body:
- **Face**: flat surface. **Edge**: line where two faces meet. **Vertex**: corner where edges meet.
- Cube / cuboid: F 6, E 12, V 8
- Triangular prism: F 5, E 9, V 6
- Square pyramid: F 5, E 8, V 5
- Triangular pyramid (tetrahedron): F 4, E 6, V 4
- Cylinder: 2 flat faces + 1 curved surface, 2 curved edges
- Cone: 1 flat face + curved surface, 1 edge, 1 vertex
- Sphere: 1 curved surface only

steps.title: Euler's formula (for polyhedra)
steps.body: For solids with flat faces: **F + V − E = 2**. Cube: 6 + 8 − 12 = 2 ✓.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
A pentagonal prism has 7 faces and 10 vertices. How many edges?

- F + V − E = 2 → 7 + 10 − E = 2 → **E = 15**

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Name a solid with 1 vertex, 1 flat circular face → **cone**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Counting the curved surface of a cylinder as a 'face' in polyhedron formulas — Euler's formula applies only to flat-faced solids.
- Confusing prisms (two identical ends) and pyramids (one base, triangular sides meeting at an apex).

activity.prompt: Match the solid with its (faces, edges, vertices).

quiz.why: A cuboid has 4 edges on the top, 4 on the bottom and 4 joining them: 4 + 4 + 4 = 12 edges, just like a cube.
A square pyramid has 4 corners on the square base and 1 apex at the top, so 4 + 1 = 5 vertices.
A sphere has only one smooth curved surface, with no flat faces, edges or corners. A cone has a vertex at its tip, and a pyramid and cube have many.

quiz.q: F + V − E for a tetrahedron
quiz.why: A tetrahedron has 4 faces, 4 vertices and 6 edges. F + V − E = 4 + 4 − 6 = 2, which is Euler's formula.

quiz.q: A dice is shaped like a
quiz.why: A die has 6 equal square faces, so it is a cube. A cuboid has some unequal faces, so it does not fit as well.

scenes.text: Asha draws six squares joined in a cross on card.
She folds along the lines and tapes the edges — a cube!
A flat pattern that folds into a solid is called a net.

steps.title: Nets
steps.body:
A **net** is a 2-D skeleton-outline which, when folded, gives a 3-D shape.

- Cube: 6 squares (there are **11** different nets of a cube)
- Cuboid: 6 rectangles (3 pairs)
- Cylinder: 2 circles + 1 rectangle
- Cone: 1 circle + 1 sector
- Triangular prism: 2 triangles + 3 rectangles
- Square pyramid: 1 square + 4 triangles

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Is a row of 6 squares in a straight line a net of a cube?

- No — when folded, the end squares overlap and two faces stay open. **Not a net.**

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: On a die opposite faces add to 7. In a cross-shaped net, faces with one square between them in a line are opposite. If 1 is opposite to the square two steps away, that square must show **6**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Any 6 joined squares is not automatically a cube net — check that no two faces overlap when folded.
- Forgetting that a cylinder's rectangle length equals the circumference of the circle.

activity.prompt: Match each net with its solid.

quiz.why: A cylinder has two flat circles (top and bottom). Its curved side opens out into one rectangle. So the net is 2 circles and 1 rectangle.

quiz.q: Number of different nets of a cube
quiz.why: There are exactly 11 different ways to unfold a cube into a flat net of 6 connected squares.

quiz.q: Net with 4 triangles only folds into
quiz.why: A solid with 4 triangular faces is a tetrahedron, also called a triangular pyramid. A cone has a circle and a sector, a cube has squares.

quiz.q: Opposite faces of a die add up to
quiz.why: On a standard die, opposite faces add up to 7: 1 with 6, 2 with 5, and 3 with 4.
A cone's curved surface opens out into a sector (a slice of a circle). Its flat base is a circle, so the net is a circle plus a sector.

lessons.title: Drawing solids: oblique and isometric sketches

scenes.text: Ravi must draw a brick in his notebook.
First he draws a quick freehand oblique sketch.
Then on isometric dot paper he draws one with true lengths.

steps.title: Oblique sketch
steps.body: Draw the front face as a true rectangle/square, then draw parallel slanting lines for depth and join. Lengths along the slant are not to scale, but the sketch gives a 3-D feel. Hidden edges may be dotted.

steps.title: Isometric sketch
steps.body: Drawn on **isometric dot paper** (dots forming equilateral triangles). Measurements along all three directions are **true to size**. A cube's isometric sketch looks like a hexagon with three visible faces.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Draw an isometric sketch of a cuboid 4 × 3 × 2 units: mark 4 units along one slant direction, 3 along the other, 2 vertically; complete parallel edges.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Three cubes of side 2 cm are placed end to end. The new cuboid is **6 cm × 2 cm × 2 cm**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Expecting oblique sketches to show true lengths.
- Drawing isometric lines at random angles; they follow the dot grid.

statements.s: Isometric sketches keep true measurements.
Oblique sketches show exact lengths for all edges.
statements.why: Depth edges are not to scale.

statements.s: Hidden edges can be shown dotted.
An isometric sketch of a cube shows 3 faces.

quiz.q: Isometric dot paper is made of
quiz.why: Isometric dot paper has dots placed at the corners of equilateral triangles. This lets us draw 3D shapes with lines in three directions.

quiz.q: Two cubes of side 3 cm joined face to face make a cuboid
quiz.why: Joining two 3 cm cubes face to face doubles one side to 3 + 3 = 6 cm. The other two sides stay 3 cm, so it is 6 × 3 × 3.

quiz.q: In an oblique sketch, the front face is
quiz.why: In an oblique sketch the front face is drawn in its true shape and size. Only the depth is drawn slanted.
Oblique sketches need no special paper, so they are quicker by hand. Isometric sketches need dot paper to keep the angles right.

quiz.q: An isometric drawing of a cube looks like a
quiz.why: Seen isometrically, a cube's outline has six equal sides, so it looks like a regular hexagon. The three visible faces are rhombuses.

lessons.title: Viewing different sections of a solid

scenes.text: A loaf sliced straight across shows a rectangle-like face each time.
A torch on a cone shows a triangle on the wall from the side, a circle from above.
Solids look different from the front, the side and the top.

steps.title: Cross-sections by cutting
steps.body:
Cutting a solid with a plane gives a **cross-section**.

- Cube cut parallel to a face → square
- Cylinder cut across (parallel to base) → circle; cut vertically through the axis → rectangle
- Cone cut parallel to base → circle; vertical cut through apex → triangle
- Sphere → always a circle

steps.title: Shadows
steps.body: A shadow is a 2-D view of a 3-D object. A cube's shadow (light straight on a face) is a square; a cylinder lying sideways casts a rectangle; a sphere always casts a circle (with light from far away).

steps.title: Front, side and top views
steps.body: Architects draw a solid as three views. A cylinder standing up: front view = rectangle, side view = rectangle, top view = circle.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: A cone standing on its base: front view **triangle**, top view **circle (with a centre point)**.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: A stack of 3 cubes in an L-shape (2 on the floor, 1 on top of the left): front view shows 3 squares in an L; top view shows 2 squares side by side.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking every cross-section of a cube is a square. Slanted cuts can give rectangles, triangles, even hexagons.
- Mixing up the top view and the front view.

activity.prompt: What shape is seen?

items.text: Top view of a standing cylinder
Front view of a standing cylinder
Cube cut parallel to a face
Shadow of a brick seen from above

quiz.q: Cross-section of a sphere is always a
quiz.why: Any flat cut through a sphere gives a circle. The size changes with where you cut, but the shape is always a circle.
Looking down from above, a cone shows its round base, so the top view is a circle.

quiz.q: Vertical cut of a cylinder through its axis
quiz.why: A vertical cut through the axis of a cylinder gives a rectangle. Its height is the cylinder's height and its width is the diameter.

quiz.q: Shadow of a cube with light straight onto a face
quiz.why: Light falling straight onto one face of a cube makes a shadow the same shape as that face. Every face is a square, so the shadow is a square.

quiz.q: Which solid has the same view from front, side and top?
quiz.why: A cube shows a square from the front, side and top. A cylinder or cone shows a rectangle or triangle from the side but a circle from above.

questions.q: A cube has how many faces?
questions.why: A cube has 6 faces, all squares: top, bottom, front, back, left and right.

questions.q: Which solid has 1 curved surface only?
questions.why: A sphere is one single curved surface with no flat parts. A cone and a cylinder also have flat faces.

questions.q: Vertices of a triangular prism
questions.why: A triangular prism has a triangle at each end. Each has 3 corners, so 3 + 3 = 6 vertices.

questions.q: Net of a cube has how many squares?
questions.why: A cube has 6 faces, so its net needs 6 squares, one for each face.

questions.q: Edges of a square pyramid
questions.why: A square pyramid has 4 edges around the base and 4 slanting edges up to the apex: 4 + 4 = 8 edges.

questions.q: Top view of a standing cylinder
questions.why: Looking down on a standing cylinder you see its round top, so the view is a circle.

questions.q: Euler: F = 8, V = 6, E = ?
questions.why: Euler's formula: F + V − E = 2. So 8 + 6 − E = 2, giving 14 − E = 2 and E = 12.

questions.q: Assertion (A): A cylinder is a polyhedron. Reason (R): A polyhedron has only flat polygonal faces.
questions.why: A is false: a cylinder has a curved surface, so it is not a polyhedron. R is true: a polyhedron has only flat polygon faces. R is the reason A is false.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Isometric sketches show exact measurements. Reason (R): They are drawn on isometric dot paper.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: A is true here in the sense that the drawing keeps edge lengths to scale along the three axes. R is true because they are drawn on isometric dot paper. The grid is what keeps lengths true, so R explains A.

questions.q: Cross-section of a cone parallel to its base
questions.why: A cut parallel to the base of a cone gives a circle that is smaller than the base. The cut near the tip gives a tiny circle.

questions.q: A hexagonal prism has F, E, V =
questions.why: A hexagonal prism has 2 hexagon ends + 6 side rectangles = 8 faces. It has 6 + 6 = 12 vertices and 6 + 6 + 6 = 18 edges. Check: 8 + 12 − 18 = 2.

questions.q: Case: A tent is a triangular prism. How many flat surfaces does its canvas + floor have?
questions.why: The tent has 2 triangular ends and 3 rectangles (two sloping sides and the floor). 2 + 3 = 5 flat surfaces.

questions.q: Case: 8 cubes of side 1 cm make a bigger cube. Its side?
questions.why: A big cube made of 8 small cubes is 2 layers of 2 × 2. Its side is 2 × 1 cm = 2 cm, since 2 × 2 × 2 = 8.

questions.q: A pyramid with an octagonal base has how many edges?
questions.why: An octagon base has 8 edges. Each of the 8 corners joins to the apex with one slanting edge, giving 8 more. 8 + 8 = 16 edges.

questions.q: A polyhedron has 12 faces and 30 edges. Vertices?
questions.why: Euler's formula: F + V − E = 2. So 12 + V − 30 = 2, which gives V = 20.

questions.q: Which cannot be a cross-section of a cube?
questions.why: A flat cut through a cube always gives a straight-sided polygon (triangle, rectangle, pentagon or hexagon). A circle has a curved edge, so it is not possible.

courses.title: Revision & Practice · Class 7 Maths
courses.summary: One place to revise every Class 7 Maths formula and method, followed by two full mock papers covering all chapters with questions graded from easy to challenging.
outcomes: Learners can recall every key formula and rule from the year
Learners can choose the right method for mixed questions
Learners can manage time across a full-length mock paper
Learners can identify their weak chapters and revise them

scenes.text: Ishaan has one evening left before his final exam.
Instead of rereading the whole book, he works through a one-page formula sheet.
He ticks each rule he can explain with an example.

steps.title: Integers and rationals
steps.body:
- Same signs add, different signs subtract; a − b = a + (−b)
- (−)(−) = +, (−)(+) = −; same for ÷
- a ÷ 0 undefined; 0 is the additive identity, 1 the multiplicative identity
- Rational p/q, q ≠ 0; standard form: q > 0, HCF(p, q) = 1

steps.title: Fractions and decimals
steps.body:
- (a/b) × (c/d) = ac/bd; divide → multiply by reciprocal
- × by 10ⁿ: point moves n places right; ÷: left
- Decimal × decimal: total places = sum of places

steps.title: Comparing quantities
steps.body:
- Percent = per hundred; fraction → % × 100
- Profit = SP − CP; Profit % = Profit/CP × 100
- SI = PRT/100; A = P + SI

steps.title: Algebra and equations
steps.body:
- Like terms only add; subtract = change every sign then add
- Transpose: + ↔ −, × ↔ ÷
- aᵐaⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ; aᵐ/aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ; (aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ; aᵐbᵐ = (ab)ᵐ; a⁰ = 1
- Standard form k × 10ⁿ, 1 ≤ k < 10

steps.title: Solved mixed example
steps.body:
Solve 3x − 7 = 2(x + 4).

- Expand: 3x − 7 = 2x + 8
- Transpose: 3x − 2x = 8 + 7 → x = 15
- Check: 45 − 7 = 38 and 2 × 19 = 38 ✓

steps.title: Common exam slips
steps.body:
- Sign errors with negatives — circle each sign.
- Units missing in answers.
- Not checking equation answers by substitution.

quiz.why: (−2)⁴ = 16 because an even power of a negative number is positive. 2² = 4, so 16 ÷ 4 = 4.
25% = 1/4, and 1/4 × 3/4 = 3/16. Multiply the numerators and the denominators.
500 000 = 5 × 100 000 = 5 × 10⁵. In standard form the number before the power of 10 must be at least 1 and less than 10.
Subtracting a bracket changes the signs inside: 3a − 2 − a + 5. Combine like terms: 3a − a = 2a and −2 + 5 = 3, giving 2a + 3.

lessons.title: Formula sheet: geometry, mensuration and data

scenes.text: Ishaan's sister sticks a geometry checklist on the fridge.
Every time he gets water he reads one rule aloud.
By morning, angles, areas and data rules are second nature.

steps.title: Lines, angles, triangles
steps.body:
- Complementary 90°, supplementary 180°, linear pair 180°, vertically opposite equal
- Parallel lines: corresponding equal, alternate interior equal, co-interior sum 180°
- Triangle angle sum 180°; exterior angle = sum of interior opposite angles
- Two sides sum > third side; Pythagoras: h² = a² + b²

steps.title: Mensuration
steps.body:
- Rectangle A = lb, P = 2(l + b); Square A = s², P = 4s
- Parallelogram A = bh; Triangle A = ½bh
- Circle C = 2πr, A = πr²; π ≈ 22/7 ≈ 3.14
- 1 m² = 10 000 cm²; 1 ha = 10 000 m²

steps.title: Data, symmetry, solids
steps.body:
- Mean = sum/n; Range = max − min; Mode = most frequent; Median = middle (ordered)
- Probability = favourable/total, between 0 and 1
- Regular n-gon: n lines of symmetry, rotational order n, angle 360°/n
- Euler: F + V − E = 2

steps.title: Solved mixed example
steps.body:
A circular park of radius 14 m has a path along its edge. Find the length of fencing (π = 22/7) and the area of the park.

- C = 2 × 22/7 × 14 = 88 m
- A = 22/7 × 196 = 616 m²

steps.title: Common exam slips
steps.body:
- Using diameter in πr².
- Forgetting ½ in triangle area.
- Not ordering data before finding the median.

activity.prompt: Match formula to shape.

quiz.q: Exterior angle 120°, one opposite interior 50°. Other?
quiz.why: An exterior angle equals the sum of the two opposite interior angles. So the other angle = 120° − 50° = 70°.
Area = πr² = 22/7 × 21 × 21 = 22 × 3 × 21 = 1386 cm². The answer 132 is the circumference-like value, not area.
Put the numbers in order: 2, 5, 6, 8, 9. The middle value is 6, so the median is 6.

quiz.q: Lines of symmetry of a regular hexagon
quiz.why: A regular polygon has as many lines of symmetry as it has sides. A hexagon has 6 sides, so 6 lines.
By Pythagoras, 5² + 12² = 25 + 144 = 169. The hypotenuse is √169 = 13.

lessons.title: How to attempt a mock paper

scenes.text: Meera used to get stuck on question 3 and run out of time.
Now she reads the paper, does all easy questions first, marks hard ones, and returns later.
Her score rose by 15 marks without learning anything new.

steps.title: Exam strategy
steps.body:
- First 5 minutes: read the whole paper; mark easy (✓), medium (~), hard (!) questions.
- Do ✓ questions first, then ~, then !.
- Spend time in proportion to marks.
- Leave 10 minutes to check signs, units and copying errors.

steps.title: Show steps
steps.body: Write formula → substitution → answer with unit. Steps earn marks even if the final answer slips.

steps.title: Solved example: checking an answer
steps.body: You found x = 4 for 3x + 5 = 17. Check: 3(4) + 5 = 17 ✓. Takes 5 seconds and catches many errors.

steps.title: Solved example: estimation
steps.body: Before computing 48.75 × 4.2, estimate 50 × 4 = 200. Your answer 204.75 is believable; 2047.5 would not be.

steps.title: Mistakes students make in exams
steps.body:
- Spending 15 minutes on one question.
- Leaving MCQs blank (there is no negative marking in most school tests — check your paper's rules).
- Not reading 'NOT' or 'EXCEPT' in a question.

activity.prompt: Before your mock paper, tick off:
items: I have revised the formula sheets
I have a pencil, scale, eraser and compass
I will read the whole paper first
I will do easy questions first
I will check signs and units at the end
I will note my weak chapters after marking

quiz.q: Best first step in an exam?
quiz.why: Reading the whole paper first helps you plan your time and choose the order of questions. Starting the hardest question first can waste time.
Round the numbers: 19.8 is about 20 and 5.1 is about 5. 20 × 5 = 100, so the estimate is about 100.
Writing steps shows your method, and examiners can give marks for correct steps even if the final answer has a slip.
To check a solution, put x = 3 into the equation: 2(3) − 1 = 6 − 1 = 5, which matches the right side. So x = 3 is correct.

quiz.q: A question says "Which is NOT…". You should
quiz.why: Underlining NOT reminds you the question asks for the odd one out, so you do not pick a true statement by mistake. Misreading is a common cause of lost marks.

scenes.text: Set a timer for 20 minutes and attempt these questions without notes.
Then mark yourself and read every explanation.

steps.title: Instructions
steps.body: This practice set mixes all chapters. Attempt the activity and quiz, then take the final exam of this course, which contains Mock Paper 2.

steps.title: Model answer 1
steps.body:
Q: The angles of a triangle are in ratio 1 : 2 : 3. Classify the triangle.

- 6 parts = 180 → 30°, 60°, 90°
- **Right-angled triangle**

steps.title: Model answer 2
steps.body:
Q: A sum of ₹8000 at 5% p.a. SI for 3 years. Amount?

- SI = 8000 × 5 × 3/100 = 1200
- **A = ₹9200**

steps.title: Mark yourself honestly
steps.body: If you got a question wrong, write which chapter it came from. Two or more wrong from a chapter → revise that chapter's course.

statements.why: Any non-zero number divided by itself is 1.

statements.s: The mean of 4, 6, 8 is 6
Vertically opposite angles add to 180°
Area of a circle of radius 7 cm is 44 cm²
statements.why: 44 cm is the circumference; area is 154 cm².

quiz.why: (−3) × (−4) = 12, and 12 × (−5) = −60. An odd number of negative factors gives a negative product.
4x/3 = 8, so 4x = 24 (multiply both sides by 3). Then x = 24 ÷ 4 = 6.
Profit = 540 − 450 = ₹90. Profit % = 90/450 × 100 = 20%, always taken on the cost price.
A Pythagorean triplet satisfies a² + b² = c². Here 6² + 8² = 36 + 64 = 100 = 10². The others fail the test.

quiz.q: Probability of a prime on a die
quiz.why: The prime numbers on a die are 2, 3 and 5, which is 3 outcomes out of 6. Probability = 3/6 = 1/2. (1 is not prime.)
Multiply both numbers by 100: 7.2 ÷ 0.08 = 720 ÷ 8 = 90.

questions.why: Dividing a negative by a negative gives a positive. 48 ÷ 6 = 8, so the answer is 8.
First divide 45 by 3 to get 15. Then multiply by 2 to get 30.
The mode is the value that appears most often. 5 appears 3 times, while 3 appears twice and 7 once.

questions.q: Supplement of 47°
questions.why: Supplementary angles add to 180°. So the supplement is 180° − 47° = 133°. The 43° is the complement, which uses 90°.

questions.q: Solve 7y − 3 = 25
Simple interest on ₹1200 at 6% for 2 years
questions.why: SI = P × R × T/100 = 1200 × 6 × 2/100 = ₹144. The amount would be ₹1344, which also includes the principal.
Use a common denominator of 8: 3/4 = 6/8. Then −5/8 + 6/8 = 1/8.

questions.q: Lines of symmetry of an equilateral triangle
questions.why: An equilateral triangle is a regular polygon with 3 equal sides, so it has 3 lines of symmetry, one through each vertex.

questions.q: Assertion (A): The median is unaffected by one very large value. Reason (R): The median depends on the order of values, not their sizes.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: A is true: the median is the middle value, so one very large value does not change it. R is true because the median depends on position in the order, not on size. R explains A.

questions.q: Area of a triangle with base 14 cm and height 9 cm
questions.why: Area of a triangle = ½ × base × height = ½ × 14 × 9 = 7 × 9 = 63 cm². The 126 is base × height without the half.

questions.q: Simplify (2⁴ × 3³)/(2² × 3)
questions.why: Subtract powers of the same base: 2⁴/2² = 2² = 4, and 3³/3 = 3² = 9. So 4 × 9 = 36.

questions.q: An item sold for ₹920 gives 15% profit. CP?
Case: A rectangular park 50 m × 30 m has a 2.5 m wide path outside it. Path area?
Case: Temperatures at 6 a.m. for a week: −2, 0, 3, −1, −4, 2, 5 °C. Mean?
In △ABC, ∠A : ∠B : ∠C = 2 : 3 : 4. The exterior angle at C is
questions.why: Parts total 2 + 3 + 4 = 9, so each part is 180° ÷ 9 = 20°. ∠C = 4 × 20° = 80°. The exterior angle at C = 180° − 80° = 100°.

questions.q: A wheel of radius 21 cm covers 660 m. Number of revolutions? (π = 22/7)
questions.why: Circumference = 2 × 22/7 × 21 = 132 cm. Distance 660 m = 66 000 cm. Revolutions = 66 000 ÷ 132 = 500.

questions.q: Sum of three consecutive odd numbers is 81. The largest is
questions.why: Let the numbers be x, x + 2 and x + 4. Then 3x + 6 = 81, so x = 25; the numbers are 25, 27, 29 and the largest is 29.

questions.q: If a = −1, b = 2, c = −3, find a²b − b²c + abc

school-c7-science-a.title: Class 7 Science · Part A
school-c7-science-a.description: Every chapter of Class 7 Science (NCERT 2023–24 rationalised order) as its own course: nutrition, heat, acids, light, electricity and more, explained with everyday examples and chapter tests.

courses.title: Ch 1 · Nutrition in Plants
courses.summary: How green plants make their own food by photosynthesis, how we test a leaf for starch, and how other plants survive as parasites, insect-eaters, saprotrophs or partners in symbiosis — plus how soil nutrients are replenished.
outcomes: Learners can distinguish autotrophic and heterotrophic nutrition
Learners can explain photosynthesis: raw materials, conditions and products
Learners can describe parasitic, insectivorous, saprotrophic and symbiotic nutrition with examples
Learners can explain how nitrogen is returned to the soil

scenes.text: Ria's mother cooks food for the family. "Who cooks for our mango tree?" Ria asks.
Mother smiles: "The tree is its own cook — its leaves make food using sunlight."
"And the cow?" — "The cow eats grass. It depends on plants."

steps.title: Nutrients and nutrition
steps.body: Food gives energy and materials for growth and repair. The components of food — **carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins and minerals** — are **nutrients**. **Nutrition** is the way an organism takes in food and uses it.

steps.title: Two modes
steps.body:
- **Autotrophic** (auto = self, trophos = nourishment): organisms make their own food from simple substances. Green plants are **autotrophs**.
- **Heterotrophic**: organisms take food made by others. Animals, fungi and most bacteria are **heterotrophs**.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Classify: rose plant, human, mushroom, grass, lion.

- Autotrophs: **rose, grass**
- Heterotrophs: **human, mushroom, lion**

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
Q: Why are green plants called producers?

A: Because they make (produce) food, and all other organisms depend on them directly or indirectly for food.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking mushrooms are plants that make food — they are fungi and cannot photosynthesise.
- Thinking plants take 'food' from the soil. Soil gives water and minerals; food is made in the leaves.

activity.prompt: Autotroph or heterotroph?

quiz.why: Auto means self and troph means feeding. Autotrophs, such as green plants, make their own food rather than eating other organisms.
A mushroom is a fungus. It has no chlorophyll, so it takes ready-made food from other sources and is a heterotroph. Wheat, mango and algae make their own food.
Nutrients are the components of food, such as carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins and minerals. Sunlight and oxygen are not nutrients.
Green plants make food by photosynthesis, so they are producers. Consumers and decomposers get food from other organisms.
Hetero means other. Heterotrophic organisms cannot make their own food and feed on others.

scenes.text: A leaf is like a kitchen. Its green pigment, chlorophyll, captures sunlight.
Water and minerals come up from the roots; carbon dioxide enters through tiny pores.
Out comes sugar (food) and oxygen — the oxygen we breathe!

steps.title: What happens
steps.body:
**Photosynthesis** (photo = light, synthesis = to combine) is the process by which green plants make carbohydrates from carbon dioxide and water using sunlight, in the presence of chlorophyll. Oxygen is released.

Word equation:

**Carbon dioxide + Water → (sunlight, chlorophyll) → Carbohydrate + Oxygen**

steps.title: Parts involved
steps.body:
- **Leaves**: food factories; contain **chlorophyll** in chloroplasts.
- **Stomata**: tiny pores mainly on the leaf surface, surrounded by **guard cells**; they let CO₂ in and O₂ out, and water vapour escapes through them.
- **Roots** absorb water and minerals; **vessels (xylem)** carry them to leaves.
- The carbohydrate made is stored as **starch**.

steps.title: Not only leaves
steps.body: Green stems and other green parts can also photosynthesise. Leaves of other colours (red, brown, violet) also contain chlorophyll; the green colour is masked by other pigments. **Algae** (green slimy patches in ponds) photosynthesise too.

steps.title: Solved example 1: starch test
steps.body:
Test a leaf for starch:

1. Boil the leaf in water, then in alcohol (on a water bath) to remove chlorophyll.
2. Wash it and add a few drops of **iodine solution**.
3. A **blue-black** colour shows starch is present.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: A potted plant is kept in a dark room for 3 days, then a leaf is tested with iodine. Result: no blue-black colour. Reason: without sunlight there is no photosynthesis, and the stored starch is used up.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying plants 'breathe in CO₂ and breathe out O₂' as respiration. That describes photosynthesis; plants also respire all the time, taking in O₂.
- Writing that the product of photosynthesis is starch directly. Glucose (a carbohydrate) is made first and then converted to starch.

activity.prompt: Order the steps of the starch test on a leaf.
items: Pluck a leaf from a plant kept in sunlight
Boil it in water
Boil it in alcohol on a water bath to remove chlorophyll
Wash it in water
Add iodine solution and look for blue-black colour

quiz.why: Plants take in carbon dioxide from the air through stomata. It is a raw material, along with water, for making food in photosynthesis.
Chlorophyll is the green pigment in leaves that traps sunlight energy for photosynthesis. Haemoglobin and melanin are found in animals.
Stomata are tiny pores on leaves that let gases in and out. Villi and alveoli are found in animals, and veins carry fluids.
Iodine solution turns blue-black when starch is present. This is the standard test to show that a leaf has made starch.
In photosynthesis plants make glucose and release oxygen as a by-product. The oxygen goes out into the air through stomata.
Water moves from the roots up to the leaves through xylem vessels. Stomata let gases pass, and guard cells only control stomata.

scenes.text: Aman sees yellow, wire-like threads wrapped around a hedge plant.
His teacher says it is Cuscuta (amarbel). It has no chlorophyll and steals food from the host.
At home, fuzzy patches on old bread are fungi — they feed on dead matter.

steps.title: Parasitic nutrition
steps.body:
A **parasite** lives on or inside another organism (**host**) and takes food from it, harming it.

- **Cuscuta (amarbel)**: yellow, tubular, no chlorophyll; twines around host plants.
- Mosquitoes, lice and leeches are animal parasites.

steps.title: Insectivorous plants
steps.body:
Some plants trap and digest insects to get extra nutrients (especially nitrogen) because they grow in nitrogen-poor soil.

- **Pitcher plant**: a leaf forms a pitcher with a lid; insects slip in, hairs stop their escape, digestive juices digest them. These plants are green and still photosynthesise.
- Venus flytrap is another example.

steps.title: Saprotrophic nutrition
steps.body:
Organisms that get nutrients from **dead and decaying matter** are **saprotrophs**. They secrete digestive juices onto the matter, convert it to solution and absorb it.

- Fungi: mushrooms, bread mould. Fungi grow well in **warm, humid** conditions — that is why food and leather spoil in the rainy season.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Q: Cuscuta is called a parasite. Give two reasons.

A: (1) It has no chlorophyll, so it cannot make food. (2) It takes ready-made food from a living host plant and harms it.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
Q: Why do pickles and leather goods get fungus in the monsoon?

A: Fungal spores are always in the air. In warm, humid weather they germinate on moist food or leather and grow.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking the pitcher plant is a total heterotroph. It photosynthesises; insects only add nutrients.
- Calling saprotrophs 'parasites' — saprotrophs feed on dead matter, parasites on living hosts.

activity.prompt: Match the organism with its mode of nutrition.

quiz.why: Cuscuta (amarbel) has no chlorophyll and takes ready-made food from the host plant it grows on. That makes it a parasite.

quiz.q: The pitcher in a pitcher plant is a modified
quiz.why: In a pitcher plant the pitcher-shaped part is a modified leaf. It traps insects.
Fungi are saprotrophs, which feed on dead and decaying matter. They break it down and absorb the nutrients.

quiz.q: Insectivorous plants mainly need insects for
quiz.why: Insectivorous plants grow in soil poor in nitrogen. They trap insects to get this missing nutrient. They still make food by photosynthesis.
Fungi grow best where it is warm and moist. Moisture helps them grow, while cold and dry conditions slow them down.

scenes.text: After harvesting wheat, Kisan Babulal sows gram (chana) in the same field.
Gram roots have nodules with bacteria that turn nitrogen from the air into a form plants can use.
Next season, the soil is richer and wheat grows well with less fertiliser.

steps.title: Symbiosis
steps.body:
