**Symbiosis** is a close relationship in which two different organisms live together and **both benefit**.

- **Lichens**: a fungus and an alga (or cyanobacterium). The alga makes food by photosynthesis; the fungus provides shelter, water and minerals.
- Some fungi live in the roots of trees, getting food and giving nutrients.

steps.title: Replenishing nutrients
steps.body:
Plants keep absorbing minerals, so soil nutrients get used up. They are replenished by **manures and fertilisers**, and naturally by bacteria.

- **Rhizobium** bacteria live in the **root nodules of leguminous plants** (gram, peas, moong, beans). They convert atmospheric **nitrogen** into a usable form for the plant; the plant gives them food and shelter. This is also symbiosis.

steps.title: Why nitrogen matters
steps.body: Nitrogen is needed to make **proteins**. Air is about 78% nitrogen, but plants cannot use nitrogen gas directly.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Q: Why do farmers grow pulses between cereal crops?

A: Pulses are legumes; Rhizobium in their root nodules fixes nitrogen, enriching the soil, so less fertiliser is needed for the next crop.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
Q: In a lichen, what does each partner provide?

A: Alga → food (by photosynthesis). Fungus → shelter, water and minerals.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying Rhizobium is a fungus — it is a bacterium.
- Thinking plants absorb nitrogen gas through leaves.

statements.s: Rhizobium lives in root nodules of legumes.
Lichens are made of an alga and a fungus.
In symbiosis only one partner benefits.
Plants can directly use nitrogen gas from the air.
Nitrogen is needed to make proteins.

quiz.why: Rhizobium is a bacterium that lives in root nodules of legumes. It changes nitrogen from air into a form the plant can use.
Root nodules with Rhizobium are found in legume plants such as gram, peas and beans. Rice, maize and wheat are not legumes.

quiz.q: In a lichen, food is made by
quiz.why: In a lichen the alga has chlorophyll, so it makes the food. The fungus gives shelter and water. Both gain, which is symbiosis.

quiz.q: Soil nutrients can be replenished by
quiz.why: Crops remove nutrients from soil, so we add manures and fertilisers to replenish them. Sunlight and pesticides do not add nutrients.
Symbiosis is a partnership in which both organisms benefit, like the alga and fungus in a lichen.

questions.q: Mode of nutrition of green plants
questions.why: Green plants make their own food using sunlight, so their mode of nutrition is autotrophic. Heterotrophs, parasites and saprotrophs depend on others.

questions.q: Food factories of a plant
questions.why: Leaves have most of the chlorophyll and stomata, so most photosynthesis happens there. That is why they are called the food factories.

questions.q: Gas released in photosynthesis
questions.why: Photosynthesis takes in CO₂ and water and gives out oxygen (O₂). CO₂ is taken in, not released.

questions.q: Iodine with starch gives
questions.why: Iodine solution turns blue-black with starch. So a blue-black colour on a leaf shows that starch is present.

questions.q: Cuscuta lacks
questions.why: Cuscuta has no chlorophyll, so it cannot make food by photosynthesis. It depends on its host plant.

questions.q: Bread mould is an example of
questions.why: Bread mould grows on dead, decaying matter and absorbs food from it. So it is a saprotroph.

questions.q: Openings controlled by guard cells
questions.why: Guard cells surround each stoma and open or close it. Root hairs and nodules are on roots, and veins carry fluids.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Pitcher plants trap insects. Reason (R): They grow in soil that is poor in nitrogen.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: A is true: pitcher plants trap insects. R is true: they live in nitrogen-poor soil. Insects give them nitrogen, so R explains A.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Plants with red leaves cannot photosynthesise. Reason (R): Red leaves have no chlorophyll.
questions.why: A is false because red leaves still have chlorophyll, hidden by other pigments, so they photosynthesise. R is false for the same reason. Both are false.

questions.q: Why is a destarched plant kept in the dark before an experiment?
questions.why: Keeping a plant in the dark uses up its stored starch. If starch is found later in sunlight, we know it was made during the experiment.

questions.q: Which pair is symbiotic?
questions.why: Rhizobium lives in gram root nodules, gets food from the plant and gives it nitrogen. Both gain, which is symbiosis. Cuscuta and mosquito harm their host.

questions.q: Case: A leaf is partly covered with black paper and kept in sunlight. After the starch test, the covered part
questions.why: The covered part gets no light, so no photosynthesis and no starch are made there. It will not turn blue-black with iodine.

questions.q: Case: A farmer notices his wheat yield falling every year. Best natural remedy?
questions.why: Growing legumes in rotation lets Rhizobium put nitrogen back into the soil. That restores fertility naturally. Burning stubble or growing wheat again does not help.

questions.q: Raw materials of photosynthesis come from
questions.why: Carbon dioxide comes from the air, and water and minerals come from the soil. Sunlight gives energy but is not a raw material.

questions.q: Desert plants like cactus have spines instead of leaves. Where does photosynthesis occur?
questions.why: A cactus has spines in place of leaves, to save water. Its stem is green and has chlorophyll, so it carries out photosynthesis.

questions.q: If all green plants disappeared, the first major problem for animals would be
questions.why: Green plants are the producers of food and release oxygen. Without them animals would lose their food supply and the oxygen would fall.

courses.title: Ch 2 · Nutrition in Animals
courses.summary: Different ways animals take food, the human digestive system from mouth to anus, how teeth, saliva, stomach, liver, pancreas and intestines work, digestion in grass-eaters, and feeding in Amoeba.
outcomes: Learners can describe ways animals take in food
Learners can trace food through the human digestive system and name each part's role
Learners can explain digestion of starch, proteins and fats and absorption by villi
Learners can explain rumination in cattle and feeding in Amoeba

lessons.title: How animals take food; the five steps

scenes.text: In a nature film a snake swallows a frog whole.
A butterfly sucks nectar through a long tube.
Meanwhile Vikram chews his roti. Every animal has its own way to eat!

steps.title: Ways of taking food
steps.body:
- Bees, hummingbirds: **sucking** nectar
- Snakes: **swallowing** whole
- Starfish: pushes out its stomach to eat soft animals inside shells
- Mosquito: **sucking** blood
- Ant, humans: **chewing**
- Amoeba: **capturing** with pseudopodia

steps.title: Five steps of nutrition
steps.body:
1. **Ingestion** – taking food into the body
2. **Digestion** – breaking complex food into simple soluble substances
3. **Absorption** – digested food passes into blood
4. **Assimilation** – absorbed food is used to build and repair, and for energy
5. **Egestion** – removing undigested waste

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Arrange: absorption, ingestion, egestion, digestion, assimilation → **ingestion, digestion, absorption, assimilation, egestion**.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
Q: Why must food be digested?

A: Complex food (starch, proteins, fats) is too large to pass into blood. Digestion turns it into small, soluble molecules (sugars, amino acids, fatty acids and glycerol) that can be absorbed.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing **egestion** (removing undigested food) with **excretion** (removing wastes made by cells, e.g. urine).
- Thinking absorption happens in the stomach mostly — it mainly happens in the small intestine.

activity.prompt: Put the steps of nutrition in order.
items: Ingestion
Digestion
Absorption
Assimilation
Egestion

quiz.q: Taking food into the body is
quiz.why: Ingestion means taking food into the body, usually through the mouth. Egestion is the removal of waste.
A starfish pushes its stomach out through its mouth to cover its prey and digest it outside, then pulls it back.

quiz.q: Using absorbed food to build the body is
quiz.why: Assimilation is when the body uses the absorbed food to build parts and get energy. Absorption is only passing the food into the blood.
Egestion is removing undigested food from the body as faeces. Excretion is removing waste made by the body's cells.
A mosquito has a needle-like mouth to pierce skin and suck blood. It does not chew.

lessons.title: Mouth, teeth and the food pipe

scenes.text: Grandpa tells Isha to chew a piece of bread for a whole minute.
Slowly it starts tasting sweet!
Saliva has turned some starch into sugar. Digestion begins in the mouth.

steps.title: Buccal cavity and teeth
steps.body:
Food enters through the mouth (**buccal cavity**). Teeth break it into pieces.

- **Milk teeth** (first set, 20) fall during childhood; **permanent teeth** (32 in adults) replace them.
- **Incisors** (8) cut and bite; **canines** (4) tear; **premolars** (8) and **molars** (12) chew and grind.

steps.title: Saliva and tongue
steps.body:
- **Salivary glands** release saliva, which **breaks down starch into sugar**.
- The **tongue** is a fleshy muscular organ attached at the back; it mixes saliva with food, helps swallowing and has **taste buds** for sweet, salty, sour and bitter tastes. It also helps in speaking.

steps.title: Tooth decay
steps.body: Bacteria in the mouth break down sugars left on teeth and release **acids** that slowly damage the tooth. Brush twice a day, floss, and rinse after meals; avoid sticky sweets between meals.

steps.title: Food pipe (oesophagus)
steps.body: Swallowed food goes down the **oesophagus** by wave-like contractions of its walls (**peristalsis**), which happen all along the alimentary canal. Sometimes food is pushed back up (vomiting) when the stomach rejects it.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Q: A child has 20 teeth; an adult has 32. Explain.

A: Children have milk teeth (20). These fall out and 32 permanent teeth grow, including extra molars.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
Q: Why does a choking cough happen when we talk while eating?

A: The windpipe and food pipe open near each other. A flap (epiglottis) normally covers the windpipe during swallowing; talking can let food enter the windpipe, causing choking.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying digestion starts in the stomach — it starts in the mouth with saliva.
- Thinking peristalsis happens only in the food pipe; it moves food all through the canal.

activity.prompt: Match the tooth to its job.

quiz.why: Saliva has an enzyme that begins to break starch down into sugar. This is why rice or bread tastes a little sweet when chewed for a long time.

quiz.q: Number of permanent teeth in adults
quiz.why: Adults usually have 32 permanent teeth. Children have 20 milk teeth.
Canines are pointed teeth used for tearing food. Incisors cut, and molars and premolars grind.

quiz.q: Wave-like movement of the food pipe is called
quiz.why: Peristalsis is the wave of muscle contractions that pushes food along the food pipe and the gut.

options: acids made by bacteria from sugars
quiz.why: Bacteria in the mouth use sugars left on teeth and make acids. These acids damage the enamel and cause decay.

lessons.title: Stomach, small intestine, liver and pancreas

scenes.text: Vikram's dal-rice slides into his stomach — a thick-walled bag.
Acid and juices churn it for hours, then it moves into a 7-metre-long coiled tube.
Millions of tiny finger-like villi soak up the nutrients into his blood.

steps.title: Stomach
steps.body:
A thick-walled, J-shaped bag. Its inner lining releases:

- **mucus** – protects the lining
- **hydrochloric acid** – kills many bacteria and makes the medium acidic for digestive juices
- **digestive juices** – break down **proteins** into simpler substances

steps.title: Small intestine, liver, pancreas
steps.body:
- **Small intestine**: highly coiled, about **7.5 m** long. Receives juices from the liver and pancreas, and its own wall secretes juices.
- **Liver**: reddish-brown, **largest gland** in the body; secretes **bile**, stored in the **gall bladder**. Bile helps in digesting **fats**.
- **Pancreas**: cream-coloured gland below the stomach; **pancreatic juice** acts on **carbohydrates, fats and proteins**.

End products: carbohydrates → **glucose** (simple sugars), fats → **fatty acids + glycerol**, proteins → **amino acids**.

steps.title: Absorption by villi
steps.body: The inner wall of the small intestine has thousands of finger-like **villi** that greatly **increase the surface area** for absorption. Each villus has a network of thin blood vessels. Digested food passes into the blood and is carried to all parts (**assimilation**). Glucose is broken down in cells with oxygen to release energy; unused glucose is stored as glycogen in the liver.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: Which organ digests each? Starch (mouth, small intestine), proteins (stomach, small intestine), fats (small intestine with bile and pancreatic juice).

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
Q: Why does the small intestine have villi?

A: Villi increase the surface area for absorption, so more digested food can pass into the blood quickly.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking bile is made in the gall bladder — it is made by the liver and only stored in the gall bladder.
- Thinking the stomach acid digests food by itself; it mainly kills bacteria and helps enzymes work.

activity.prompt: Match the part to its role.
pairs: Juice for carbohydrates, fats and proteins

quiz.why: The liver is the largest gland in the body. It makes bile and does many other jobs.
Bile, made by the liver, breaks fats into tiny droplets so they can be digested. It does not act on starch or proteins.
Proteins are broken down into amino acids. Glucose comes from carbohydrates, and fatty acids come from fats.
Hydrochloric acid in the stomach kills bacteria that come in with food. It also gives the acidic medium that stomach enzymes need.
The small intestine is about 7.5 m long. The great length gives more time and surface for digestion and absorption.
Villi are tiny finger-like projections on the inner wall of the small intestine. They increase the surface for absorbing digested food.

scenes.text: In the evening the cow sits quietly but keeps chewing. Nothing is in front of her!
She brings up partly digested grass (cud) from her stomach and chews it again.
In her rumen, bacteria break down cellulose — something humans cannot digest.

steps.title: Large intestine
steps.body: Wider and shorter than the small intestine (about **1.5 m**). It **absorbs water and some salts** from the undigested material. The remaining waste is stored in the **rectum** as semi-solid faeces and removed through the **anus** (egestion).

steps.title: Digestion in ruminants
steps.body:
Cows, buffaloes, goats and deer are **ruminants**. They swallow grass quickly and store it in a part of the stomach called the **rumen**, where it is partially digested into **cud**. Later the cud returns to the mouth in small lumps and is chewed again — **rumination**.

Grass is rich in **cellulose**. Bacteria in ruminants help digest cellulose. Many animals including horses and rabbits have a large **caecum** (a sac between the small and large intestines) where bacteria digest cellulose. **Humans cannot digest cellulose.**

steps.title: Feeding in Amoeba
steps.body: **Amoeba** is a single-celled organism in pond water. It has finger-like projections called **pseudopodia** (false feet) for movement and for capturing food. It surrounds the food and traps it in a **food vacuole**. Digestive juices are secreted into the vacuole; digested food is absorbed and undigested residue is thrown out.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Q: Why do we need fibre (roughage) if we can't digest cellulose?

A: Fibre adds bulk and helps the movement of food and waste through the intestines, preventing constipation.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
Q: How is diarrhoea dangerous and what immediate help is given?

A: Frequent watery stools cause loss of water and salts (dehydration), which can be dangerous. Give **ORS** (oral rehydration solution: boiled cooled water with a pinch of salt and sugar, or a packet) and see a doctor.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying ruminants have 'four stomachs'. Their stomach has four chambers; the rumen is one of them.
- Thinking the large intestine digests food — it mainly absorbs water and salts.

statements.s: Humans can digest cellulose.
The rumen stores partly digested grass.
Amoeba uses pseudopodia to capture food.
The large intestine is longer than the small intestine.
ORS helps replace lost water and salts.

quiz.q: Partly digested food that a cow chews again
quiz.why: Cattle swallow grass quickly, store it, then bring it back to chew again. This chewed food is called cud.

quiz.q: Main job of the large intestine
quiz.why: The large intestine absorbs water and salts from the leftover food. The rest passes on as faeces.

quiz.q: In Amoeba, food is digested in
quiz.why: Amoeba takes food into a food vacuole. Digestive juices work inside it, and the useful parts are absorbed.

quiz.q: Cellulose is digested with the help of bacteria in
quiz.why: Grass-eaters have bacteria in the rumen and a large caecum that digest cellulose. Humans cannot digest cellulose well.
Faeces are stored in the rectum, the last part of the large intestine, and leave through the anus.

questions.q: Breaking down complex food into simple substances is
questions.why: Digestion is breaking down large, complex food into small simple substances the body can absorb.

questions.q: Digestion of starch begins in the
questions.why: Starch digestion starts in the mouth, because saliva contains an enzyme that acts on starch.

questions.q: Bile is produced by the
questions.why: The liver makes bile. The gall bladder only stores it until it is needed.

questions.q: Finger-like projections in the small intestine
questions.why: Villi are finger-like folds in the small intestine that absorb food. Cilia and pseudopodia belong elsewhere, and stomata are in leaves.

questions.q: Number of canines in adult humans
questions.why: Adults have 4 canines, which are pointed teeth for tearing: one on each side of the upper and lower jaw.

questions.q: Fats are digested into
questions.why: Fats are digested into fatty acids and glycerol. Amino acids come from proteins and glucose from carbohydrates.

questions.q: Rumination is seen in
questions.why: Cows are ruminants: they swallow food, bring it back as cud, and chew again. Lions, dogs and humans do not.

questions.q: Assertion (A): The inner wall of the small intestine has villi. Reason (R): Villi increase the surface area for absorption.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: A is true: the small intestine has villi on its inner wall. R is true: they increase the surface area for absorption. R explains why A exists, so R explains A.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Digestion of proteins begins in the mouth. Reason (R): Saliva acts on starch.
questions.why: A is false: protein digestion begins in the stomach, not the mouth. R is true, because saliva acts on starch, but it does not explain A.

questions.q: Which juice acts on all three — carbohydrates, fats, proteins?
questions.why: Pancreatic juice has enzymes that digest carbohydrates, fats and proteins. Saliva acts only on starch, and bile only helps with fats.

questions.q: Undigested food in Amoeba is
questions.why: Amoeba cannot digest everything. The undigested part is pushed out of the cell through its surface.

questions.q: Case: Rohan ate a lot of sweets and did not brush for days. His tooth hurts. Most likely cause?
options: bacteria made acid that damaged enamel
questions.why: Sweets left on teeth feed bacteria. They make acid, which damages enamel and causes decay and pain. Brushing removes the sugar.

questions.q: Case: A child has severe diarrhoea. Best immediate step at home while contacting a doctor?
questions.why: Diarrhoea makes the body lose water and salts. ORS replaces them and prevents dehydration. Medical help should still be sought.

questions.q: Glucose is broken down in cells with the help of oxygen to give
questions.why: Cells use oxygen to break down glucose in respiration. This releases energy and gives carbon dioxide and water.

questions.q: Why can a horse live on grass while a human cannot?
options: Horse has a large caecum with cellulose-digesting bacteria
questions.why: Grass is mostly cellulose. A horse has a large caecum with bacteria that digest cellulose. Humans do not have these bacteria in enough number.

questions.q: Arrange the path of food: stomach, oesophagus, large intestine, mouth, small intestine, rectum
options: mouth, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine, rectum
mouth, stomach, oesophagus, small intestine, rectum, large intestine
mouth, oesophagus, small intestine, stomach, large intestine, rectum
oesophagus, mouth, stomach, large intestine, small intestine, rectum
questions.why: Food passes mouth → oesophagus → stomach → small intestine → large intestine → rectum. The other orders skip or swap parts of the canal.

courses.title: Ch 3 · Heat
courses.summary: Hot and cold, measuring temperature with clinical and laboratory thermometers, the three ways heat travels — conduction, convection, radiation — and why we wear dark woollen clothes in winter and light cotton in summer.
outcomes: Learners can read clinical and laboratory thermometers safely and correctly
Learners can explain conduction and classify conductors and insulators
Learners can explain convection, including sea and land breezes
Learners can explain radiation and choose suitable clothing for weather

scenes.text: Dhruv feels warm. Mother touches his forehead — "Hmm, maybe a fever."
Touch can mislead, so she uses a thermometer: 38.5 °C.
Normal is about 37 °C, so Dhruv has a fever. They call the doctor.

steps.title: Temperature
steps.body: **Temperature** tells us how hot or cold something is. It is measured with a **thermometer**, commonly in **degrees Celsius (°C)**. Our sense of touch is not reliable: a hand from cold water feels lukewarm water as warm.

steps.title: Clinical thermometer
steps.body:
- Measures **body temperature**; range **35 °C to 42 °C** (human body range).
- **Normal body temperature ≈ 37 °C** (it can vary slightly from person to person).
- Has a **kink** near the bulb that stops the mercury from falling back on its own, so it can be read after removal.
- Shake it to bring the level below 35 °C before use. Hold it by the stem, not the bulb.
- Many homes now use **digital thermometers**; mercury is toxic, so broken mercury thermometers must be handled carefully.

steps.title: Laboratory thermometer
steps.body:
- Range usually **−10 °C to 110 °C**. No kink, so read it **while the bulb is still in the substance**.
- Keep it upright, bulb surrounded by the substance and not touching the container; read with the eye level with the mercury top.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Q: Why should a clinical thermometer not be used to measure the temperature of boiling water?

A: Its maximum is 42 °C; boiling water is about 100 °C, so it may break.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
A lab thermometer reads between 20 and 30 with 10 small divisions. The mercury is 6 divisions above 20. Reading?

- Each division = (30 − 20)/10 = 1 °C
- Reading = **26 °C**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Removing a lab thermometer before reading — the reading changes immediately.
- Holding a thermometer by its bulb (body heat changes the reading).
- Assuming 37 °C is exactly everyone's normal; small variations are normal.

bands.text: Below the usual range — could be low body temperature; re-check and consult a doctor if unwell.
Fever — rest, fluids, and see a doctor if it continues.
High fever — seek medical help promptly.

quiz.why: A clinical thermometer measures body temperature, so its range is about 35–42 °C. The 0–100 °C range is for a laboratory thermometer's boiling use, which is a different type.
Normal human body temperature is about 37 °C (98.6 °F). The value 98 is in °F, not °C.

quiz.q: Why does a clinical thermometer have a kink?
options: To stop mercury falling back on its own
quiz.why: The kink stops the mercury from falling back on its own once the thermometer is taken out. This lets us read the temperature calmly.

options: while the bulb is in the substance
quiz.why: A laboratory thermometer has no kink, so the mercury would fall if removed. It must be read while the bulb stays in the substance.
Temperature is commonly measured in degrees Celsius (°C). Litre, metre and kilogram measure volume, length and mass.

story.title: The steel spoon in hot tea

scenes.text: Neha leaves a steel spoon in her hot tea.
A minute later the handle is hot too!
A wooden spoon stays cool. Steel conducts heat; wood does not.

steps.title: Transfer of heat
steps.body: Heat flows from a **hotter** object to a **colder** one until both reach the same temperature.

steps.title: Conduction
steps.body:
In **conduction**, heat passes from particle to particle from the hotter end to the colder end of a material, **without the particles moving from their places**. It happens mainly in **solids**.

- **Conductors**: allow heat to pass easily — metals like aluminium, copper, iron, silver.
- **Insulators (poor conductors)**: wood, plastic, cloth, glass, air, water.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Q: Why do cooking pans have plastic or wooden handles?

A: The metal pan conducts heat to cook food quickly; the handle is an insulator so we can hold it safely.

steps.title: Solved example 2 (activity)
steps.body: Wax drops are stuck along an iron rod; one end is heated. The drops nearest the flame melt first, then the next, and so on — showing heat moves along the rod by conduction.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking air or water are good conductors — they are poor conductors (that is why air layers keep us warm).
- Saying 'cold flows into the hand'. Heat flows out of the hand into the colder object.

activity.prompt: Conductor or insulator?

quiz.why: Heat always flows from a hotter object to a colder one until both are at the same temperature.
In conduction heat passes from particle to particle without the material moving. This works best in solids, especially metals.
Copper is a metal, and metals are good conductors of heat. Wood, plastic and rubber are poor conductors.
Air is a poor conductor, so it is an insulator. That is why trapped air keeps things warm.

quiz.q: Wax drops on a heated rod melt
quiz.why: Heat travels along the rod from the flame, so the wax nearest the flame melts first, then the rest in order.

lessons.title: Convection, sea breeze and land breeze

scenes.text: At Goa beach, the cool breeze blows from the sea during the day.
At night, fishermen notice the breeze reverses and blows from land to sea.
Both are caused by convection in air.

steps.title: Convection
steps.body:
In **liquids and gases**, the heated part becomes lighter (less dense) and **rises**; cooler, heavier fluid comes down to take its place. This movement carries heat and is called **convection**.

Activity: a crystal of potassium permanganate in a beaker of water heated at one side shows coloured water rising above the flame and circulating.

steps.title: Sea breeze and land breeze
steps.body:
- **Day**: land heats faster than water. Warm air over land rises; cooler air from the sea moves in → **sea breeze**.
- **Night**: land cools faster. Air over the (warmer) sea rises; cooler air from land moves out → **land breeze**.

Houses near coasts are often built with windows facing the sea to catch the sea breeze.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Q: Why is a room heater placed near the floor but an air conditioner near the ceiling?

A: Warm air from the heater rises and spreads; cool air from the AC sinks. Convection circulates the air through the room.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
Q: In a pan of water heated from below, which water gets warm first at the top — and how?

A: Water at the bottom heats, rises; cooler water sinks to be heated. Convection currents warm the whole pan.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying convection happens in solids. Particles in solids cannot flow.
- Mixing up sea and land breeze direction. Name the breeze by where it **comes from**.

statements.s: Sea breeze blows from sea to land during the day.
Land breeze blows at noon.
Hot air rises because it is lighter.
Convection can occur in solids.
Water is heated mainly by convection when heated from below.

quiz.why: In convection the heated fluid itself moves and carries heat. This can happen only in liquids and gases, not in solids or vacuum.

quiz.q: During the day, the breeze at a beach usually blows
quiz.why: In the day land heats faster than sea, so warm air over land rises. Cooler air from the sea moves in, giving a sea breeze from sea to land.
Land has lower heat capacity than water, so it warms up faster for the same heat. Water warms slowly.
Warm air is lighter (less dense), so it rises. Cooler air moves in to replace it.
At night land cools faster than the sea, so the air over the sea is warmer and rises. The breeze then blows from land to sea.

lessons.title: Radiation and the clothes we wear

scenes.text: On a hot May afternoon, Arjun touches a black car and a white car.
The black car is much hotter!
Dark colours absorb more heat radiation; light colours reflect most of it.

steps.title: Radiation
steps.body: Heat from the Sun reaches us through space where there is no air. This transfer without any medium is **radiation**. All hot bodies radiate heat; when we stand near a fire or a heater, we feel heat by radiation.

steps.title: Absorbing and reflecting
steps.body:
- **Dark surfaces absorb** more radiation and heat up faster; they are also better radiators.
- **Light/white surfaces reflect** more radiation.
- So light clothes are comfortable in summer; dark clothes in winter. Solar cookers are painted black inside.

steps.title: Woollen clothes
steps.body: Wool is a poor conductor, and its fibres **trap air** between them. Air is also a poor conductor, so heat from our body does not escape easily. **Several thin layers** keep us warmer than one thick layer because more air is trapped between the layers.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Q: Two identical cans, one painted black and one white, are filled with equal water and kept in the sun. Which warms faster?

A: The **black** can, because it absorbs more radiation.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
Q: Why are many houses in hot regions painted white outside?

A: White reflects sunlight, so the house absorbs less heat and stays cooler.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying 'woollen clothes give heat'. They only stop body heat from escaping.
- Thinking radiation needs air — it travels even through empty space.

activity.prompt: Match each situation to the way heat is transferred.
pairs: Spoon handle in hot tea getting hot
Water in a pan heated from below
Iron tava getting hot on a stove

quiz.q: Heat from the Sun reaches Earth by
quiz.why: Space is nearly empty, so there is no medium for conduction or convection. Heat from the Sun reaches us by radiation.
Dark, black surfaces absorb more heat than light or shiny ones. Shiny foil and mirrors reflect heat.

quiz.q: Woollen clothes keep us warm because
quiz.why: Wool traps air between its fibres, and air is a poor conductor. This stops our body heat from escaping, so we feel warm.
Light colours reflect more heat, and cotton lets sweat evaporate so we stay cool. Dark and thick clothes absorb heat and trap it.

quiz.q: Several thin layers are warmer than one thick layer because
options: more air is trapped between layers
quiz.why: Air trapped between layers is a poor conductor and insulates the body. More layers mean more trapped air than one thick layer.

questions.q: Instrument to measure temperature
questions.why: A thermometer measures temperature. A barometer measures air pressure, a hygrometer humidity, and an odometer distance.

questions.q: Normal body temperature
questions.why: Normal body temperature is about 37 °C. 100 °C is the boiling point of water.

questions.q: Metal spoon in hot milk gets hot by
questions.why: Heat passes along the solid metal spoon from the hot milk to your hand by conduction.

questions.q: Heat from the Sun reaches us by
questions.why: Heat from the Sun crosses empty space, which has no medium, so it travels by radiation.

questions.q: Range of a laboratory thermometer
questions.why: A laboratory thermometer typically reads from −10 °C to 110 °C. The 35–42 °C range belongs to a clinical thermometer.

questions.q: Which is an insulator?
questions.why: Wood is a poor conductor, so it is an insulator. Iron, silver and aluminium are metals and good conductors.

questions.q: Light-coloured clothes are preferred in summer because they
questions.why: Light colours reflect most of the heat falling on them, so we stay cooler. Dark colours absorb heat.

questions.q: Assertion (A): A clinical thermometer should not be washed in hot water. Reason (R): Its range is only up to 42 °C.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: A is true: hot water could break the thermometer. R is true since its range tops out at 42 °C, and hot water is well above this. So R explains A.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Sea breeze blows during the day. Reason (R): Water heats up faster than land.
questions.why: A is true: in the day land heats faster, so cooler air flows from the sea. R is false, because water heats more slowly than land.

questions.q: A lab thermometer reads between 30 and 40 with 5 divisions; mercury is at the 3rd division above 30. Reading?
questions.why: Between 30 and 40 with 5 divisions, each division = 10 ÷ 5 = 2 °C. Three divisions above 30 is 30 + 3 × 2 = 36 °C.

questions.q: Why is a frying pan base sometimes made of copper?
questions.why: Copper is a good conductor of heat, so a copper base spreads heat quickly and evenly to the food. An insulator would not.

questions.q: Case: In a hostel, a geyser's heating element is placed at the bottom. Why?
options: Heated water rises by convection, heating all of it
questions.why: Water at the bottom heats, becomes lighter and rises. Cooler water moves down to take its place. These convection currents heat all the water.

questions.q: Case: Two identical bottles of water, one wrapped in black cloth, one in white, kept in sunlight for an hour. Result?
questions.why: Black cloth absorbs more heat radiation than white cloth, which reflects it. So the water in the black cloth gets warmer.

questions.q: Why should you not hold a thermometer by its bulb?
options: Bulb may break and body heat changes reading
questions.why: Holding the bulb warms it by hand, which would change the reading, and it could also break. Hold the thermometer by the top end.

questions.q: Two people sit by a campfire: one in front, one directly above the smoke. Above the fire, heat reaches mainly by ___; in front, by ___.
questions.why: Above the fire, hot air rises, which is convection. In front of the fire, we feel the heat travelling straight through the air by radiation.

questions.q: Igloos made of snow keep the people inside warm because
options: snow is a poor conductor and traps air
questions.why: Snow has air trapped in it, and trapped air is a poor conductor. So it slows the loss of heat from inside, and people stay warm.

courses.title: Ch 4 · Acids, Bases and Salts
courses.summary: Sour acids and soapy bases around us, testing them safely with litmus, turmeric and china rose indicators, neutralisation that makes a salt, and how it helps with indigestion, ant bites, soil and factory wastes.
outcomes: Learners can name common acids and bases in daily life
Learners can use natural indicators to test substances
Learners can explain neutralisation and write its word equation
Learners can apply neutralisation to daily-life problems

scenes.text: Lemon juice tastes sour; so do curd, tamarind and vinegar.
Soap solution feels slippery and tastes bitter (please do not taste!).
Sour substances are acids; bitter, soapy ones are bases.

steps.title: Acids
steps.body:
The word acid comes from the Latin *acere* meaning sour. Acids found naturally:

- Vinegar → **acetic acid**
- Ant sting → **formic acid**
- Citrus fruits (lemon, orange) → **citric acid**
- Curd → **lactic acid**
- Spinach → **oxalic acid**
- Amla, citrus → **ascorbic acid (vitamin C)**
- Tamarind, grapes, unripe mangoes → **tartaric acid**

steps.title: Bases
steps.body:
Bases are bitter and **soapy to touch**.

- Lime water → **calcium hydroxide**
- Window cleaner → **ammonium hydroxide**
- Soap → sodium hydroxide / potassium hydroxide
- Milk of magnesia → **magnesium hydroxide**
- Baking soda (sodium hydrogencarbonate) is basic in nature.

steps.title: Safety first
steps.body: Never taste or touch unknown substances to test them. Strong acids and bases in labs can burn skin and damage eyes. We use **indicators** instead.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Classify: lemon juice, soap, vinegar, lime water, curd, baking soda.

- Acidic: **lemon juice, vinegar, curd**
- Basic: **soap, lime water, baking soda**

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: Which acid does an ant inject when it stings? → **formic acid**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking all acids are dangerous — many in food are safe and useful.
- Calling baking soda an acid because it is used in cooking; it is basic.

activity.prompt: Match the source with its acid.

quiz.why: Acids taste sour, like lemon and tamarind. The word acid comes from the Latin acere, meaning sour.
Lime water is a solution of calcium hydroxide, which is a base. Citric, acetic and formic acids are acids.
Milk of magnesia contains magnesium hydroxide, which is a base. It is used as an antacid.
Bases feel soapy or slippery to the touch and taste bitter. (Never taste unknown substances.)
Ascorbic acid is another name for vitamin C, found in amla, lemon and orange.

lessons.title: Natural indicators: litmus, turmeric, china rose

scenes.text: A drop of curry falls on Riya's white shirt — a yellow stain.
When she scrubs it with soap, it turns red!
After rinsing and drying, it slowly becomes yellow again. Turmeric is an indicator.

steps.title: Indicators
steps.body: **Indicators** change colour in acidic or basic solutions. **Neutral** solutions (pure water, sugar solution, common salt solution) do not change them.

steps.title: Litmus
steps.body:
Extracted from **lichens**. Available as red and blue litmus paper/solution.

- **Acid turns blue litmus red.**
- **Base turns red litmus blue.**
- Neutral: no change in either.

steps.title: Turmeric and china rose
steps.body:
- **Turmeric** paper is yellow; a **base turns it red**. Acids do not change it.
- **China rose (gudhal) indicator**: acids turn it **dark pink (magenta)**; bases turn it **green**.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
A solution turns red litmus blue. Is it acidic, basic or neutral?

- **Basic.** (Example: soap solution, lime water.)

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
You have three unlabelled bottles: an acid, a base and water, and only red litmus. How do you identify them?

1. Dip red litmus in each. The one turning it blue is the **base**.
2. Mix a drop of each remaining liquid with the base and test with the blue litmus you just made: the liquid that turns it back red is the **acid**; the other is **water**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying acids turn turmeric red — only bases do.
- Mixing up the litmus colours. Memory aid: a **B**ase turns red litmus **B**lue; so an acid turns blue litmus red.

activity.prompt: What happens? Sort each observation.

quiz.why: Litmus is a natural dye extracted from lichens. It turns red in acids and blue in bases.
An acid turns blue litmus red. A base turns red litmus blue.
Turmeric stays yellow in acids and neutral solutions but turns red in bases such as soap solution.

quiz.q: China rose indicator in an acid becomes
quiz.why: China rose indicator turns dark pink (magenta) in acids and green in bases.
Sugar solution is neutral. It does not change the colour of red or blue litmus.
Soap is basic, and bases turn red litmus blue. An acid would leave red litmus red.

scenes.text: In the lab, the teacher adds drops of a base to an acid with a few drops of an indicator.
The colour changes exactly when the acid is used up.
The test tube also feels warm: heat is given out. A salt and water have formed.

steps.title: What neutralisation is
steps.body:
When an acid reacts with a base, they cancel each other's effect. This is **neutralisation**. A **salt** and **water** are formed and **heat is evolved**.

**Acid + Base → Salt + Water (+ heat)**

Example: Hydrochloric acid + Sodium hydroxide → Sodium chloride (common salt) + Water.

steps.title: Salts
steps.body: Salts can be acidic, basic or neutral in nature. Common salt solution is neutral.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Activity: Fill a test tube with dilute hydrochloric acid, add 2–3 drops of phenolphthalein (colourless in acid). Add sodium hydroxide drop by drop. When the solution just turns **pink**, it has become slightly basic — the acid is fully neutralised. Adding a drop of acid makes it colourless again.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
Q: Write the word equation for the reaction of an acid with a base and name the type.

A: Acid + Base → Salt + Water; it is **neutralisation** and it is **exothermic** (gives out heat).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying neutralisation gives 'only water'. A salt is also formed.
- Thinking the products are always neutral. The salt may be slightly acidic or basic depending on the acid and base used.

activity.prompt: Complete the word equation.
activity.text: Acid + Base → ___ + ___ (heat is also given out).

quiz.why: In neutralisation an acid and a base react to form salt and water.
Neutralisation releases heat, so the mixture becomes warmer. Such reactions are called exothermic.
Hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide react to give sodium chloride (common salt) and water: HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O.
Phenolphthalein is colourless in acids and neutral solutions but turns pink in a basic solution.
Common salt is made from a strong acid and a strong base, so its solution is neutral and does not change litmus.

story.title: The ant bite at the picnic

scenes.text: At a picnic Kunal is bitten by an ant. It stings!
His aunt rubs moist baking soda on the bite.
The base neutralises the formic acid and the pain eases.

steps.title: Indigestion
steps.body: The stomach contains **hydrochloric acid**. Too much acid causes **indigestion** (acidity) and pain. An **antacid** such as **milk of magnesia** (magnesium hydroxide), a mild base, neutralises the excess acid. (Take medicines only as advised by an adult or doctor.)

steps.title: Ant bite
steps.body: An ant's sting injects **formic acid**. Rubbing a mild base — moist **baking soda** or **calamine** solution (contains zinc carbonate) — neutralises it.

steps.title: Soil treatment
steps.body:
- Soil too **acidic** (excess chemical fertilisers) → add **quick lime (calcium oxide)** or **slaked lime (calcium hydroxide)**.
- Soil too **basic** → add **organic matter (compost)**, which releases acids.

Plants grow best when soil is neither too acidic nor too basic.

steps.title: Factory wastes
steps.body: Wastes of many factories contain **acids**. Dumped directly into water bodies, they kill fish and other organisms. So factory wastes are **neutralised with basic substances** before disposal.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Q: A farmer's soil test shows it is acidic. What should he add and why?

A: Quick lime or slaked lime (bases), to neutralise the excess acid.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
Q: Why should toothpaste be basic? (extension)

A: Bacteria in the mouth produce acids that damage teeth; a basic toothpaste helps neutralise them.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Putting vinegar on an ant bite — that adds more acid.
- Thinking lime is added to basic soil. Lime is for acidic soil.

a.text: Your little cousin is stung by an ant (formic acid) and cries. What do you reach for?

choices.label: Moist baking soda
choices.feedback: Yes — a mild base neutralises the acid.

choices.label: Lemon juice
choices.feedback: Lemon is an acid; it may make it worse.

c.text: Lemon adds citric acid. Try a mild base instead.

b.text: Later your uncle has a burning feeling in his stomach after a heavy, spicy meal. What could help (as advised by an adult or doctor)?

choices.label: An antacid like milk of magnesia
choices.feedback: Right — it neutralises extra stomach acid.

e.text: More acid would add to the problem. Choose again.

choices.label: An antacid like milk of magnesia

d.text: Both times you used neutralisation: a base cancels an acid. If pain is severe or keeps returning, see a doctor.

quiz.why: Antacids contain a mild base such as milk of magnesia, which neutralises extra acid in the stomach. Lemon juice and vinegar are acids and would make it worse.
Acidic soil is treated with a base such as quicklime or slaked lime. The base neutralises the acid.
Basic soil is treated with organic matter such as compost, which releases acids that neutralise the base. Quicklime and slaked lime are bases and would make it worse.
Ant stings contain formic acid. A mild base such as calamine or baking soda eases the sting.

quiz.q: Factory wastes are neutralised before disposal because
options: they contain acids that harm aquatic life
quiz.why: Factory waste may contain acids that would harm fish and plants in water. Neutralising it first protects water bodies.

questions.q: Taste of acids
questions.why: Acids taste sour. The word acid comes from the Latin acere, meaning sour.

questions.q: Base turns red litmus
questions.why: Bases turn red litmus blue. Acids turn blue litmus red.

questions.q: Acid found in curd
questions.why: Curd contains lactic acid. Vinegar has acetic acid, citrus fruits have citric acid and ant stings have formic acid.

questions.q: Product of neutralisation besides water
questions.why: Neutralisation gives salt and water. So besides water, the product is a salt.

questions.q: Turmeric turns red with
questions.why: Turmeric turns red with bases. Soap solution is basic, while vinegar and lemon juice are acids and sugar solution is neutral.

questions.q: Which is neutral?
questions.why: A common salt solution is neutral and does not change litmus. Vinegar is acidic, and soap and lime water are basic.

questions.q: Litmus is extracted from
questions.why: Litmus is a natural dye got from lichens. Turmeric, china rose and beetroot are other natural dyes but not the source of litmus.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Calamine solution is applied on an ant bite. Reason (R): It contains zinc carbonate, which is basic.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: A is true: ant bites have formic acid, so calamine is applied. R is true: calamine has basic zinc carbonate. The base neutralises the acid, so R explains A.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Neutralisation is exothermic. Reason (R): The reaction mixture becomes warm.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: A is true: neutralisation gives out heat. R is true: the mixture becomes warm. The warming is the evidence of heat release, so R explains A.

questions.q: A solution turns china rose indicator green. It could be
questions.why: China rose turns green in bases. Lime water is a base, while tamarind water, lemon juice and vinegar are acids.

questions.q: Which pair shows the correct acid–base reaction products? Hydrochloric acid + Sodium hydroxide →
questions.why: The acid–base reaction of HCl and NaOH gives sodium chloride (salt) and water. It does not break water or form sodium metal.

questions.q: Case: Paheli has three liquids — A turns blue litmus red, B turns red litmus blue, C changes neither. A, B, C are
questions.why: An acid turns blue litmus red, so A is an acid. A base turns red litmus blue, so B is a base. C changes neither, so it is neutral.

questions.q: Case: A farmer used too much chemical fertiliser and his soil became acidic. What should he do?
questions.why: Acidic soil needs a base to neutralise it, so slaked lime is added. More fertiliser or vinegar would not help; vinegar is an acid.

questions.q: Why is phenolphthalein used in neutralisation activity?
options: It shows when the solution turns basic (pink)
questions.why: Phenolphthalein is colourless in acid but turns pink once the solution becomes basic. This shows the end point of neutralisation.

questions.q: A student adds NaOH drop by drop to HCl with phenolphthalein. At the moment the solution turns faint pink, the solution is
questions.why: Phenolphthalein turns pink only in a basic solution. A faint pink means all the acid has just been used up and a tiny excess of NaOH is present.

questions.q: Which household situation does NOT use neutralisation?
questions.why: Dissolving sugar in water is a physical change, not an acid–base reaction. Antacids, lime for soil and treating factory acid all neutralise acids.

courses.title: Ch 5 · Physical and Chemical Changes
courses.summary: Changes in shape, size and state that make no new substance, chemical changes that do, the signs that tell them apart, rusting and how to prevent it, and growing crystals.
outcomes: Learners can classify changes as physical or chemical with reasons
Learners can write word equations for common chemical changes
Learners can explain rusting and ways to prevent it
Learners can describe crystallisation

scenes.text: Mira folds paper into a boat, then unfolds it — still paper.
Ice in her glass melts into water; in the freezer the water becomes ice again.
Nothing new was made. These are physical changes.

steps.title: What a physical change is
steps.body: A **physical change** alters properties such as **shape, size, colour or state** (solid, liquid, gas), but **no new substance is formed**. Many physical changes are **reversible**.

steps.title: Examples
steps.body:
- Cutting paper, tearing cloth, crushing a can
- Melting wax/ice, boiling water, condensation of steam
- Dissolving salt or sugar in water (you can get the salt back by evaporation)
- Heating a glass tube until soft and bending it
- Magnetising an iron needle

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Q: Is melting of wax physical? Burning of a candle?

A: Melting of wax: **physical** (wax → liquid wax → solid again). Burning: **chemical** — the wax reacts with oxygen, forming carbon dioxide, water vapour, heat and light. A burning candle shows **both** changes.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
Q: Is 'irreversible' the same as 'chemical'?

A: No. Cutting a tree trunk into logs cannot be undone but no new substance forms — physical. Always ask: **is a new substance formed?**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling dissolving a chemical change — the dissolved substance can be recovered.
- Using reversibility alone to decide. Use the 'new substance' test.

activity.prompt: Physical or chemical change?

quiz.why: In a physical change no new substance is formed. Only things like shape, size or state change.
Melting of ice is a change of state from solid to liquid. It is still water, so no new substance forms. Burning, rusting and souring form new substances.
When salt dissolves in water no new substance forms. You can get the salt back by evaporating the water, so it is a physical change.
A candle shows both changes: the wax melts, which is physical, and the wax burns to form new substances, which is chemical.
Melting, freezing, boiling and condensing only change the state of a substance. No new substance forms, so changes of state are physical and can be reversed.

scenes.text: For a science fair, Arjun mixes vinegar and baking soda in a model volcano.
It fizzes and bubbles — a gas is forming!
He passes the gas through lime water: it turns milky. The gas is carbon dioxide.

steps.title: What a chemical change is
steps.body: A **chemical change** (chemical reaction) forms **one or more new substances**. It is usually not easily reversible.

steps.title: Signs of a chemical change
steps.body:
- **Heat, light or sound** given out or absorbed
- **Colour change**
- **Gas** given off (bubbles)
- **Change in smell**

(Not every chemical change shows all signs.)

steps.title: Important reactions (word equations)
steps.body:
1. **Burning magnesium ribbon**: gives a dazzling white light.
   Magnesium + Oxygen → Magnesium oxide (white ash)
   Magnesium oxide + Water → Magnesium hydroxide (turns red litmus blue — basic)
2. **Copper sulphate + iron**: blue solution turns **green**; brown copper coats the nail.
   Copper sulphate (blue) + Iron → Iron sulphate (green) + Copper (brown)
3. **Vinegar + baking soda**: Vinegar (acetic acid) + Baking soda (sodium hydrogencarbonate) → Carbon dioxide + other substances
4. **CO₂ + lime water**: Carbon dioxide + Lime water (calcium hydroxide) → Calcium carbonate (milky) + Water

steps.title: Chemical changes in life
steps.body: Burning fuels, digestion, ripening of fruits, fermentation, cooking, photosynthesis, the ozone layer absorbing UV radiation, and making new materials (plastics, medicines) are chemical changes.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Q: A blue copper sulphate solution with an iron nail turns green after an hour. Explain.

A: Iron is more reactive and displaces copper: iron sulphate (green) forms and copper (brown) deposits on the nail. A new substance formed → chemical change.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
Q: When an apple is cut, the cut surface turns brown. Physical or chemical?

A: **Chemical** — substances in the apple react with oxygen in the air, forming coloured substances.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking colour change always means chemical change (paint mixing or dissolving coloured ink is physical).
- Forgetting to name the white ash from magnesium: **magnesium oxide**.

activity.prompt: Match the reaction to the observation.

quiz.q: Gas produced from vinegar + baking soda
quiz.why: Vinegar (an acid) reacts with baking soda to give carbon dioxide gas, seen as fizzing. The gas turns lime water milky, which proves it is CO₂.

quiz.q: Magnesium oxide dissolved in water is
quiz.why: Magnesium oxide dissolves in water to form magnesium hydroxide, a base. A base turns red litmus blue, so the solution is basic.
When iron reacts with copper sulphate, iron sulphate forms. Its solution is green, while copper sulphate solution is blue.

quiz.q: Lime water turns milky due to formation of
quiz.why: Carbon dioxide reacts with lime water (calcium hydroxide) to form calcium carbonate. It is a white solid that does not dissolve, so the water looks milky.
Ripening changes the chemicals in a fruit, forming new substances with a new taste, colour and smell. Melting, tearing and magnetising give no new substance.

quiz.q: Which is NOT a sign of chemical change?
quiz.why: A change of shape alone gives no new substance, so it is physical. Colour change, gas and heat are signs that a new substance has formed.

scenes.text: Rahul left his bicycle in the rain all monsoon.
Now its chain and bell have a flaky brown coating.
His uncle explains: rust forms when iron meets oxygen and water. Paint and grease would have protected it.

steps.title: Rusting
steps.body:
Iron objects left in moist air get a brown flaky coating called **rust** (iron oxide). Rust is a new substance → **chemical change**.

**Iron (Fe) + Oxygen (from air) + Water → Rust (iron oxide)**

Both **oxygen and water (moisture)** are needed. Rusting is faster in humid areas and near the sea (salty air). Rusting slowly eats away iron, causing great loss.

steps.title: Preventing rust
steps.body:
Stop iron from contacting oxygen and moisture:

- **Paint** or **grease/oil** the surface
- **Galvanisation**: coat iron with **zinc** (used for water pipes, buckets)
- Make **stainless steel**: mix iron with carbon and metals like chromium, nickel, manganese — it does not rust

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Q: Three test tubes: (A) nail in dry air with a drying agent, (B) nail in boiled water covered with oil, (C) nail in tap water open to air. Where does rust form?

A: Only in **C**: A lacks moisture; B lacks oxygen (boiling removes dissolved air and oil stops more air).

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
Q: Why do ships rust faster than iron objects in a desert town?

A: Sea water is salty and the air is moist, which speed up rusting. Desert air is dry.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying rust needs only water or only air — it needs both.
- Thinking painting is needed only once; chipped paint lets rusting start again.

statements.s: Rusting is a chemical change.
statements.why: Iron oxide is a new substance.

statements.s: Iron rusts in completely dry air.
Galvanisation means coating iron with zinc.
Stainless steel rusts quickly.
Rusting is faster near the sea.

quiz.why: Rust forms when iron reacts with oxygen and water. It is iron oxide, a reddish-brown new substance.
Iron rusts only when both oxygen (air) and water (moisture) are present. With only one of them, there is no rusting.
Galvanised iron has a thin coat of zinc. The zinc keeps air and water off the iron and protects it from rust.

quiz.q: Stainless steel is made by mixing iron with
quiz.why: Stainless steel is an alloy: iron mixed with carbon and metals like chromium, nickel and manganese. It does not rust easily.

quiz.q: Best way to protect a gate from rust
quiz.why: Paint forms a barrier that stops air and water from touching the iron, so it does not rust. Wetting or salt would speed up rusting.

scenes.text: Sana dissolves copper sulphate powder in hot water with a few drops of dilute sulphuric acid.
She filters it and lets it cool undisturbed overnight.
In the morning — beautiful blue crystals with neat shapes!

steps.title: What crystallisation is
steps.body:
Large crystals of pure substances can be obtained from their solution. This process is **crystallisation**. It is a **physical change** — no new substance forms, only a pure solid separates.

Salt obtained by evaporation of sea water is not pure and its crystals are small; crystallisation gives purer, well-shaped crystals.

steps.title: Solved example 1: steps
steps.body:
1. Take water in a beaker, add a few drops of dilute sulphuric acid.
2. Heat it; add copper sulphate powder while stirring until no more dissolves (saturated solution).
3. Filter the hot solution.
4. Let it cool **undisturbed**.
5. Crystals of copper sulphate form.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
Q: Why is the solution left undisturbed while cooling?

A: Disturbing it produces many tiny crystals; undisturbed cooling allows large, well-shaped crystals to grow.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling crystallisation a chemical change.
- Confusing it with evaporation, which gives small, impure crystals.

activity.prompt: Order the steps to grow copper sulphate crystals.
items: Add a few drops of dilute sulphuric acid to water in a beaker
Heat and dissolve copper sulphate until no more dissolves
Filter the hot solution
Leave the filtrate to cool undisturbed
Collect the crystals that form

quiz.why: In crystallisation, a substance comes out of solution as crystals. No new substance forms, so it is a physical change.
Crystallisation gives pure, well-shaped crystals because impurities stay behind in the liquid.

quiz.q: Salt from sea water by evaporation is
quiz.why: Evaporating sea water leaves salt with impurities, and the crystals are small. Slow crystallisation of a pure solution gives purer and bigger crystals.
Copper sulphate crystals are blue, and so is their solution.
The solution should cool undisturbed. Slow, still cooling lets large, well-shaped crystals grow, whereas shaking or fast stirring gives tiny crystals.

questions.q: Melting of ice is
questions.why: Ice melting to water is a change of state, and the substance is still water. So it is a physical change.

questions.q: Rusting of iron needs
questions.why: Iron rusts when both oxygen and water are present. Light, heat alone or zinc do not cause rust; zinc actually protects iron.

questions.q: Burning of magnesium gives
questions.why: Magnesium burns in air with a bright white flame and joins with oxygen. The white ash left is magnesium oxide.

questions.q: Gas that turns lime water milky
questions.why: Carbon dioxide turns lime water milky because it forms white calcium carbonate. Oxygen, hydrogen and nitrogen do not.

questions.q: Galvanisation uses
questions.why: Galvanisation means coating iron with a layer of zinc to prevent rusting.

questions.q: Which is a chemical change?
questions.why: Cooking food makes new substances (taste, colour and smell change) and it cannot be reversed. Breaking glass, dissolving sugar and folding paper are physical.

questions.q: Copper sulphate + iron gives a ___ solution
questions.why: Iron displaces copper from copper sulphate, forming iron sulphate. Iron sulphate solution is green, and the blue colour fades.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Crystallisation is a physical change. Reason (R): No new substance is formed.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: A is true: crystallisation only separates a dissolved solid as crystals. R is true: no new substance forms. That is why it is physical, so R explains A.

questions.q: Assertion (A): All irreversible changes are chemical. Reason (R): Chemical changes form new substances.
questions.why: A is false: some irreversible changes are physical, like cutting a tree or tearing paper. R is true, but it does not make A true.

questions.q: Which shows both physical and chemical changes?
questions.why: A burning candle shows both: wax melting is physical, and wax burning to form new substances such as CO₂ and water vapour is chemical.

questions.q: Magnesium oxide solution turns
questions.why: Magnesium oxide in water forms a base, which turns red litmus blue. It does not turn blue litmus red.

questions.q: Case: A nail is kept in boiled water with a layer of oil on top. After a week, it shows
questions.why: Boiled water has no dissolved air, and the oil layer stops air from getting in. With no oxygen, the nail does not rust.

questions.q: Case: A student says, "Dissolving salt in water is a chemical change because the salt disappears." Correct reply?
options: It is physical; salt can be recovered by evaporation
questions.why: Dissolving salt is a physical change. The salt is still there, and evaporating the water gets it back. Disappearing is not the same as forming a new substance.

questions.q: Why is iron used for ships coated with paint and also with zinc blocks?
options: To keep away oxygen and moisture and reduce rusting
questions.why: Paint and zinc blocks keep oxygen and moisture from reaching the iron hull, so rusting is reduced. They do not change weight, heat flow or colour in a useful way.

questions.q: In the reaction copper sulphate + iron → iron sulphate + copper, which observation is NOT expected?
questions.why: Iron takes the place of copper, so blue copper sulphate changes to green iron sulphate and brown copper coats the nail. The solution gets paler blue, not deeper.

questions.q: Which set has only chemical changes?
questions.why: Rusting, burning and digestion all form new substances, so all are chemical. The other sets include boiling, cutting, dissolving, freezing or melting, which are physical.

courses.title: Ch 6 · Respiration in Organisms
courses.summary: Why every cell needs respiration, aerobic and anaerobic respiration (including yeast and tired muscles), how we breathe in and out, what we breathe out, breathing in other animals and under water, and respiration in plants.
outcomes: Learners can explain cellular respiration and compare aerobic and anaerobic respiration
Learners can describe the mechanism of breathing in humans
Learners can compare inhaled and exhaled air and test exhaled air for carbon dioxide
Learners can describe respiratory organs of cockroach, earthworm, fish and frog, and respiration in plants

lessons.title: Why we respire: aerobic and anaerobic

scenes.text: Boojho runs the 400 m race as fast as he can.
Afterwards his legs ache with cramps.
His coach says: "Your muscles ran short of oxygen and made lactic acid. A warm bath and massage will help."

steps.title: Cellular respiration
steps.body: All living things are made of **cells**. Each cell needs **energy** for its work. Food (glucose) is broken down inside cells to release energy — **cellular respiration**. It happens in every cell, all the time.

steps.title: Aerobic respiration
steps.body:
Uses **oxygen**:

**Glucose → (with oxygen) → Carbon dioxide + Water + Energy**

It releases much energy. Humans and most organisms respire aerobically.

steps.title: Anaerobic respiration
steps.body:
Without oxygen (less energy released):

- **Yeast**: Glucose → (without oxygen) → **Alcohol + Carbon dioxide + Energy**. Yeasts are single-celled; this is why they are used to make bread rise and in making wine/beer.
- **Our muscles** during heavy exercise: Glucose → (without oxygen) → **Lactic acid + Energy**. Lactic acid build-up causes **muscle cramps**; hot water baths or massage improve blood circulation, bringing oxygen to break it down.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Q: Why do we breathe faster after running?

A: Muscles need more energy, so more oxygen is needed. Faster, deeper breathing supplies more oxygen.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: Organisms that can live without air are called anaerobes. Name one. → **Yeast** (some bacteria too).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling breathing and respiration the same. Breathing is taking in and giving out air; respiration is breakdown of food in cells.
- Thinking anaerobic respiration releases more energy — it releases less.

activity.prompt: Aerobic or anaerobic?

items.text: Happens in muscles during a sprint when oxygen runs short

quiz.why: Respiration happens in every living cell, where food is broken down to release energy. Breathing only brings oxygen to the cells.
In aerobic respiration, glucose with oxygen gives carbon dioxide, water and energy. Lactic acid and alcohol come from anaerobic respiration.
Yeast can respire without oxygen, called fermentation. It gives alcohol and carbon dioxide.
With heavy exercise, muscle cells may run short of oxygen and break down glucose partly. This makes lactic acid, which causes cramps.

options: taking in and giving out air
quiz.why: Breathing is taking in air and giving out air. It is only one part of respiration, which also happens in the cells.

scenes.text: The teacher asks everyone to count breaths for a minute while sitting.
Most count about 15–18. After running on the spot, counts jump to 25 or more.
Then they place hands on their chests and feel the ribs move.

steps.title: Breathing
steps.body: **Inhalation**: taking in oxygen-rich air. **Exhalation**: giving out air rich in carbon dioxide. One inhalation + one exhalation = **one breath**. The number of breaths per minute is the **breathing rate**. An adult at rest breathes about **15–18 times a minute**; it rises during exercise.

steps.title: Path of air
steps.body:
Nostrils → **nasal cavity** → windpipe → **lungs**. Lungs lie in the **chest cavity**, protected by the **rib cage**. A large muscular sheet, the **diaphragm**, forms the floor of the chest cavity.

Hairs and mucus in the nasal cavity trap dust; sneezing expels irritants.

steps.title: Mechanism
steps.body:
- **Inhalation**: ribs move **up and outwards**, diaphragm moves **down** → chest cavity becomes larger → air rushes in.
- **Exhalation**: ribs move **down and inwards**, diaphragm moves **up** → chest cavity becomes smaller → air is pushed out.

Model: a bell jar with balloons (lungs) and a rubber sheet at the bottom (diaphragm). Pulling the sheet down inflates the balloons.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Q: Why should we not breathe through the mouth?

A: The nose filters dust and germs with hairs and mucus and warms the air; mouth breathing skips this.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
Q: In the bell-jar model, what happens when the rubber sheet is pushed up?

A: The space inside decreases, air is pushed out, and the balloons deflate — like exhalation.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the diaphragm moves up during inhalation — it moves down.
- Thinking lungs pull in air by themselves; they expand because the chest cavity enlarges.

activity.prompt: Order the events during inhalation.
items: Diaphragm moves down and ribs move up and out
Chest cavity becomes larger
Air pressure inside lungs falls
Air rushes in through the nostrils
Lungs fill with air

quiz.q: Floor of the chest cavity is the
quiz.why: The diaphragm is a large muscular sheet at the floor of the chest cavity. It moves down and up as we breathe.
When we breathe in, the ribs move up and out. This makes the chest cavity bigger, so air rushes in.

quiz.q: Normal resting breathing rate of an adult (per min)
quiz.why: An adult at rest breathes about 15–18 times per minute. It is faster after exercise.
During exhalation the ribs move down and in and the diaphragm moves up. The chest cavity gets smaller and pushes air out.
Sneezing is a reflex that pushes out dust and irritants from the nose. It protects the breathing passage.

lessons.title: What we breathe out; breathing in other animals

scenes.text: Using a straw, Paheli blows into a test tube of clear lime water.
It turns milky quickly. Air pumped by a syringe takes much longer.
Exhaled air has much more carbon dioxide!

steps.title: Inhaled vs exhaled air (approx.)
steps.body:
- Inhaled air: oxygen ~21%, carbon dioxide ~0.04%
- Exhaled air: oxygen ~16.4%, carbon dioxide ~4.4%

Nitrogen is about 78% in both. Exhaled air also has more water vapour — that is why breathing on a mirror fogs it.

steps.title: Other animals
steps.body:
- **Elephants, lions, cows, goats, frogs, lizards, snakes, birds**: lungs (like us).
- **Cockroach**: small openings called **spiracles** on the sides of the body, leading to air tubes called **tracheae**. Insects have this tracheal system.
- **Earthworm**: breathes through its **moist, slimy skin**; gases pass easily through it.
- **Frog**: lungs, and also through its moist skin.
- **Fish**: **gills** — projections of the skin with many blood vessels; they take oxygen dissolved in water.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Q: Why do earthworms come out of the soil after heavy rain?

A: Water fills the air spaces in soil, so earthworms cannot get oxygen through their skin; they come up for air.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
Q: Why does a fish die when taken out of water?

A: Its gills are made to take dissolved oxygen from water; in air they collapse and cannot absorb enough oxygen.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying exhaled air has no oxygen — it still has about 16%.
- Saying fish breathe the oxygen in H₂O molecules; they use oxygen **dissolved** in water.

activity.prompt: Match the animal with its breathing organ.

quiz.why: Exhaled air has more carbon dioxide (about 4.4%) than inhaled air (about 0.04%), because cells make CO₂ in respiration.
Insects have small openings called spiracles on the body. They lead to air tubes (tracheae) that carry air to the cells.
Earthworms breathe through their moist skin. Gases dissolve in the wet skin and pass in and out.
Fish use oxygen dissolved in water. Their gills take it out of the water as it passes over them.

quiz.q: Mirror fogs when we breathe on it because exhaled air has
quiz.why: Exhaled air has more water vapour. On the cool mirror it condenses into tiny droplets, so it fogs.

lessons.title: Breathing under water and respiration in plants

scenes.text: Scuba divers carry oxygen cylinders to breathe under water.
Meanwhile at home, Kiran overwaters her potted plant every day. Its leaves start yellowing.
Roots need air too — waterlogged soil has no air spaces.

steps.title: Under water
steps.body: Humans cannot take oxygen from water. Divers use **oxygen cylinders**. Whales and dolphins have lungs and come to the surface to breathe through **blowholes** (nostrils on top of the head).

steps.title: Plants respire too
steps.body:
Plants also respire: they take in **oxygen** and give out **carbon dioxide**, day and night. Glucose is broken down to CO₂ and water with release of energy.

- **Leaves**: gases exchange through **stomata**.
- **Roots**: take in air from the **spaces between soil particles**.
- **Stems**: in some woody plants through small openings called lenticels.

steps.title: Photosynthesis vs respiration in plants
steps.body: In bright sunlight, photosynthesis is faster than respiration, so a plant releases more oxygen than it uses. At night, only respiration takes place.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Q: Why do potted plants die if watered too much?

A: Excess water fills the air spaces in soil; roots cannot get oxygen for respiration.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
Q: Is it true that plants only photosynthesise and never respire?

A: No. Every living cell respires. Plants respire all the time; they photosynthesise only in light.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'Plants give oxygen and animals give CO₂' — plants give out CO₂ too, from respiration.
- Thinking roots respire through stomata. Roots take air from soil spaces.

statements.s: Plants respire only at night.
Roots take in oxygen from air spaces in soil.
Whales breathe using gills.
Overwatering can harm roots.
Leaves exchange gases through stomata.

quiz.why: Plants respire like other living things. They take in oxygen and give out carbon dioxide, using food made by photosynthesis.
Roots take oxygen from the air spaces between soil particles. Waterlogged soil has little air, so roots can suffer.
Dolphins are mammals. They breathe air into lungs through a blowhole on the top of the head, and come up to the surface for it.
At night there is no light, so plants cannot photosynthesise. They still respire, taking in oxygen and giving out CO₂.

quiz.q: Gas exchange in leaves happens through
quiz.why: Stomata on the leaf surface let oxygen and carbon dioxide move in and out. Veins carry water and food.

questions.q: Breakdown of food in cells to release energy
questions.why: Respiration is the breakdown of food in cells to release energy. Digestion breaks food down outside the cells, and breathing just moves air.

questions.q: Organ of breathing in fish
questions.why: Fish breathe using gills, which take oxygen dissolved in water. Spiracles belong to insects and lungs to land animals.

questions.q: Lime water turns milky with
questions.why: Carbon dioxide turns lime water milky. Oxygen, nitrogen and water vapour do not.

questions.q: Earthworm breathes through
questions.why: An earthworm breathes through its moist skin. It has no lungs or gills.

questions.q: Anaerobic respiration in yeast produces
questions.why: In anaerobic respiration yeast makes alcohol and carbon dioxide. This is fermentation. Lactic acid is made in muscle cells.

questions.q: During inhalation the diaphragm
questions.why: On inhalation the diaphragm moves down (flattens) and the ribs move up and out. The chest gets bigger and air flows in.

questions.q: Percentage of CO₂ in exhaled air (approx.)
questions.why: Exhaled air has about 4.4% carbon dioxide. Inhaled air has only about 0.04%, and 78% is nitrogen and 21% oxygen.

questions.q: Assertion (A): We feel muscle cramps after heavy exercise. Reason (R): Muscles respire anaerobically and lactic acid accumulates.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: A is true: cramps are felt after heavy exercise. R is true: muscles run short of oxygen, respire anaerobically and lactic acid builds up. R explains A.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Plants do not respire during the day. Reason (R): Plants photosynthesise in sunlight.
questions.why: A is false: plants respire all the time, day and night. R is true, since plants photosynthesise in sunlight, but that does not stop respiration.

questions.q: Which releases more energy from the same glucose?
questions.why: Aerobic respiration breaks glucose down completely using oxygen, and so releases much more energy. Anaerobic respiration breaks it down only partly.

questions.q: Air tubes in a cockroach are called
questions.why: The air tubes in insects are called tracheae. Spiracles are the small openings on the body that lead into them.

questions.q: Case: Dough with yeast kept in a warm place rises in a few hours. Why?
options: Yeast releases CO₂ during anaerobic respiration
questions.why: Yeast respires without oxygen in the dough and gives off CO₂. The gas bubbles make the dough rise and puff up.

questions.q: Case: After a 1 km run, Ravi's breathing rate rises from 16 to 30 per minute. Main reason?
options: Muscles need more oxygen for energy
questions.why: Running makes muscles work hard, and they need more energy. More oxygen is needed to release it, so breathing speeds up.

questions.q: Why do we feel hungry after physical activity?
options: Cells used up energy from food
The stomach is empty of air
questions.why: Activity uses up energy that cells got from food by respiration. Hunger is the body asking for more food to restore it.

questions.q: In a bell-jar model of lungs, the balloons represent ___ and the rubber sheet represents ___
questions.why: In the bell-jar model the balloons stand for the lungs and the rubber sheet at the bottom stands for the diaphragm. Pulling the sheet down makes the balloons fill with air.

questions.q: Which statement is correct?
questions.why: Exhaled air still has about 16% oxygen, since only part is used. It has about 4% CO₂ while inhaled air has about 0.04%. Plants do release CO₂ in respiration.

courses.title: Ch 7 · Transportation in Animals and Plants
courses.summary: Blood and its parts, arteries, veins and capillaries, the four-chambered heart and heartbeat, how kidneys remove wastes, and how water, minerals and food move in plants through xylem and phloem, with transpiration.
outcomes: Learners can describe the components of blood and their functions
Learners can compare arteries, veins and capillaries and explain the pulse
Learners can describe the heart and circulation of blood
Learners can describe the human excretory system
Learners can explain transport in plants and transpiration

scenes.text: Paheli cuts her finger while slicing vegetables. Blood oozes out.
After a few minutes it stops by itself — a clot forms.
Her teacher explains: tiny cells called platelets helped seal the cut.

steps.title: Circulatory system
steps.body: The heart, blood and blood vessels form the **circulatory system**. It carries oxygen, digested food and other substances to every cell and carries wastes away.

steps.title: Blood
steps.body:
Blood is a fluid flowing in blood vessels.
